training_text: Titanium alloys are important structural materials, while nickel-based alloys are considered superalloys. Due to their high thermal expansion coefficients, cracks are prone to develop during deposition. In the WAAM process, no cracks were observed in the deposited layers at deposition currents below 50 A. However, at a deposition current of 50 A, cracks were detected in the deposited layer. Figure 9 illustrates the macroscopic view of the partial cracks, as well as high-rate SEM images. No cracks were found in the first layer, but the crack section in the second layer Ti6Al4V/Inconel 718 appeared disconnected, with an uneven crack morphology. High-magnification SEM images (shown in Figure 9b–d) of the crack section reveal a microfracture morphology characterized by river and cleavage patterns, indicating a cleavage fracture mechanism. To investigate the phase composition of the crack section, an EDS scanning analysis of its microstructure was conducted. Figure 10 presents a high-magnification SEM image of the fracture bottom, revealing a precipitated phase A. EDS analysis indicates that the atomic ratio of oxygen to iron is approximately 1.6:1, suggesting that the precipitate is likely iron oxide. At position B, the ratio of nickel to titanium atoms is about 1:1, with the chromium and iron content being similar to that of titanium and nickel. However, the carbon content is relatively high, leading to the speculation that the main phase at position B is MC carbide. Previous studies have shown that small amounts of MC carbide can impede dislocation movement and stabilize grain boundaries, thus providing strengthening; however, excessive MC can result in stress concentration, reducing the alloy’s durability and contributing to crack formation [15]. At position C, the nickel atom content is highest, with titanium, chromium, and iron content being comparable. This leads to the speculation that the phase at this position may be a eutectic structure of brittle intermetallic compounds formed by Ni, Ti, Cr, and Fe. Figure 9. training_text: To study the effect of different heat inputs on the microstructure of the same composite material (VInconel 718: VTi6Al4V=2:1), the metallographic morphology of the samples was observed under different deposition currents using an optical microscope. Figure 4 displays the optical microscopy characterization for each deposition current. Figure 4a shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 35 A, with the Ti6Al4V/Inconel 718 composite in the upper part and the Inconel 718 layer in the lower part. The upper section is predominantly composed of columnar crystals, intermingled with some long black bars among the branches of the columnar crystals. In the WAM process, the solid–liquid interface gradually advances into the liquid phase region. During this advancement, the solute undergoes redistribution, resulting in a phenomenon of component supercooling within a certain distance. This instability of the flat solid–liquid interface ultimately leads to the formation of columnar crystals. As the liquid phase region is influenced by solute redistribution, solute aggregation occurs, which is manifested as microscopic segregation [27]. From the Figure 4a, it can be observed that tiny secondary dendrites are present on the sides of the columnar crystals, with an average distance of 5.16 μm between these secondary dendrites. With the increase in the deposition current, the columnar crystals in the deposited layer gradually undergo differentiation. Figure 4b shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 40 A. From the Figure 4b, it can be observed that some of the grains are arranged in an orderly manner, while a discontinuous black phase is present between the grains. In addition, long straight columnar crystals can be observed in the Figure 4b, which is formed due to the instability of the solid–liquid interface resulting from the supercooling of the composition. Under conditions of rapid cooling, columnar crystals are formed more readily. In comparison to Figure 4a, when the deposition current is 40 A, the heat input increases, leading to a longer temperature residence time on the workpiece under the same heat dissipation conditions. As a result, the cooling rate becomes relatively slower. At the microscopic level, the number of columnar crystals decreases, with some larger columnar crystals gradually transforming into smaller grains, leading to an increase in the spacing between columnar crystals. As some of the heat is conducted in the direction of the deposited additive, a negative temperature gradient develops in the liquid phase, perpendicular to the crystal axis. This results in the formation of a secondary crystal axis along the primary crystal axis [27]. The presence of secondary dendrites can be observed in the Figure 4b, with the average distance between the secondary dendrites measuring 6.38 μm. Figure 4. DSC Test The shape memory effect (SME) of the built specimen was evaluated using DSC by comparing its phase transformation temperatures with those of the untreated NiTi SMA wire. A DSC setup was employed to investigate the phase transformation temperature of specimens by using a heating/cooling rate of 10 \(^\circ\)C/min under a constant nitrogen flow. A small sample was extracted from the built L-shaped wall structure for the DSC test. The test consists of heating and cooling of the specimens, during which a plot illustrating the relationship between temperature and phase changes is generated. Table 3 shows the transformation temperatures obtained for the untreated NiTi SMA wire and WAAM specimen. Figure 11a,b show the DSC curve obtained for the untreated NiTi SMA wire and WAAM specimen sample, respectively. Transformation temperatures were identified by locating the intersections between the baseline and tangents drawn to each peak. During the cooling phase, exothermic peaks signified the forward transformation from austenite (B2) to martensite (B19') in both the NiTi wire and WAAM sample. Conversely, endothermic peaks appeared upon heating, corresponding to the reverse transformation from martensite (B19') back to austenite (B2). The transformation temperatures observed in both the base metal wire and WAAM samples were comparable, suggesting that the shape memory effect remained intact after the fabrication of the L-shaped wall structure using the GMAW-based WAAM process. Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

training_text: The shapes and distribution of pores within multilayer specimens processed with each different parameter are displayed in Fig. 12 (a) – Fig. 12 (e). As shown in Fig. 12 (a) and (b), pores in cubes A1 and A2 (with highest energy densities of 249.69 J/mm\(^3\) and 229.41 J/mm\(^3\)) were mostly spherical in shape and small in size, and mostly distributed within melt pools. This suggests the pores were gas-induced by high laser energy, turbulent melt pool dynamics, vaporization of low melting point constituents (Zhang et al., 2017) or gas-induced voids embedded within the powder feedstock (Hao et al., 2009). However, cubes A3, A4, and A5 (with lower energy densities than cubes A1 and A2) showed irregular, non-spherical and larger pores, suggesting process-induced porosity formed by insufficient melting or lack of fusion between adjacent scan tracks and/or successive layers (King et al., 2014). The pores in cube A3, A4, and A5 (Fig. 12(c–e) were mainly located beneath the boundaries of the melt pools and some un-melted powders were observed adjacent to a triangular void, which suggests lack of fusion due to insufficient energy density input. Although cube A5 had a higher energy density (157.23 J/mm\(^3\)) than cubes A3 and A4 (82.02 J/mm\(^3\) and 72.97 J/mm\(^3\)), ~4% lower density was exhibited. This can be explained by the discontinuous melt pools produced in single laser scans using the A5 parameters, which would lead to inconsistent overlap between adjacent scans, and a melt pool size (height plus depth of 29.2 \( \mu \)m) slightly smaller than the powder layer thickness of 30 \( \mu \)m. training_text: Probability density function of pixel intensities of metallurgical phases: (a) well-discriminated ferrite and pearlite phases, and (b) overlapped ferrite, pearlite, and martensite phases. | Image segmentation is a digital image processing technique that is widely used in the fields of engineering, medicine, food science, remote sensing, etc., to identify the distinct regions/objects in an image that possess distinguishable visual characteristics or features [10]. Grayscale level, color, contrast, spectral values, or textural features are some examples of such distinguishing features [11]. In general, two types of approaches are employed for segmentation of images: a discontinuity approach and a similarity approach [12]. While a discontinuity approach involves computation of abrupt changes or discontinuity of some object (e.g., edges) in the image to identify distinct regions, a similarity approach involves extraction and a one-to-one comparison of similar features (e.g., pixel intensity) for identification of distinct regions. Techniques of discontinuity approach include Sobel operator [13], Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) operator [14], Laplacian operator [15], and canny operator [15]. Techniques of similarity approach include histogram-based thresholding [16], region splitting and merging [17], level-set [18], clustering, and water shedding [11]. Among these techniques, histogram-based thresholding (or Otsu’s method [16]) is extensively used for image analysis or segmentation of microstructures [19]. In this technique, threshold-based criteria are established from the multimodal histogram of pixel intensities, which is used for the segmentation of distinct phases. Implementation of such a technique results in an accurate segmentation of metallurgical phases whose pixel intensity distributions are distinct (multimodal) and do not overlap significantly (see Figure 1). However, when there are multiple metallurgical phases whose pixel intensity distributions overlap with each other (see Figure 1), employing histogram-based thresholding may lead to misclassification of phases. training_text: The fractographic analysis of the fracture planes shows a development of different structural characteristics during the various heat treatments, as shown in Figure 7. For the as-built state, a very plane surface with a very fine-grained structure occurs, not showing big breakouts. Furthermore, microscopic pores are shown (cf. Figure 7a), diminishing the fatigue behavior, as the different regimes of fatigue behavior fall below the heat-treated states. During the SR, the material structure changes, showing a very plane, but coarse-grained fracture surface. The surface is mostly formed by bigger breakouts, as the ductile material leads to bigger dimples.[30] For the SR + DA and HIP components, the surface structure differs significantly, as fibrous shaped fractures occur at heat-treated states. Furthermore, the HIP components show plane breakout regions, as depicted in Figure 7d, alluding more homogeneous material properties.[21] Within the SR, a very ductile material structure develops, as stated in the microstructural analysis. Microstructural changes lead to a decreased UTS and a good fatigue behavior (cf. Figure 2). For a testing at a load of \( \sigma = 250 \) MPa, performing about \( n = 1.5 \times 10^6 \), a crack initiation point can be identified. Emanating from the crack initiation point (cf. Figure 8a), the fracture develops into the structure, diminishing the applicable load capacity. Finally, the crack propagation and the strength reduction of the material lead to a failure of the component. Furthermore, porosities within the material structure can cause the final rupture, as the structure gets weakened significantly (cf. Figure 8b).[31] Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

This phenomenon was intensified under the presence of porosity and other printing defects, which can stimulate internal cracking and shift the velocity of crack propagation. training_text: Microstructure and grains distribution greatly affect the mechanical properties of fabricated parts produced through WAAM [140]. Min Qi et al. [141] explained that complex thermal cycling in the manufactured material from AM processes results in columnar coarse grains. Haden et al. [134] performed a wear scar of platinum in Z axis (facing towards test equipment) over the deposited MS, they performed SEM and FIB imaging and observed grain refinement immediately below the wear scar as shown in Fig. 17. Wang et al. [142] utilized H13 as feeder wire for the WAAM process with 4-Axis CNC-assisted MIG welding powder as shown in Fig. 18. They found multiple microstructural formations which was due to local heating histories. Also, the elongation and tensile strength were maximum which was farthest from the substrate. Liu et al. [143] developed an Al based fabricated part through TIG and MIG. They revealed that the GTAW welding of Al part results in higher hardness and strength over the GMAW welds due to the precipitate strengthening and less porosity development. In GTAW weldment, there are large amount of localised plasticity observed, while there is a considerable amount of porosity in GMAW weldments which could figure out the difference in mechanical characteristics between both the kinds. GTAW bonded Al part is mechanically more reliable than GMAW welded one [143,144]. However, cold metal transfer for Al based WAAM improves mechanical characteristics by allowing for better control of porosity formation, controlled metal deposition, and lower heat input. Lower welding heat input results in decreased weld pool temperature as well as fine grain structure, which minimizes H2 trapping and hence the porosity formation [145,146]. With WAAM microstructure and phase transformation is dependent on the materials used, High temperature developed, cooling rate and deposition rate [147]. Defects produced in the process also affect the mechanical properties [140]. To increase the mechanical properties, recent studies concentrated mostly on reducing the defects such as porosity, surface cracking, deformations and gas inclusions by introducing some post-processing techniques. This paper will see the recent post-processing techniques which have been done for the enhancing of mechanical properties of as-fabricated (AF) produced parts. Delamination is usually a visible deficiency which cannot be eliminated by post-processing techniques or heat treatments, but can be avoided by following proper process parameters in order to reduce repeated fluctuated stresses and also by considering the characteristics of deposited alloy [148,149], there are various categories of defects as can be briefly seen in Table 7. Scope of defect in WAAM processes with various metals can be seen in Fig. 19. Material: s GMAW 1400 NAB. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

The as-built microstructure (Figure 5a) is characterized by columnar β-grains containing hcp α′-martensite laths (white arrows in Figure 5a). As investigated in several studies [10,31,40], the LPBF process promotes, first, the nucleation of the β-grain directly on the build platform and, secondly, its growth along the build direction, namely, across the several molten pools. For this reason, columnar β-grains are disposed parallel to the build direction. The high cooling rate controlling the solidification process of the molten pools induces the diffusionless \( \beta \rightarrow \alpha'\)-martensite transformation and forms a cross-hatched structure of α′-martensite laths (dotted circle in Figure 5a). As deeply studied by Yang et al. [8], the cross-hatched structure is composed of a twine of several laths disposed perpendicular and/or parallel to each other. In detail, primary α′-martensite laths always extend across the whole columnar grain. Secondary, tertiary, and quartic α′-martensite laths, characterized by finer dimensions, are instead disposed of parallel and/or perpendicular to the primary ones. As widely investigated in our previous works [30,31], the heat treatments performed at temperatures below the β-transus (704 °C and 740 °C, Figure 1) induced the α′-martensite → α + β decomposition due to the diffusion of the β-stabilizer alloying elements (i.e., V, Fe) from the supersaturated hcp lattice to the α-phase grain boundary. The EBSD observations in [31] showed the presence of about 3% of the newly formed β-phase and that the newly formed α-phase retains the same orientation as its progenitor α′-martensite lath. The same EBSD maps in [31] indicated that the α-phase has an orientation relation with the retained columnar β-grain (yellow dotted line in Figure 5b). Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: significantly decreased after cyclic annealing, especially for the elongation (EL), achieving a reduced anisotropy of 6.34% compared with the distinct anisotropy of 43.40% for as-built specimens. The anisotropic degree of the specimens after cyclic annealing is comparable to that of the equiaxed \( \beta \) grain microstructures fabricated by DED [14, 31]. Figure 13 shows the tensile fracture morphologies of the specimens after cyclic annealing in horizontal and vertical directions. The fibrous zone and shear rupture zone appear in both samples, and the dimples is also similar, which further demonstrates that the mechanical properties are almost isotropic. Although the yield tensile strength (YS) and the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) decrease after cyclic annealing, the EL, especially in horizontal direction, is significantly improved. The main reason for this may be attributed to the globularization of \( \alpha \) phase in prior-\( \beta \) grains and the elimination of grain boundary \( \alpha \) phase (\( \alpha_{GB} \)) between prior-\( \beta \) grains [32]. Dislocation theory can be applied to clarify the difference of the mechanical properties between the as-built and heat-treated specimens. For the as-built specimens, lots of dislocations pile up at the grains boundaries during the tensile test in horizontal direction due to the continuous \( \alpha_{GB} \) between prior-\( \beta \) grains (Fig. 10a), causing a high back stress to block the slip of dislocation. Besides, the pile up of dislocations also leads to a stress concentration triggering crack along the \( \alpha_{GB} \), which is detrimental to the ductility [32]. Therefore, the elimination of \( \alpha_{GB} \) after cyclic annealing (Fig. 10b) avoids the initiation of crack at the \( \beta \) grain boundaries and favors the improvement of ductility in the horizontal direction. On the other hand, the magnitude of elongation is also proportional to the glide distance of dislocations or to the size of \( \alpha \) in the direction of tensile axes. In the specimens after cyclic annealing, the shape of the primary \( \alpha \) is globular (Fig. 10b) and, thus, the slide distance is comparable in the vertical and horizontal tensile axes. In contrast, the shape of the primary \( \alpha \) is lamellar for the as-built specimens (Fig. 3), and the size of \( \alpha \) sections in different tensile directions is diverse, easily contributing to nonuniform dislocation slide and stress concentration in \( \alpha\text{-}\beta \) interfaces. Therefore, the anisotropy of tensile properties of the as-built specimens is higher than that of the cyclic annealing specimens. Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: To examine the spatial elemental distribution in AM IN625, we performed EDS mapping of an as-built IN625 specimen. Typical elemental maps of Ni, Cr, Nb and Mo for the same area of sample are shown in Fig. 3. A segregated dendritic microstructure is observed. Such microstructure is closely tied to the rapid and nonequilibrium solidification conditions inherent to the AM process [60,61]. We observed local enrichment of Nb and Mo and corresponding deficits of Ni and Cr in the interdendritic regions. The trends within the dendrites were the opposite. Such elemental microsegregations occur due to solute rejection and redistribution during a solidification process, a process, not surprisingly, also broadly identified in the welding literature [62,63]. Furthermore, Fig. 3 shows that the microsegregation is not homogeneous across the probed sample area. This behavior is consistent with previous experimentally observed and theoretically predicted microstructure heterogeneities [64,65]. Here, we surmise that the extent of microsegregation is related to the complex heating (reheating) profile at a local level. We performed quantitative analysis of the extent of micro-segregation by using an EDS line scan with a step size of 2 μm and a dwell time of 300 s over ≈200 μm, as highlighted by the arrow in Fig. 3(c). The calibrated, spatially-resolved mass fractions of two heavy elements (Mo and Nb) are shown in Fig. 4. The Nb and Mo mass fractions were measured between 2.81% and 5.84% and 9.35% and 10.85%, respectively. Fig. 4 shows that these mass fractions are not confined to bounds set forth by the chemically allowable values of IN625. Similar fluctuation was also observed for Ni and Cr. We emphasize that these results were acquired using a 2 μm beam size, hence the measured mass fractions were the average value within the probed volume. Our previous synchrotron experiment, by analyzing the lengths of X-ray streaks in the two-dimensional SAXS patterns, indirectly demonstrated that the atomic concentration profile within the microsegregated interdendritic regions has a nominal width on the order of 10 nm [24]. This result was further validated by both thermodynamic and phase-field modeling. A CALPHAD-based solidification modeling effort was carried out using both DICTRA software and a Scheil-Gulliver model, where the temperature profile was supplied by a finite-element thermal model [22]. Similarly, two dimensional and three dimensional phase-field models were studied using the same finite-element thermal model [66]. All of these models predict that most of the microsegregation occurs within a 10 nm region, and that the upper bound of local Mo and Nb mass fractions are predicted at as high as 20 mass % and 29 mass %, respectively. Such observations strongly suggest that, due to microsegregation, local composition of as-built IN625 alloy does not consistently meet the alloy specifications and must be further processed via heat treatments so that the expected performance requirements can be achieved. It is also important to point out that the existing experimental evidence, while consistent with modeling predictions, is nevertheless indirect. Direct evidence using techniques that can resolve compositional changes with a nm resolution is needed to validate predictions made by thermodynamic and phase field models. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

We observed local enrichment of Nb and Mo and corresponding deficits of Ni and Cr in the interdendritic regions. The trends within the dendrites were the opposite. Such elemental microsegregations occur due to solute rejection and redistribution during a solidification process, a process, not surprisingly, also broadly identified in the welding literature [62,63]. Furthermore, Fig. 3 shows that the microsegregation is not homogeneous across the probed sample area. This behavior is consistent with previous experimentally observed and theoretically predicted microstructure heterogeneities [64,65]. Here, we surmise that the extent of microsegregation is related to the complex heating (reheating) profile at a local level. We performed quantitative analysis of the extent of micro-segregation by using an EDS line scan with a step size of 2 μm and a dwell time of 300 s over ≈200 μm, as highlighted by the arrow in Fig. 3(c). The calibrated, spatially-resolved mass fractions of two heavy elements (Mo and Nb) are shown in Fig. 4. The Nb and Mo mass fractions were measured between 2.81% and 5.84% and 9.35% and 10.85%, respectively. Fig. 4 shows that these mass fractions are not confined to bounds set forth by the chemically allowable values of IN625. Similar fluctuation was also observed for Ni and Cr. We emphasize that these results were acquired using a 2 μm beam size, hence the measured mass fractions were the average value within the probed volume. Our previous synchrotron experiment, by analyzing the lengths of X-ray streaks in the two-dimensional SAXS patterns, indirectly demonstrated that the atomic concentration profile within the microsegregated interdendritic regions has a nominal width on the order of 10 nm [24]. This result was further validated by both thermodynamic and phase-field modeling. A CALPHAD-based solidification modeling effort was carried out using both DICTRA software and a Scheil-Gulliver model, where the temperature profile was supplied by a finite-element thermal model [22]. Similarly, two dimensional and three dimensional phase-field models were studied using the same finite-element thermal model [66]. All of these models predict that most of the microsegregation occurs within a 10 nm region, and that the upper bound of local Mo and Nb mass fractions are predicted at as high as 20 mass % and 29 mass %, respectively. Such observations strongly suggest that, due to microsegregation, local composition of as-built IN625 alloy does not consistently meet the alloy specifications and must be further processed via heat treatments so that the expected performance requirements can be achieved. It is also important to point out that the existing experimental evidence, while consistent with modeling predictions, is nevertheless indirect. Direct evidence using techniques that can resolve compositional changes with a nm resolution is needed to validate predictions made by thermodynamic and phase field models.

training_text: The x-ray diffractograms for the as-cast and as-built IN718 samples are shown in Fig. 3. It is evident that the as-cast sample consists of Laves_C14 and NbC phases in the γ matrix. On the other hand, the as-built sample comprises of the Laves_C14 phase only along with the γ matrix. Figure 4 shows the comparison of the microstructure between as-cast and as-built IN718 samples. The as-cast sample shows the presence of blocky NbC phase and irregular Laves_C14 phase dispersed in the γ matrix (Fig. 4a). These secondary phases were found to form as co-existing precipitates, predominantly along the grain boundaries. In the as-built IN718 sample, Laves_C14 phase is the only secondary phase observed as shown in Fig. 4(b). It is found to form along the boundaries of columnar and cellular subgrains due to the segregation of Nb.[17] NbC was not observed in the as-built alloys probably since its precipitation was suppressed by the fast solidification rate during the LPBF process. Moreover, the grains formed during the solidification were found to be equiaxed with a diameter in the range of 10-20 μm for the as-cast IN718 sample while, large columnar grains consisting of fine columnar subgrains of ~1 μm width and cellular subgrains of ~2 μm diameter were observed in the as-built IN718 alloy.[17] The Fig. 4. BSE-SEM micrographs of (a) as-cast and (b) as-built IN718 alloys phase evolution in both as-cast and as-built samples observed under SEM correlates well with the phases determined using XRD. Though the equilibrium phase fraction plot and Scheil solidification path predict the formation of δ phase in these alloys, it was not found to form in the as-cast and as-built alloys. Material: s. Columnar grain structure perpendicular to the crescent edge in additive manufacturing arises from rapid solidification and significant vertical temperature gradients, prompting metal material to develop columnar grains along the solidification direction. Slower cooling rates in the middle and top sections facilitate carbon diffusion, leading to the formation of larger carbide particles and carbide coarsening within the bainitic structures. During solid state cooling, the α dendrites transform into α2/γ lamellar structure, and the γ phase remains interdendritic (Ref 10). As shown in Fig. 12(d), the α2/γ lamellar structure has a different orientation with an angle of approximately 45°. The SEM image of the bottom region of the cold-wire weld metal specimen is shown in Fig. 13(a). The heating of the arc causes an obvious substrate dilution in the bottom region of the weld metal specimen, which is dominated by coarse α2 equiaxed grains with γ laths precipitating in different directions inside the grains and at the grain boundaries. Figure 13(b) shows a magnified SEM image of the grain boundaries. White (point A) and black (point B) structures are observed at the grain boundaries. According to the EDS point analysis results (Fig. 13c and d), the white region has a relatively high Al content (48.2 at.%), while the black region has a lower Al content (45.4 at.%). In Fig. 8, the α2 phase content in the bottom region of the weld metal decreases gradually as the preheating temperature of the Ti wire increases. Combined with the droplet transfer analysis, the droplet grows continuously after deflecting toward the side of the Al wire during the cold-wire process, so that it cannot be transferred to the weld pool in time. As a result, the arc heat is applied directly to the substrate for a longer period of time, resulting in the obvious substrate dilution in the bottom region of the weld metal specimen. With the increase of the preheating temperature of Ti wire, the melting of Ti wire and Al wire tends to be synchronized, and the droplet transfer is gradually continuous and stable. As a result, the arc heat acts primarily on the droplet rather than the substrate, which reduces the dilution of the substrate. Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

training_text: Pores can be observed to be critical in both the IMC and aluminum areas, as shown in Fig. 6 (a). Two types of pores are observed: one with a circular boundary and the other with an irregular boundary. The circular boundaries are located in the Al alloy area, whereas the irregular boundaries are located at the IMC and 316 L boundary areas. The size of the circular pore was similar to the Al powder size of ~100 μm used in the LDED process. Thus, it is believed to be a gas pore which was generated by boiling. The overheating of the deposited aluminum was considered due to the obstruction effect which reduced the aluminum powder feeding. The irregular pore is believed to result from a lack-of-fusion (Lof). The larger pore, located on the bottom-left side of Fig. 6 (a), is believed to originate from the neck of the anchor. Melted aluminum appears not to fill the neck of the anchor although the outside is covered because of the metallic reaction with 316 L. Similarly, other Lof can be generated. The reason why the melted aluminum cannot penetrate the pores in Fig. 6 (a) is unclear because no Lof is observable (Fig. 6 (b)) and aluminum is presumed to penetrate into the neck of the anchor (Fig. 6 (c)). Small gas pores can be observed in Fig. 6 (b) and (c), which is characteristic of aluminum alloys manufactured via LDED [18]. Consider this, the higher porosity observed in the 1.8 mm (Fig. 6 (c)) sample compared to the 1.5 mm sample (Fig. 6 (b)) is attributed to the greater energy density applied during the filling process. Traces of the anchor neck geometry can be observed when they appear as cracks in Fig. 6 (b) and Lof in Fig. 6 (c). The cracks and pores are mainly located in the left boundary of the aluminum alloy between the anchors and appear to be bonded well in the right boundary (Fig. 7(a)). Therefore, detailed results were introduced, as shown in Fig. 8, providing the total detected element spectrum and a private elemental mapping image of the main elements: Al, Fe, Si, Cr, and Mg. training_text: Micrographs of the wrought and LPBF 316L were captured and compared in Figure 4. The wrought material has equiaxed grains containing twins which is a typical microstructure for rolled and annealed austenitic sheets, see Figure 4. In contrast, individual weld beads or molten pools are visible in the LPBF 316L, see Figure 5a,b. The alloy components segregate during the rapid solidification of the melt. Also, the top surface of the melt pool reacts with the atmosphere of the pressure chamber. Consequently, the micrographs along the building direction show a layer-like structure, where the melt pool boundaries become visible. This microstructure is totally different from typical austenitic microstructure, as observed for the examined wrought material. The epitaxial crystal growth results in stem crystals, which grow polyhedrally beyond the so-called layered structure. Therefore, the LPBF 316L contains large elongated grains, which favor anisotropic mechanical properties.[45] As reported in refs. [45,46], LPBF leads to highly nonequilibrium microstructures with tortuous and irregular grain morphologies, a high density of dislocations, cellular structures, and chemical segregation. Thus, significantly different mechanical properties are expected in comparison with conventional manufacturing routes, such as wrought and cast.[47,48] The xy plane micrograph shows several parallel scan paths or tracks in a longitudinal section, see Figure 5c. The AM material examined was not cut out 100% parallel to the xy plane of the sample. Accordingly, the sectional plane shown is inclined minimally to the xy plane. Consequently, several superimposed layers with a relative 67° angle between the scan paths of the successive layers can be identified in the micrograph. The grain size distribution and morphology of the wrought and LPBF 316L samples are characterized by EBSD, see Figures 6–9. As shown in Figure 6, wrought 316L is composed of equiaxed grains and twins, corresponding to the results obtained from the OM micrographs shown in Figure 4. The microstructure is characterized by no pronounced texture and a relatively uniform grain size of \( \approx 30 \) µm, see Figures 6a–c and 8a–c. As indicated in the GB maps, the red lines represent low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) with a misorientation angle ranging from 2° to 15°, whereas the black lines characterize high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs), i.e., GBs with a misorientation angle higher than 15°. The microstructure of the wrought sample mainly consists of HAGBs with an average misorientation angle of about 44°, see Figures 6d–f and 8d–f. The fraction of HAGBs is 95 ± 1%. These results are in good agreement with those reported by Kong et al.[49] Scale bar: 100 µm µm.

In the STAed state, the alloy’s matrix is reinforced by the precipitates, thereby imparting a high strength but a reduced degree of ductility. Therefore, the fracture mechanism appears brittle-dominated with emergence of cleavages (Fig. 19b). 3.3 Studies on Microhardness It is observed that the as-built microhardness exceeds the conventionally manufactured wrought samples. The wrought maraging steel’s microhardness value as reported by Tascioglu et al. (Ref 48) is 301 HV. In the present work, the as-built alloy’s microhardness value of 359 ± 9 HV_{0.5} is obtained. On the other side, Bodziak et al. (Ref 6) obtained 370 ± 15 H microhardness in the as-built condition. The higher microhardness of the as-built L-PBFed specimen is due to the finer microstructure with higher density of dislocations as compared to the wrought counterpart (Ref 46). From Table 4, it is observed that as compared to the as-built state, increased microhardness values are obtained after the STA treatments, irrespective of the aging duration (the aging temperature being constant ~ 450 °C). Although Kladaric et al. (Ref 24) concluded that as compared to the aging time, the aging temperature is more significant in purview of microhardness of the post-heat treated alloy. In contrast to the STAed specimens, the low microhardness of the as-printed specimen is due to the lath martensitic microstructure without any strengthening precipitates (Ref 22). Investigations at different aging durations reveal that the microhardness of the STAed specimens reflects a declining trend with increase in the aging duration, as shown in Table 4; keeping in mind that while aged for 2 and 4 h, the difference in the obtained microhardness values is found insignificant (same as in the case of UTS). Therefore, it can be interpreted that the increased aging duration tends to reduce the microhardness value. This is due to the fact that the particular aging temperature and exposure time influence the precipitation kinetics. A longer aging duration causes coarsening of precipitates; as a consequence, a lower microhardness value is obtained. Moreover, the particular aging temperature and associated holding duration decide the formation of reverted austenite within the alloy. The trace of reversed austenite within the over-aged maraging steels was reported in the literature (Ref 13, 39). Similar observation is made through XRD analysis in the present study (Fig. 14). The austenite, being a soft and ductile phase, reduces the strength of the alloy. Therefore, with increase in the aging duration, the transformation of martensite-to-austenite (austenite reversal) is surely increased, which causes a decline in the microhardness value. However, reverted austenite is considered to be a desired phase constituent because by controlling the proportion of reverted austenite, the required combination of the ductility and toughness can be achieved (Ref 35). Past researchers extensively studied the phenomenon of austenite reversion, and they reported that alteration in the tensile strength and ductility in maraging steels is greatly influenced by the precipitation of nano-scaled particulates (Ref 7). On the contrary, some other research groups concluded that reversed austenite plays an important role for improving mechanical properties, especially, elongation at break through the Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) effect. As reported by Ooi et al. (Ref 30), the beneficial role of reverted austenite is mainly to increase work hardening during the tensile tests. However, a high content of reverted austenite does not necessarily incur an increased percentage of elongation rather may cause reduced yield as well as tensile strengths (Ref 32). Therefore, the role of reverted austenite in maraging steel remains still a debatable topic. Power: 300 W; Scan speed: 800 mm/s. Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

In contrast to the STAed specimens, the low microhardness of the as-printed specimen is due to the lath martensitic microstructure without any strengthening precipitates (Ref 22). Investigations at different aging durations reveal that the microhardness of the STAed specimens reflects a declining trend with increase in the aging duration, as shown in Table 4; keeping in mind that while aged for 2 and 4 h, the difference in the obtained microhardness values is found insignificant (same as in the case of UTS). Therefore, it can be interpreted that the increased aging duration tends to reduce the microhardness value. This is due to the fact that the particular aging temperature and exposure time influence the precipitation kinetics. A longer aging duration causes coarsening of precipitates; as a consequence, a lower microhardness value is obtained. Moreover, the particular aging temperature and associated holding duration decide the formation of reverted austenite within the alloy. The trace of reversed austenite within the over-aged maraging steels was reported in the literature (Ref 13, 39). Similar observation is made through XRD analysis in the present study (Fig. 14). The austenite, being a soft and ductile phase, reduces the strength of the alloy. Therefore, with increase in the aging duration, the transformation of martensite-to-austenite (austenite reversal) is surely increased, which causes a decline in the microhardness value. However, reverted austenite is considered to be a desired phase constituent because by controlling the proportion of reverted austenite, the required combination of the ductility and toughness can be achieved (Ref 35). Past researchers extensively studied the phenomenon of austenite reversion, and they reported that alteration in the tensile strength and ductility in maraging steels is greatly influenced by the precipitation of nano-scaled particulates (Ref 7). On the contrary, some other research groups concluded that reversed austenite plays an important role for improving mechanical properties, especially, elongation at break through the Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) effect. As reported by Ooi et al. (Ref 30), the beneficial role of reverted austenite is mainly to increase work hardening during the tensile tests. However, a high content of reverted austenite does not necessarily incur an increased percentage of elongation rather may cause reduced yield as well as tensile strengths (Ref 32). Therefore, the role of reverted austenite in maraging steel remains still a debatable topic.

training_text: Overall schematic of the experimental in-situ XCT tensile testing set-up (a) with Deben tensile unit illustrating the load axis movement independent of the load frame (b) | Samples were tested until failure on a Deben CT20kN Open Frame tensile test rig with a 100 μm/s crosshead speed following ASTM E8/E8M. Tensile testing was carried out in 2 parts. The first is straightforward tensile loading until failure to ascertain the general tensile behavior of the two PBF-LB parameter sets. These data were used to determine the best approach for the second part of testing involving in-situ tensile testing inside an X-ray Computed Tomography (XCT) unit. The Deben load frame was custom-designed for in-situ tensile testing within the XCT unit. In this setup, the load frame is fixed and remains stationary throughout the test to prevent interference with the X-ray beam. The tensile axis rotates independently of the load frame, enabling simultaneous CT imaging without obstruction from the dense steel load frame, as illustrated in Fig. 2. The acquisition time for a typical XCT scan is relatively long compared to a standard tensile test. Therefore, to obtain in-situ data, the applied load must be held constant during scanning. After each scan, the load is increased to the next level, followed by another scan, and so on. After pre-loading the sample to 100 N, the stress was increased in 1000 N increments until failure. During each XCT scan, the tensile unit was switched to position control to maintain a constant applied strain. An equilibration period was implemented before each scan until significant load changes were no longer observed. XCT images were then acquired, and porosity was analyzed as described previously. To minimize scanning time, the following parameters were adjusted: integration time of 750 ms, geometric magnification of 13.3, and a continuous capture strategy. This resulted in a voxel resolution of 15.04 μm for the in-situ scans Fig. 2. Scale bar: 20 µm µm.

training_text: SEM observations and EDS analysis of the HSDA sample were conducted, as illustrated in Fig. 7. The homogenization treatment induced recrystallization, leading to the formation of annealing twins. The presence of MC carbides and the \( \delta \)-phase was observed, as shown in Fig. 7a. During multi-step heat treatment of the HSTDA sample, pronounced microstructural changes occur involving the dissolution of Laves phases and the precipitation of \( \delta \)-phase (Ni$_3$Nb) as shown in Fig. 7a. The Nb-rich Laves phase, formed during rapid solidification, becomes thermodynamically unstable at elevated homogenization temperatures [44]. At 1100 °C, Nb diffuses from the Laves phase into the \( \gamma \)-matrix, and the phase gradually dissolves as the system approaches equilibrium. The subsequent 980 °C solution treatment step further promotes redistribution of Nb and mitigates residual segregation [44]. According to the thermodynamic assessments for Inconel 718 [45], the \( \delta \)-phase (orthorhombic) becomes stable in the temperature range of 850–980°C, where Nb supersaturation in the \( \gamma \)-matrix promotes its heterogeneous precipitation along grain boundaries. The presence of \( \delta \)-phase at these locations reduces Nb segregation and improves microstructural stability by acting as a grain-boundary pinning phase. This dissolution-precipitation sequence also provides abundant Nb for subsequent \( \gamma'' \) (body-centered tetragonal) strengthening during aging [45]. Additionally, the magnified image in Fig. 7b revealed cuboid structures associated with \( \gamma' \) precipitates, consistent with findings reported in the literature [42]. A plate-like structure, indicative of \( \gamma'' \) precipitates, was also identified, as depicted in the inserted of Fig. 7b. The presence of these phases aligns with findings reported by various authors in the literature [38, 42, 43]. EDS analysis was conducted to determine the elemental composition of specific phases, and based on these results, the expected phase composition is listed in Table 5. XRD was performed to confirm the major phases and precipitates in the as-built and heat-treated Inconel 718 samples as shown in Fig. 7c. All conditions exhibit characteristic reflections of the face-centered cubic \( \gamma \) (Ni-Cr-Fe) matrix corresponding to the (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes. The (200) reflection is dominant in the AB, ST, and DDA samples, whereas the (111) reflection shows the highest intensity in the HT, HST, and HSTDA conditions. This shift in dominant plane orientation from (200) to (111) after heat treatment indicates structural relaxation and redistribution of lattice strain. A distinct Laves-phase peak is observed near 2θ≈49° in the AB sample, confirming Nb segregation during rapid solidification. In contrast, this peak disappears in the HT, HST, and HSTDA conditions, indicating complete dissolution of the Laves phase during high-temperature solution treatment. Weak \( \delta \)-phase (Ni$_3$Nb) peaks are detected in the DDA condition, while the HSTDA condition shows very low \( \delta \) intensity, reflecting near-complete phase transformation after double aging. training_text: shows representative micrographs of the L-PBF and L-DED specimens in as-built (NHT) condition, heat treated at 1000 °C (HT-1000), and heat treated at 1210 °C (HT-1210). As previously discussed, NHT specimens display grains and so-called subgrains, formed during the rapid solidification process. The feature defined as a subgrain is a solidification cell, i.e. the solidification morphology observed during both L-PBF and L-DED of austenitic stainless steels. Each cell is surrounded by a thin layer with slightly altered composition, which refers to the fraction of liquid phase that solidifies after cell solidification, i.e. the intercellular region. Cell and intercellular region are often referred to as a core-rim structure, respectively. The rims, enriched in elements (Cr, Mo) that prefer to accumulate in the liquid during solidification, tend to form an interconnected network. The solidification cells have an average diameter of 0.42 ± 0.04 μm in the L-PBF sample (Figure 1a), while they have an average diameter of 4.72 ± 0.58 μm for the L-DED specimen (Figure 1d). The cellular structure of the L-DED sample is about 10 times coarser than that of the L-PBF sample. This is, as reported in several earlier works, due to the intrinsic differences in cooling rate between the two fabrication techniques. When heat treated at temperatures of 1000 °C or higher, the cellular structure disappears (see Figures 1b, 1c, 1e, and 1f). Numerous inclusions can be seen within the matrix of all the samples. A detailed characterization of these inclusions is presented below in a dedicated section. Figure 1. High magnification secondary electron micrographs of the surface of the L-PBF (a, b, c) and the L-DED (d, e, f) specimens in as-built (NHT) state (a, d), heat treated at 1000 °C – HT-1000 (b, e), and heat treated at 1210 °C – HT-1210 (c, f). EBSD-IPF maps, indexing the FCC austenite phase, and the corresponding kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps of all the specimens analyzed are shown in Figure 2. As seen in this figure, the austenite grain structure of the L-DED samples does not change significantly after any of both heat treatments (HT-1000 as well as HT-1210). On the other hand, the austenite grain size in L-PBF specimens after heat treatment at either 1000 or 1210 °C differs significantly. While the austenite grain size in NHT and HT-1000 L-PBF samples is similar, the microstructure of the HT-1210 sample undergoes full recrystallization, without significant change in crystallographic texture. The microstructural features that can be quantified from the EBSD analysis are summarized in Table 2. As can be seen from these values and the accompanying IPF maps, L-DED samples display a lower high-angle grain boundary (HAGB) density than L-PBF samples, confirming that L-DED samples have larger grain size than L-PBF specimens. Almost no twin grain boundaries (TGBs) were seen in any of the NHT specimens (L-DED and L-PBF). Furthermore, none to very low amount of TGBs were detected in all L-DED samples. Since twin boundaries are known to form during recrystallization of low stacking fault metals such as 316L SS [52], this suggests that no recrystallization event occurred in the L-DED material after any of the heat treatments investigated. For the L-PBF material, after the HT-1000 heat treatment, only a marginal increase in TGBs density was observed compared to the NHT condition, indicating that negligible recrystallization had taken place. However, a significantly higher density of TGBs was detected in the L-PBF specimens after heat treatment at 1210 °C, which confirms the observed recrystallization behavior. From the microstructure morphology, it was confirmed that the L-PBF sample that was heat treated at 1210°C (HT-1210) (Figure 2f1) was fully recrystallized. In summary, heat treatment at 1000 °C did not significantly alter the grain structure of either one of the AM fabricated specimens (L-DED and L-PBF). The grain structure of the L-DED samples was also not notably affected Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

The wire arc additive manufacturing process, characterized by high thermal gradients and repeated thermal cycling, results in a heterogeneous dendritic morphology, reflecting variations in cooling rate, heat flow direction, and local alloy chemistry. From Fig. 2(a), the IN825 alloy predominantly exhibits equiaxed dendrites in regions of low thermal gradient and high undercooling, typically located at the top of deposition passes where nucleation is favored over growth. In contrast, columnar dendrites develop when the heat flow is unidirectional, aligning their growth axes with the build direction. The formation of secondary arms on dendrites suggests that the cooling rate in certain zones was slow enough to allow lateral growth and solute redistribution, promoting segregation of alloying elements such as Ni, Fe, and Cr into interdendritic regions. The refinement or coarsening of dendritic structures across layers is no visible cracks, unmelted inclusions, or porosity, confirms good metallurgical compatibility between the two alloys during deposition. The variation in thermal expansion coefficients and solidification behavior between SS304 and IN825 could potentially introduce residual stresses; however, the presence of graded dendritic morphologies suggests that the interface solidification process may have helped in stress accommodation. The microstructure of SS304 (Fig. 2c) is characterized by columnar dendrites growing along the build direction, interspersed with equiaxed dendritic regions particularly evident near deposition boundaries. The primary matrix phase is austenite (\( \gamma \)-Fe), while interdendritic regions contain \( \delta \)-ferrite, formed due to the segregation of ferrite-stabilizing elements (Cr, Mo) during solidification. The ferrite fraction is small, which is beneficial for toughness but enhances resistance to hot cracking during solidification. Clear deposition layer boundaries are observed, which mark the thermal history differences between layers. The transition from equiaxed to columnar dendrites and the presence of phase segregation are expected to affect local yield strength, work-hardening behavior, and fracture modes. The IN825 region, with finer equiaxed dendrites, is anticipated to have higher yield strength but potentially lower ductility, whereas the SS304 region, dominated by columnar grains, may exhibit better elongation due to slip along extended grain boundaries. The delta-ferrite phase in SS304 is known to act as a crack-arresting feature, reducing hot cracking tendency and improving resistance to brittle fracture. training_text: The high-speed camera was used to analyze the solidification behavior of molten pool during CMT-WAAM process, as shown in Fig. 7. However, in order to obtain thicker walls, the oscillated path made the heat accumulation further increased. The measured diameter of molten pool with the oscillated path process was about 5-6 mm. The calculated solidification time of molten pool was about 8 s, which provide enough time for the molten pool to absorb the oxygen in atmosphere. The long solidification time and large molten pool will cause the lower cooling rate during CMT-WAAM process. Figure 8 presents the inner-layer microstructure of WAAM built Ti-6Al-4V samples at the center of cross sections. The lower cooling rate during this study was in the range of \( \alpha \) lamellar microstructure formation, and could effectively avoid the formation of martensitic \( \alpha' \) microstructure (Ref 28). With the increase in oxygen level in the shielding atmosphere, the content of \( \alpha \) colony was increased, and the ratio of length to width for \( \alpha \) lamellar was improved. The Gaussian energy profile generates a thermal gradient (G ≈ 10^6 °C/m) and solidification rate (R = 25 mm/s) that produce a high G/R ratio (~4 × 10^4 °C/s·mm^2), favoring planar growth at the initial solid-liquid interface. As solidification progresses, constitutional supercooling triggers a transition to cellular morphology, with cell alignment paralleling the laser’s travel direction. The ER70S-6’s low carbon content (0.13 wt.%) minimizes micro-segregation, while nickel from the AISI 316L filler segregates to inter-dendritic regions (up to 14 wt.% Ni via EDS), stabilizing austenite and preventing δ-ferrite formation. The absence of porosity here, compared to the AISI 308L interface, reflects ER70S-6’s inherent advantages: lower hydrogen solubility and faster hydrogen effusion through its ferritic matrix. Figure 5d’s dilution zone reveals intricate mixing between the AISI 316L filler and 308L WAAM substrate. Laser remelting achieves 5–8% dilution, creating a compositional gradient from AISI 308L (20% Cr, 10% Ni) to 316L (18% Cr, 14% Ni). The solidification sequence progresses through three stages: initial δ-ferrite dendritic growth (Cr-rich cores, Ni-depleted boundaries), peritectic γ formation at 1420–1450°C, and final σ-phase (FeCr) precipitation at γ/δ interfaces during cooling. The resulting microstructure contains 10–15 vol.% vermicular δ-ferrite within an austenitic matrix, with dendritic arm spacing (8–12 μm). The transition zone in Fig. 5(e) illustrates the WAAM 308L’s layered response to thermal exposure. Near the fusion line (Layer 1), temperatures reaching 1300 °C completely erase the original columnar dendritic structure (60–80 μm long), replacing it with 15–20 μm equiaxed grains through full recrystallization. At the subsurface (Layer 2), where plateau temperatures are between 800 and 1000 °C, partial recrystallization creates a duplex structure, with recrystallized equiaxed grains alongside retained columnar grains. This thermal gradient effect was quantified through microhardness, with recrystallized zones reaching 230–250 HV due to grain boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch relationship). The defect-free weld in Sample #2 (Fig. 5a) ultimately stems from optimized parameter synergy. The 316L filler’s high Cr/Ni ratio (1.6) counters solidification cracking risks in ER70S-6 by promoting austenite stability, while controlled heat input (40 J/mm) minimizes distortion. For 308L, the higher alloy content narrows the processing window, and its greater thermal expansion (16.5 μm/m°C versus ER70S-6’s 11.5 μm/m°C) exacerbates interfacial stresses, explaining the contrasting porosity behavior between material pairs. These observations collectively highlight the critical role of thermal management and alloy compatibility in LHW of dissimilar WAAM components. Scale bar: 100 µm µm.

This visual evidence aligns with the quantitative electrochemical data, conclusively demonstrating the enhanced corrosion resistance of HT LPBF-fabricated 440C stainless steel compared to its wrought counterpart. This superior performance highlights the potential of additive manufacturing to produce AISI 440C components with improved corrosion resistance, offering a compelling advantage over traditional manufacturing techniques. The findings of this study are consistent with previous reports regarding the absence of martensite in as-LPBF-fabricated 440C steel and its associated undesirable properties [28–30]. However, this work presents a systematic investigation into the mechanisms underlying the absence of martensite, which has not been explored previously. The results reveal that a high solute concentration in the austenite parent phase leads to a significantly reduced Ms temperature, without the formation of a substantial amount of carbides, as observed in wrought samples following heat treatment. These findings underscore the critical importance of applying a full heat treatment to LPBF-fabricated 440C steel to promote martensitic transformation and achieve desirable properties. Looking ahead, compositional modifications aimed at reducing the solute content in austenite and increasing the Ms temperature may provide a more efficient pathway to martensitic transformation, thereby minimising the need for extensive post-processing. training_text: SEM fractography of as-built specimens is shown in Figure 6. From a macroscopic perspective, no signs of necking are visible, and the fracture exhibits characteristic features of fatigue failure. Independent of the applied stress, fatigue crack initiation sites consistently appear at the surface of the specimens. In L-PBF 316L, defects are inevitable, and fatigue failure in almost all investigated specimens invariably originates from these defects, as illustrated in Figure 6b,f,h. Only a few specimens exhibited fatigue failure initiation at the surface without defects, as depicted in Figure 6d. Porosity was observed in the subsurface region but did not initiate fatigue cracks. Morphological analysis of the defects reveals that the primary type of defect is gas porosity, characterized by circular pores typically smaller than 50μm, as depicted in Figure 6f,h. Additionally, one instance of fatigue failure was traced to a large-scale LoF defect, depicted in Figure 6b. SEM fractographs of specimens tested after the combined treatment are presented in Figure 7. After combined treatment, a notable difference from the as-built condition is that the location of fatigue initiation has shifted from the surface to the interior of the specimens (see Figure 7a,c,g). Pores are the main location for fatigue crack initiation, as illustrated in Figure 7b,d,h. Also, fatigue crack initiation at the surface was observed, as shown in Figure 7e. This is caused by an LoF defect exceeding 100μm in size, with irregularly shaped edges. Overall, the fatigue initiation sites after combined treatment occur at defects, especially porosities. To evaluate the benefits of combined treatment, fatigue tests of specimens subjected to only HT or only LTGC at an applied stress of 364MPa are given in Figure 8. It is observed that the combination of HT and LTGC has a synergistic effect, resulting in a significantly larger improvement of the fatigue performance than the addition of the effects of HT and LTGC individually. Interestingly, HT alone shows almost no contribution to the fatigue life at this applied stress. Zeng et al. [41] reported similar findings for L-PBF 316L subjected to HT at 900°C, noting that the improvement in fatigue performance due to HT was not significant. After only LTGC, there is an approximate five-fold increase in fatigue life, demonstrating the effectiveness of the LTGC process in enhancing the fatigue performance of L-PBF 316L. Notably, after the combined treatment, the fatigue life of L-PBF 316L improved about 50-fold. This illustrates that the combined treatment provides a superior improvement, significantly surpassing the sum of the individual effects of HT and LTGC. Scale bar: 100 µm µm.

training_text: The microstructure of the layers deposited via L-DED-wire was investigated at various locations and under different magnifications using SEM, as shown in Fig. 8. The figure shows that the steel processed by the L-DED-wire method in this study had a hierarchical microstructure composed of various layers of metal deposited upon each other and separated by interlayer boundaries, marked by red lines in Fig. 8a. The Schaeffler diagram has been seen to be reliable for evaluating the overall microstructural features of the type of stainless steel filler wire used in this study processed via direct deposition techniques due to the similarities such methods share with conventional welding technologies [22]. Thus, the \( Cr_{eq} \) and \( Ni_{eq} \) values of the 316LSi were calculated following the nominal chemical composition of the alloy and marked on the Schaeffler diagram in Fig. 9; the results show that the filler wire used is expected to have a mixture of around 92% austenite and 8% ferrite after deposition. However, the low-magnification SEM images in Fig. 8a and b did not show any clear sign of ferritic features being present in the deposited metal, and the dominant microstructure seemed austenitic with a hierarchical structure of grains and subgrain features, as can be seen in Fig. 8b. The absence of ferrite Fig. 8(a) and (b) SEM images can be attributed to the relatively rapid cooling rates associated with L-DED, which potentially refined the ferritic features along the austenitic boundaries to the extent that they could not be detected in such magnifications. However, the presence of ferrite in the microstructure was experimentally confirmed since the deposited metal was noticeably ferromagnetic. Hence, the material was investigated using SEM under higher magnifications, as shown in Fig. 8c to f, and refined ferritic features with different morphologies were detected. The morphology of ferritic features was dependent upon the area of investigation. As shown in Fig. 8c, ferrite had mainly a vermicular network in the top section, while it turned into sporadic spots in the middle section. Furthermore, ferritic features in the bottom center are mainly lacy, trapped between austenitic dendrites and stretched toward the primary thermal gradient direction (Fig. 8e), while ferrite morphology turned into a combination of vermicular and lacy close to the bottom corner areas (Fig. 8f). Moreover, the austenitic grains, as the main phase, could be made out by backscatter electron channeling imaging, as can be seen in Fig. 8b, where they are separated by red dashed lines, while cellular and dendritic subgrain constituents are apparent within the grains, indicating the hierarchical nature of the main microstructure. Accordingly, the various ferritic morphologies were scattered between the hierarchical austenitic features. Accordingly, the various ferritic morphologies were scattered between the hierarchical austenitic features [24–26]. The low thermal conductivity and high melting point (>2500 °C) of the MC materials slow the migration of elements in the melt pool, resulting in a narrower diffusion zone. Additionally, this leads to a decrease in the area of the planar crystal and cellular crystal regions at the bottom of the coating as the MC addition rate increases. A representative plot highlighting changes in the hysteresis loop area across a single fatigue test is shown in Fig. 8a. Within the first two to three cycles, the material experiences cyclic hardening, which is then followed by continuous cyclic softening that continues through to specimen separation. If fatigue crack initiation was solely driven by near-surface defects, the hysteresis loop area should eventually stabilize prior to crack initiation [50]. The lack of stabilization in the hysteresis loop area is indicative of the presence of a continuously changing dislocation substructure generated during fatigue loading [29], which is associated with the presence of incoherent or semi-coherent secondary phase–matrix interfaces that are interacting with dislocation generation [51, 52]. When the fatigue testing data are broken out as a function of both strain amplitude and build angle, similar trends in the measured hysteresis loops were observed, indicative of a microstructural-driven mechanism for crack initiation. These increases in hysteresis loop area correspond with a decrease in fatigue life that is observed with a decrease in build angle, which can be connected to changes in the width of the brittle fracture regions. The widths of the brittle fracture regions were determined by identifying the location where fatigue striations began to appear on the fracture surface, as shown in Fig. 7b, c. training_text: SFE plays a crucial role in shaping the microstructure and properties of 3D-printed CoCrMo alloys. Lower SFE promotes the formation of partial dislocations and stacking faults, which impede dislocation motion and enhances alloy strength through increased dislocation density.[376] This lower SFE also facilitates the nucleation of hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lamellae at stacking faults during rapid cooling, resulting in a fine microstructure with improved mechanical properties. Conversely, higher SFE can inhibit the γ-fcc to ε-hcp transformation, leading to fcc phase dominance and potentially reduced wear resistance.[386] The formation of nanotwins and increased stacking fault density in low-SFE conditions creates additional barriers to dislocation motion, enhancing strength. These unique microstructural features, including cell boundaries and planar defects, are fundamental to optimizing the alloy’s mechanical performance.[387] Thermal history fundamentally shapes the phase composition of 3D-printed CoCrMo alloys through various mechanisms. In Material Extrusion (MEX), extrusion temperature and flow rate affect microstructural development and carbon content, where optimal thermal management prevents detrimental carbide precipitation, enhancing wear performance and biocompatibility.[374] LPBF creates rapid cooling rates that yield refined microstructures with fine grains and cellular structures, contrasting with traditional casting’s coarser grains and brittle sigma phase formation. training_text: Microstructure analysis of the WLAM 316L alloy on the XZ plane (printing direction-front cross-section view) clearly showed the presence of melt pool boundaries, along with an epitaxial solidification tendency of a secondary phase [38,39], as introduced in Figure 3. Further analysis on the XY plane (printing path-top cross-section view) revealed the existence of a duplex microstructure composed of an austenitic matrix and a secondary ferritic phase [13], as expected from the Schaeffler diagram [40] and introduced in Figure 4. This microstructure of WLAM 316L alloy is in contrast to the pure austenitic morphology of its counterpart AISI 316L alloy, which has the same chemical composition [6,40]. In terms of printing defects, Figure 5 clearly demonstrates the presence of macroporosity and microporosity with sizes of 1 μm and up to 6 μm, respectively, in both the XY and XZ planes. This porosity can be identified as “keyholing porosity” or intralayer porosity, usually generated due to the use of an inert protective gas atmosphere and consequent gas entrapment [32], as can be expected from DED processes [41–43]. It should be pointed out that such porosity can have a significant detrimental effect on the mechanical properties and, in particular, on the fatigue endurance due to the fact that pores can act as fatigue initiation sites. X-ray microtomography (CT) analysis of WLAM 316L and its counterpart AISI 316L alloy is shown in Figures 6 and 7, respectively. This reveals the rough surface of the WLAM alloy compared to the smooth surface of the counterpart alloy that did not include any abnormal defects. Close examination of the WLAM alloy showed the presence of porosity with a spherical shape that is in line with the observation of the electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 5. The corrosion performance of WLAM 316L and its counterpart AISI 316L alloy in terms of pitting density and the pitting factor after the immersion test in 1 M of HCl solution for 100 h is shown in Figure 8, along with quantitative analysis in Table 1. This reveals that both alloys suffered from a localized corrosion attack, mainly in the form of pitting. However, the extent of the corrosion attack in the WLAM 316L alloy was significantly increased compared to its counterpart AISI 316L. For example, the pitting density in WLAM 316L was 14-times higher than that obtained by the counterpart AISI 316L alloy. This could be mainly related to the inherent process defects of the WLAM 316L alloy and the fact that this alloy contains a ferritic phase with reduced corrosion resistance [6,11]. Material: in 1 M HCl solution. Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: In a study on FG Ti-Rene88DT superalloy prepared using Laser rapid forming (LRF) from 100 Ti to 60 wt.% Rene88DT, Lin et al. (2006) (Ref 115) observed evolution of a series of different phases along the graded compositions: \( \alpha + \beta \) \( \alpha + \beta + \mathrm{Ti}_2\mathrm{Ni} \) (10 wt.% Rene88DT) \( \beta + \mathrm{Ti}_2\mathrm{Ni} \) (20-40 wt.% Rene88DT) Ti\(_2\)Ni + TiNi (50 wt.% Rene88DT) TiNi (60 wt.% Rene88DT). Figure 3 shows optical micrographs at different wt.% of Rene88DT. From Fig. 3 it is suggested that with increase in wt.% of Rene88DT there was a transition in microstructure from cellular to dendritic accompanied by the decrease in cellular spacing. This conclusion was derived based on earlier studies (Ref 116). As mentioned earlier, with further increase in wt% of Rene88DT a series of phases were developed. This series involved the growth of \( \beta + \mathrm{Ti}_2\mathrm{Ni} \) anomalous eutectic which was discussed by the same team in a different study (Ref 117). The hardness of the FGM was found to greatly depend on the morphology of phases like Ti\(_2\)Ni, TiNi and \( \alpha + \mathrm{Ti}_2\mathrm{Ni} \) eutectoid. Also, studies involving comparison of Ti-Ni-based graded materials and homogenous alloys have shown that the dominant phases are same in both systems; however, there was a variation in evolution of different phases (Ref 118). The Ti-Ni system can also be tailored to obtain properties that are suitable for bio-medical applications (Ref 119). Abioye et al. (2015) successfully developed FG Ni-Ti system using concurrent feeding of Ni powder and commercially pure (CP) Ti wire via direct laser metal deposition process. The microstructural characterization revealed the presence of NiTi and NiTi\(_2\) phases where the fraction of NiTi\(_2\) decreased and NiTi increased with increase in Ni powder feed rate. Also, these hard phases caused the maximum hardness to rise up to 1.5 times CP Ti (Ref 120). Also alloys like Inconel 718, Inconel 625 have been successfully used to develop graded structures with Ti, but the major issue with these structures is development of cracks at certain compositions due to development of brittle intermetallic phases. Even though the literature available on additively manufactured Ti-Ni(alloy)-based FGM systems are very limited, successful attempts have been made by different authors to eliminate cracking. However this requires additional processing like preheating of the substrate (Ref 59, 109). Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

Image analysis of a series of three unetched 2D sections in both the AB and HT condition revealed an average density of 99.96%, which corresponds well with previous studies on LPBF DSS 2205 [10,15]. The micrographs of the AB specimens (Fig. 3b, c) show the microstructure is dominated by ferrite. This phenomena occurs due to the molten powder solidifying as delta ferrite coupled with the rapid cooling rates in the LPBF process [21]. In the build direction, the AB specimens exhibit a columnar grain structure with a more equiaxed type structure on the orthogonal face in the build plane. The melt pool boundaries are somewhat visible in the AB specimens, indicated by white arrows, which helps to reveal two features in the AB microstructure. Firstly, the elongated grains in the build direction extend over several melt pools, revealing the epitaxial growth mechanism which occurs due to the remelting and solidification of previously deposited layers. Secondly, in the AB build plane, there is evidence of finer grains on the overlap of the melt pool boundaries. The micrographs of the HT specimens (Fig. 3e, f) show that the HT schedule has resulted in a significant increase in the austenite fraction, which arises due to the formation and movement of high angle grain boundaries at the solution annealing temperature [10]. The formed austenite can generally be divided into three groups; (i) formed along the melt pool boundaries during the process and grown during HT, (ii) needle-like laths and (iii) small islands of intragranular secondly austenite [14], indicated by the red, yellow and black arrows respectively in Fig. 3f. When examining the grain size distributions, particularly in the graph between area fractions versus grain size, it is evident that the proportion of grains sized between 40 \( \mu \)m and 80 \( \mu \)m is significantly reduced in the FSP-treated wall sample compared to the WAAM sample which underscores a marked difference in the microstructures between two samples. The reduction in the number of large grains in the FSP-treated sample can be attributed to the grain refinement effect of FSP, which involves intense plastic deformation and localized heating, thereby breaking down larger grains and promoting the formation of finer ones [41,42]. In the WAAM wall, the average grain size is approximately 16.28 \( \mu \)m in the ER5356 zone and 118.92 \( \mu \)m in the ER4043 zone. This smaller average grain size in the ER5356 side occurs because of the presence of a thermal gradient among both filler wires [28]. In the FSP-treated wall, the average grain size is reduced to ~5.57 \( \mu \)m in the stirred area, while in the unstirred area, it is around 72.40 \( \mu \)m. This grain size reduction of the stirred area indicates that FSP treatment on the WAAM sample has significantly influenced grain growth during fabrication, resulting in grain refinement. This finer grain structure likely contributes to the improved hardness of the wall, which is in line with the Hall–Petch equation [43]. Additionally, the IPF map shows most grains with high-angle boundaries, consistent with observations made in the optical images. This microstructure refinement is mostly attributed to the stringent plastic deformation and geometric dynamic recrystallization experienced by the alloy in the stirred zone caused by the rotating pin. The direction of grain growth aligns with the rotational direction of the stirring head. This process results in the formation of fine equiaxed grains and eliminates pore defects [14,34,35]. In the 1200 °C-annealed specimens, the dislocation density further decreased and dislocation-free grains were noted. Moreover, numerous spherical inclusions (0.02–1.0 μm, average 0.11 ± 0.03 μm; 64% of <0.1 μm) (Figure 8g) were revealed. Many coarse inclusions resided at grain boundaries, suggesting either their interaction with moving boundaries or boundary-related nucleation and coarsening (Figure 8h,i). Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

Some micro-cracks can be observed at the fracture surface, as shown in Fig. 12d. The initiation and propagation of these micro-cracks accelerated the failure of the tensile specimen, thereby limiting the increase in elongation. The deformation temperature has been shown to have a significant effect on the deformation mode of NiTi alloys due to the thermoelastic martensitic transformation [42]. The formation of stress-induced martensite upon loading and the reversible transformation upon unloading occurs only at temperatures above \( A_f \), contributing to the superelasticity. Thereby, to better reflect the superelastic behavior of the current WAAM NiTiTa alloys, cyclic tensile tests were carried out at 100 °C (above \( A_f \)), and the results are presented in Fig. 13. The WAAM NiTiTa sample shows obvious superelasticity during the loading-unloading process, as shown in Fig. 14a. The critical stress (\( \sigma_c \)) for stress-induced martensitic transformation is about 380 MPa at 100 °C, while at room temperature it decreases to 252 MPa. This is due to the increased thermodynamic resistance for the martensitic transformation, which is a function of temperature as expressed by the Clausius-Clapeyron relation [43]. The calculated recovery ratio as a function of the cycle times is shown in Fig. 13b. The reversible strain in the first cycle is about 1.8 %, and the corresponding recovery ratio (ratio of recoverable strain to total imposed strain) is 91.5 %. With the increase of the number of cycles, the recovery ratio gradually reduced and then maintained at nearly 86.8 % after 10 loading-unloading cycles. The reduced recovery ratio is due to the gradual accumulation of defects and retained martensite, which promotes the decrease of transformation strain and the increase of the volume fraction of untransformed austenite within the shear bands during cycling tests [44].
