training_text: In the context of this study, \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) represent batch CG and any other sample with a distinct building direction than 0° (i.e., batch CG), respectively, while \( x \) denotes Yield stress, UTS, and elongation at break. The calculated \( D_{\alpha \beta} \) values in samples constructed with varying build directions are as follows: (i) 1.2, 3.5, and 22.2% for BD_15; (ii) 3.7, 1.3, and 14.8% for BD_30; and (iii) 2.4, 1.7, and 7.4% for BD_90. It is evident that the anisotropy index of Yield stress and UTS remained relatively consistent across all build directions, while it decreased for elongation with larger build directions. Consequently, under the specified PPPs, the specimens demonstrated a high degree of mechanical isotropy. The metal AM machine used for this work exhibited capability to generate components with nearly isotropic mechanical behavior across different building directions. In addition, microscopic examinations were conducted to elucidate the correlation between mechanical characteristics and microstructure of the material resulting from printing with varying parameters. Figure 18 illustrates the fractographies obtained from the fractured surfaces of the tensile specimens. The presence of porosity in the printed specimens instigated void expansion, thereby leading to a fracture with the escalation of scanning speed and thus lack of fusion. Upon analysis of the fractured surfaces, segments printed at comparatively lower speeds exhibited a ductile fracture microstructure. According to the SEM investigations, CG, SS_1400, LT_30, BD_30, and BD_90 showed nearly similar results as it can be seen in Fig. 18a. At low magnification, large dimples were discernible on the fractured surfaces of components. This surface images conformed to the characteristics of a typical ductile fracture, characterized by a terraced and opaque surface. Figure 18b shows a closer look at the dimpled surface which is the final fracture region of the optimized sample. The conspicuous large dimples served as evidence of considerable ductility and a substantial volume fraction of voids within the ultimate fracture zones, as expected. Initial voids, originating from the manufacturing process, expand concurrently with the initiation of new voids during deformation. The sub-micrometric size of these dimples was indicative of the cell dimensions within the solidified microstructure of the printed components. The coalescence of nano-voids formed within structure contributed to the ductile fracture behavior of the components. As necking commences, intrinsic voids and newly nucleated voids congregated locally, resulting in ductile fracture. Consequently, the increasing number of large dimples served as an indicator of the degree of elongation at the point of fracture. This escalation in the final fracture zone, relative to the initial state, can be attributed to the high ductility of the alloy. Conversely, when the scanning speed was increased to 2000 mm/min, the fracture surface displayed a flatter profile, accompanied by an escalation in brittle fracture regions as displayed in Fig. 18c. Local brittle zones were the indication of the reduction in ductility. Despite the presence of larger brittle fracture surfaces, the fracture behavior can still be categorized as ‘ductile’ due to the matte and terraced surface characteristics. The brittle zones are attributed to a possible result of lack of fusion. Further, alteration of the building direction to 15°, resulted in a decrease in the ductility. Figure 18d demonstrates the localized flat surfaces accompanied by the ductile fracture. SEM micrographs revealed a more pronounced manifestation of brittle fracture surfaces. For the building directions of 30° and 90°, the fracture surfaces of the specimens exhibited characteristics indicative of a conventional ductile fracture, characterized by the presence of dimples. When scrutinizing the dimpled regions in detail, a consistent profile emerged: a mixture of small and medium-sized dimples alongside terraced surfaces. The parts generated using a laser power of 100 W exhibit characteristics of brittle fracture, featuring a shiny-surface devoid of any discernible necking. The stress–strain curve also displayed a non-uniform deformation region with a pronounced sharp decline, signifying brittle fracture when the material loses its capacity to bear an elastic load, see P_100 batch in Fig. 17. Figure 18e effectively illustrates the consequences of reducing the laser power to 100 W, revealing the presence of unmelted powders within the microstructure, which are highlighted in Fig. 18e. Consequently, remelting strength between layers were notably poor. The component displayed a considerable degree of porosity, which consequently affects HRB hardness measurements adversely, as shown in Fig. 6. On the contrary, when the laser power was increased to 150 W, there was an enhancement in remelting strength. Similar to the 100 W samples, narrow-melted regions were observed, as depicted in Fig. 18f. Strikingly, the fracture behavior within these narrow-melted regions was characterized by a dimpled surface. The expansion in melted regions influenced the Yield stress and UTS. However, the presence of non-melted powders primarily governed the elongation at break, and the increase in power from 100 to 200 W did not significantly impact this aspect. BF denotes brittle fracture Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: To study the effect of different heat inputs on the microstructure of the same composite material (VInconel 718: VTi6Al4V=2:1), the metallographic morphology of the samples was observed under different deposition currents using an optical microscope. Figure 4 displays the optical microscopy characterization for each deposition current. Figure 4a shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 35 A, with the Ti6Al4V/Inconel 718 composite in the upper part and the Inconel 718 layer in the lower part. The upper section is predominantly composed of columnar crystals, intermingled with some long black bars among the branches of the columnar crystals. In the WAM process, the solid–liquid interface gradually advances into the liquid phase region. During this advancement, the solute undergoes redistribution, resulting in a phenomenon of component supercooling within a certain distance. This instability of the flat solid–liquid interface ultimately leads to the formation of columnar crystals. As the liquid phase region is influenced by solute redistribution, solute aggregation occurs, which is manifested as microscopic segregation [27]. From the Figure 4a, it can be observed that tiny secondary dendrites are present on the sides of the columnar crystals, with an average distance of 5.16 μm between these secondary dendrites. With the increase in the deposition current, the columnar crystals in the deposited layer gradually undergo differentiation. Figure 4b shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 40 A. From the Figure 4b, it can be observed that some of the grains are arranged in an orderly manner, while a discontinuous black phase is present between the grains. In addition, long straight columnar crystals can be observed in the Figure 4b, which is formed due to the instability of the solid–liquid interface resulting from the supercooling of the composition. Under conditions of rapid cooling, columnar crystals are formed more readily. In comparison to Figure 4a, when the deposition current is 40 A, the heat input increases, leading to a longer temperature residence time on the workpiece under the same heat dissipation conditions. As a result, the cooling rate becomes relatively slower. At the microscopic level, the number of columnar crystals decreases, with some larger columnar crystals gradually transforming into smaller grains, leading to an increase in the spacing between columnar crystals. As some of the heat is conducted in the direction of the deposited additive, a negative temperature gradient develops in the liquid phase, perpendicular to the crystal axis. This results in the formation of a secondary crystal axis along the primary crystal axis [27]. The presence of secondary dendrites can be observed in the Figure 4b, with the average distance between the secondary dendrites measuring 6.38 μm. Figure 4. training_text: Light metallographic images of fracture surfaces for T1 and T3 rings at low magnification are displayed in Fig. 18. The T1 ring fracture surface (Fig. 18 (a)) does not display any large pores. The T3 ring displays numerous large pores between 25 and 72 \( \mu \)m diameter in which striations are visible on the surface of each pore. The rib-like feature on the surface of Ti-6Al-4 V was concluded to be a characteristic of keyhole porosity [41,56], and modelling of keyhole induced pores displayed similar surface striations in Ti-6Al-4 V [19]. It is unlikely these features developed in the keyhole pores during dynamic ring expansion. Although with tensile plastic deformation the large pores on the fracture surface would stretch from a more spherical to an elongated shape [57] aligned to the major axis (in the ring hoop direction), together with some lateral growth before fracture. The striations on the surface of the large pores in the T3 rings are a distinguishing feature of keyhole porosity in the LPBF IN718 alloy. Similar striations were observed in Ti-6Al-4 V (PD: 50 \( \mu \)m) [56] and was associated with increased turbulence in the melt pool which suggests a high energy density was applied. Kasperovich et al [41] mentioned that the features around each of the large pores contain sharp trenches that can act as stress concentrators. It was suggested they could have formed due to surface tension forces exerting a shear force on the liquid surface [58,59]. The largest PD identified in the T1 ring (Table 3) was 25 \( \mu \)m diameter which was fabricated under stable conduction melting and this cannot be a keyhole pore. Therefore, an appreciable portion of the distribution in the left tail of Fig. 9c may not be attributed to keyhole porosity. T1 and T3 ring fracture surfaces at high magnification are displayed in Fig. 19 at the same scale. Fracture is transgranular for all ring samples. The fracture surfaces display a dimpled character associated with a ductile fracture. Many small sub-micron size pores can be observed in Fig. 19 (a and b) at the centre of a dimple. These may have developed from micro pores and nucleated from the second phase precipitates within the \( \gamma \) matrix that serve to impede dislocation slip. The dimples in the T1 ring are equiaxed typically from 1 to 5 \( \mu \)m across ligaments, and fracture was by tensile void coalescence [60–63]. The dimples identified in LPBF IN718 [28,43], in the as-built and unaged condition obtained from quasi-static uniaxial tensile testing, although equiaxed were smaller spanning submicron to a few microns. In the T1 fractograph a few long dimpled channels had coalesced which could be associated with a higher concentration of precipitates or grain boundaries. Some very small dimples which are just visible have nucleated within the ligaments of some larger dimples. This feature has been attributed to void sheeting with coalescence by shear [64] as a secondary instability stage preceding final fracture. Hardness: 299. Scale bar: 100 µm µm.

DDC in fusion-based AM Nickel-based superalloy is referred to the cracking caused by creep like mechanism [226]. They concluded that during the reheating of welded Nickel-base superalloy, grain boundary sliding causes high strain and void coalescence. These voids segregate at the stress concentration sites such as triple point junction of grain boundaries and forms cracking eventually. It was noted that continuous carbide particles are harmful to ductility-dip cracking resistance since the voids near the carbide particles nucleate into the cracking [227]. training_text: Microstructure and grains distribution greatly affect the mechanical properties of fabricated parts produced through WAAM [140]. Min Qi et al. [141] explained that complex thermal cycling in the manufactured material from AM processes results in columnar coarse grains. Haden et al. [134] performed a wear scar of platinum in Z axis (facing towards test equipment) over the deposited MS, they performed SEM and FIB imaging and observed grain refinement immediately below the wear scar as shown in Fig. 17. Wang et al. [142] utilized H13 as feeder wire for the WAAM process with 4-Axis CNC-assisted MIG welding powder as shown in Fig. 18. They found multiple microstructural formations which was due to local heating histories. Also, the elongation and tensile strength were maximum which was farthest from the substrate. Liu et al. [143] developed an Al based fabricated part through TIG and MIG. They revealed that the GTAW welding of Al part results in higher hardness and strength over the GMAW welds due to the precipitate strengthening and less porosity development. In GTAW weldment, there are large amount of localised plasticity observed, while there is a considerable amount of porosity in GMAW weldments which could figure out the difference in mechanical characteristics between both the kinds. GTAW bonded Al part is mechanically more reliable than GMAW welded one [143,144]. However, cold metal transfer for Al based WAAM improves mechanical characteristics by allowing for better control of porosity formation, controlled metal deposition, and lower heat input. Lower welding heat input results in decreased weld pool temperature as well as fine grain structure, which minimizes H2 trapping and hence the porosity formation [145,146]. With WAAM microstructure and phase transformation is dependent on the materials used, High temperature developed, cooling rate and deposition rate [147]. Defects produced in the process also affect the mechanical properties [140]. To increase the mechanical properties, recent studies concentrated mostly on reducing the defects such as porosity, surface cracking, deformations and gas inclusions by introducing some post-processing techniques. This paper will see the recent post-processing techniques which have been done for the enhancing of mechanical properties of as-fabricated (AF) produced parts. Delamination is usually a visible deficiency which cannot be eliminated by post-processing techniques or heat treatments, but can be avoided by following proper process parameters in order to reduce repeated fluctuated stresses and also by considering the characteristics of deposited alloy [148,149], there are various categories of defects as can be briefly seen in Table 7. Scope of defect in WAAM processes with various metals can be seen in Fig. 19. Material: s GMAW 1400 NAB. Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: To study the effect of different heat inputs on the microstructure of the same composite material (VInconel 718: VTi6Al4V=2:1), the metallographic morphology of the samples was observed under different deposition currents using an optical microscope. Figure 4 displays the optical microscopy characterization for each deposition current. Figure 4a shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 35 A, with the Ti6Al4V/Inconel 718 composite in the upper part and the Inconel 718 layer in the lower part. The upper section is predominantly composed of columnar crystals, intermingled with some long black bars among the branches of the columnar crystals. In the WAM process, the solid–liquid interface gradually advances into the liquid phase region. During this advancement, the solute undergoes redistribution, resulting in a phenomenon of component supercooling within a certain distance. This instability of the flat solid–liquid interface ultimately leads to the formation of columnar crystals. As the liquid phase region is influenced by solute redistribution, solute aggregation occurs, which is manifested as microscopic segregation [27]. From the Figure 4a, it can be observed that tiny secondary dendrites are present on the sides of the columnar crystals, with an average distance of 5.16 μm between these secondary dendrites. With the increase in the deposition current, the columnar crystals in the deposited layer gradually undergo differentiation. Figure 4b shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 40 A. From the Figure 4b, it can be observed that some of the grains are arranged in an orderly manner, while a discontinuous black phase is present between the grains. In addition, long straight columnar crystals can be observed in the Figure 4b, which is formed due to the instability of the solid–liquid interface resulting from the supercooling of the composition. Under conditions of rapid cooling, columnar crystals are formed more readily. In comparison to Figure 4a, when the deposition current is 40 A, the heat input increases, leading to a longer temperature residence time on the workpiece under the same heat dissipation conditions. As a result, the cooling rate becomes relatively slower. At the microscopic level, the number of columnar crystals decreases, with some larger columnar crystals gradually transforming into smaller grains, leading to an increase in the spacing between columnar crystals. As some of the heat is conducted in the direction of the deposited additive, a negative temperature gradient develops in the liquid phase, perpendicular to the crystal axis. This results in the formation of a secondary crystal axis along the primary crystal axis [27]. training_text: EBSD, normal to the deposition direction, was used to better understand the microstructure of the as-deposited L-DED and AFSD material, and the results of this can be observed in Figure 4. The L-DED material exhibited a typical microstructure of the material, with a high amount of martensite present and an average grain size of 24 \( \mu \)m. L-DED produces high cooling rates of the solidification structure between 103 and 106 \( ^\circ \)C/s and typically sees a dominant martensitic microstructure. The Fe-Ni lath martensitic structure is formed during the rapid cooling of austenite [31]. The AFSD material exhibited a more uniform martensitic microstructure than that of the L-DED material and exhibited a smaller grain size of 17 \( \mu \)m. Overall, the cooling rates were likely not as high in the AFSD process due to the material maintaining a solid state during deposition. The L-DED material hardness was observed to be 521 HV during the first half of the deposited region depicted in Figure 5. However, the hardness was seen to rise by ~5% closer to the substrate before significantly falling due to the weaker strength of the substrate material. paper_id: Dudziak et al. 2023 - Effect of 316L Stainless Steel Fabrication on Oxidation Resistance, Surface Morphology, and Hot Tensile Behavior
training_text: shows the surface microstructure of 316L CM SS developed in the temperature range 600-900 °C for 100 h, respectively. Figure 5 shows the SEM images in SE mode for the oxide scale development process on austenitic steel exposed to air. At the lowest temperature (600 °C), the exposed surface developed randomly distributed crystals with the size of a few nanometers. Nevertheless, not a whole surface was covered at 600 °C with tiny crystals. Instead, some areas developed a Fe-rich oxide, as shown in Fig. 5. The EDS analyses in Fe-rich region confirmed: 43.1 Fe, 46.0 O, 2.2 Cr, 0.8 Mn and finally 1.7 at.% Si. No other elements were shown during this analysis. Fe-rich oxide in austenitic steel in the air is natural since the steel is not uniform in terms of chemical composition. Some places in the matrix are enriched in Fe and develop non-protective oxides based on Fe under highly oxidizing conditions. On the other hand, the formation of tiny enriched crystals spread on the surface is shown. The detailed EDS analyses of the crystals revealed a chemical composition of 16.4 O, 0.9 Si, 0.7 Mo, 13 Cr, 4.3 Mn, 54.0 Fe and finally 7.9 at.% Ni. This composition is similar to the metal matrix of 316L grade but with O content. The matured crystals on the 316L surface are too small, and the EDX measurement mainly reveals the bulk composition. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

training_text: shows cropped panorama images of LPBF-processed CP titanium grade 1 in the as-printed state of a specimen of the first (Figure 3A) and second (Figure 3B) print jobs. As can be seen, a substantial columnar microstructure cannot be observed. Prior β-grain boundaries are not visible, but regions with similar orientations of α- or α'-grains do partially exhibit a columnar appearance, suggesting the presence of elongated, long prior β-grains aligned with the building direction, as expected. According to these panorama images, the microstructure appears to be homogeneous throughout the samples that include the last scan tracks at the top of each specimen. The latter suggests that the microstructural changes due to platform heating did not occur in situ during LPBF printing. Moreover, it can be seen that significant differences between both analyzed specimens are not present, which is supported by SEM analyses, although the second print job lasted much longer (more than 43 h) than the first (more than 9 h). Consequently, it is expected that the tensile samples printed during the second print job exhibit a similar microstructure. Figure 4 shows the SEM images (BSE detector) of the as-printed microstructure at the approximate center of the specimen that is being printed together with the tensile specimens. At lower magnifications and in accordance with the optical microscope images, a needle-like martensitic microstructure seems to be present but appears to be heterogeneous in size and shape and seems to contain broad structures as well. Regarding the latter, further features or grain boundaries within these structures are not visible at lower magnifications. However, as can be seen in the high-magnification image of Figure 4, broader structures, at least partially, consist of almost parallel, finer plates or needles. The smaller substructures are, nevertheless, not always recognizable, which is also evident from Figure 4. By contrast, much smaller, round, white particles are supposed to be artifacts from metallographic specimen preparation. In addition, pitting corrosion seems to have taken place at the grain boundaries due to etching, which is often observed with this etchant, further indicating the presence of smaller structures being not visible with lower magnification. In general, due to the very high cooling rates during LPBF printing (DebRoy et al., 2018), a martensitic β to α transformation would be expected during cooling. Although in situ decomposition of martensite might be possible (Xu et al., 2015), microstructural differences between both specimens and along the the building direction that included the last laser tracks were not observed, as has already been described, suggesting that no martensite decomposition took place. Moreover, the microstructure exhibits similarities with massive martensite, which is characterized by approximate parallel α-plates forming larger packets and microstructural areas, in which the grain boundaries are hardly visible (Lütjering and Williams, 2007). This type of martensite is thereby present, among others, in pure titanium and alloys with a very low amount of alloying elements (Lütjering and Williams, 2007). Therefore, it is concluded that the LPBF-processed samples consist of massive martensite. In the literature, the microstructure observed after LPBF printing of CP titanium has also been described as plate-like or lenticular α'-laths (Wysocki et al., 2017), α-grains, shaped as plates, or acicular α' (depending on process parameters) (Attar et al., 2014) and α'-laths or acicular α' (Attar et al., 2017). It is also reported that different α'-structures can be present within a sample (Attar et al., 2017). Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: Microstructure of the L-PBF Inconel 625 after stress-relief annealing at a temperature of 980 °C for 1 h, followed by annealing at a temperature of 600 °C for 5 h: (a) LM image, (b) SEM image, as well as TEM images of (c) dislocations arrangements, (d) precipitates of the γ'' phase (arrowed), (e) [100]γ zone axis SAED pattern with the γ'' phase diffraction spots of the [100]γ'' and [010]γ'' zone axes shows the electron diffraction pattern of the matrix γ phase [100] zone axis with the lower intensity spots of the γ'' phase [100] and [010] zone axes, which confirms that the precipitates lie on the {100} planes of the γ matrix. Body centered tetragonal Ni3Nb-based γ'' phase exhibits ordered structure and precipitates from the γ solid solution in the form of coherent precipitates (Ref 31). Precipitates of the γ'' phase were observed in the thin foils prepared from the sections parallel to the horizontal (XY) and vertical (XZ and YZ) sections of the examined specimen. The evidence of the γ'' phase was reported also in L-PBF Inconel 625 subjected to stress-relief annealing at a temperature of 870 °C for 1 h (Ref 7). Our studies did not confirm those findings for the specimen stress relieved at the higher temperature of 980 °C, whereas it was demonstrated that precipitation of the γ'' phase occurs after subsequent annealing at a temperature of 600 °C for 5 h in the whole volume of the L-PBF Inconel 625. Precipitation of the γ'' phase was also observed in wrought Inconel 625 long-time service exposed and subsequently annealed at the temperature of 650 °C for 1 h (Ref 2) as well as in TIG and GTA welds heat treated at 700 °C for 8 h (Ref 24) and 750 °C for 4 h (Ref 25), respectively. Although welding and L-PBF processes seem similar, the cooling rates in additive manufacturing are much higher, which results in a very fine and highly segregated microstructure. Our observations indicate that such refinement in L-PBF Inconel 625 contributes to precipitation of the \( \gamma'' \) phase at lower temperature and after a shorter time than in heat-treated welds. Prolongation of the annealing time up to 100 h resulted in the destabilization of the cellular microstructure manifested by breaks in the continuity of the cell walls, as observed in LM images (Fig. 4a) and more clearly in SEM images (Fig. 4b). Due to the intensification of recovery processes, dislocation density inside the cells further decreased and was equal to \( 2.55 \times 10^{14} \) m\(^{-2}\) (Fig. 4c). Moreover, the \( \gamma'' \) phase particles grew and precipitated in all three sets of the {100} planes of the \( \gamma \) phase matrix, what was demonstrated by the presence of the three sets of diffraction spots form the [100], [010] and [001] zone axes of the \( \gamma'' \) phase (Fig. 4d and e). Streaking of the \( \gamma'' \) diffraction spots in the principal cubic directions is related to the plate-like shape of the particles precipitated on the {100} \( \gamma \) phase planes. EDS spectra acquired in the locations of the \( \gamma'' \) phase precipitates revealed the presence of the strong Ni, Cr, Mo and Nb peaks (Fig. 4f). The \( \gamma'' \) phase nanoparticles were below 100 nm in size, while the foil thickness was about 210 nm; thus, this result represents the sum of the \( \gamma \) and \( \gamma'' \) phase compositions. It should be pointed out that prolongation of the annealing at a temperature of 600 °C to 100 h did not result in intensive precipitation of the \( \delta \) phase, as it was shown in other studies even already after stress relieving at a temperature of 870 °C for 1 h (Ref 12). Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: The scanning electron micrographs in Figure 5 contrast the microstructure of the specimens. It is worth noting that the resultant solidified microstructures are very similar. The solidification structure is that of columnar grains containing colonies of submicrometric cells separated by low angle grain boundaries. These columnar grains arose due to partial remelting of the previous consolidated layers, as they allowed epitaxial growth. Therefore, this epitaxial growth from the parent grains encouraged the elongation of the columnar grains, which then resulted in a highly textured columnar microstructure, as confirmed later by the electron backscatter diffraction analysis. From the shown plane of view, microstructural features of periodically layer bands are common in L-PBF specimens [31–36]. Consequently, neighbouring colonies of cells grew rather misoriented to each other in response to the influence of the layer bands to the local maximum heat flux direction. training_text: The scanning electron micrographs in Figure 5 contrast the microstructure of the specimens. It is worth noting that the resultant solidified microstructures are very similar. The solidification structure is that of columnar grains containing colonies of submicrometric cells separated by low angle grain boundaries. These columnar grains arose due to partial remelting of the previous consolidated layers, as they allowed epitaxial growth. Therefore, this epitaxial growth from the parent grains encouraged the elongation of the columnar grains, which then resulted in a highly textured columnar microstructure, as confirmed later by the electron backscatter diffraction analysis. From the shown plane of view, microstructural features of periodically layer bands are common in L-PBF specimens [31–36]. Accordingly, the behaviour of the layer bands observed in Figure 5 resulted from reheat and remelt influence by the consecutive layer deposition. In summary, these layer bands were weak barriers to prevent columnar grain size growth. However, as observed from the high magnification inset micrographs in Figure 5, layer bands did effectively break the cellular structures into small colonies. Consequently, neighbouring colonies of cells grew rather misoriented to each other in response to the influence of the layer bands to the local maximum heat flux direction. Therefore, this randomised orientation of the colonies contrasted with the columnar grains anisotropy. The benefit of this is that such subgrain features could result in strengthening and toughening effects by impeding dislocation movement and altering the course of fracture and propagation paths. training_text: The scanning electron micrographs in Figure 5 contrast the microstructure of the specimens. It is worth noting that the resultant solidified microstructures are very similar. The solidification structure is that of columnar grains containing colonies of submicrometric cells separated by low angle grain boundaries. These columnar grains arose due to partial remelting of the previous consolidated layers, as they allowed epitaxial growth. Therefore, this epitaxial growth from the parent grains encouraged the elongation of the columnar grains, which then resulted in a highly textured columnar microstructure, as confirmed later by the electron backscatter diffraction analysis. From the shown plane of view, microstructural features of periodically layer bands are common in L-PBF specimens [31–36]. Accordingly, the behaviour of the layer bands observed in Figure 5 resulted from reheat and remelt influence by the consecutive layer deposition. In summary, these layer bands were weak barriers to prevent columnar grain size growth. However, as observed from the high magnification inset micrographs in Figure 5, layer bands did effectively break the cellular structures into small colonies. Consequently, neighbouring colonies of cells grew rather misoriented to each other in response to the influence of the layer bands to the local maximum heat flux direction. Therefore, this randomised orientation of the colonies contrasted with the columnar grains anisotropy. The benefit of this is that such subgrain features could result in strengthening and toughening effects by impeding dislocation movement and altering the course of fracture and propagation paths. training_text: shows the as-built (Figure 5a) and heat-treated (Figure 5b) microstructures acquired on the xz-plane of the Ti6Al4V dog-bone samples. The as-built microstructure (Figure 5a) is characterized by columnar β-grains containing hcp α′-martensite laths (white arrows in Figure 5a). As investigated in several studies [10,31,40], the LPBF process promotes, first, the nucleation of the β-grain directly on the build platform and, secondly, its growth along the build direction, namely, across the several molten pools. training_text: Titanium alloys are important structural materials, while nickel-based alloys are considered superalloys. Figure 9 illustrates the macroscopic view of the partial cracks, as well as high-rate SEM images. No cracks were found in the first layer, but the crack section in the second layer Ti6Al4V/Inconel 718 appeared disconnected, with an uneven crack morphology. High-magnification SEM images (shown in Figure 9b–d) of the crack section reveal a microfracture morphology characterized by river and cleavage patterns, indicating a cleavage fracture mechanism. To investigate the phase composition of the crack section, an EDS scanning analysis of its microstructure was conducted. Figure 10 presents a high-magnification SEM image of the fracture bottom, revealing a precipitated phase A. EDS analysis indicates that the atomic ratio of oxygen to iron is approximately 1.6:1, suggesting that the precipitate is likely iron oxide. At position B, the ratio of nickel to titanium atoms is about 1:1, with the chromium and iron content being similar to that of titanium and nickel. However, the carbon content is relatively high, leading to the speculation that the main phase at position B is MC carbide. Previous studies have shown that small amounts of MC carbide can impede dislocation movement and stabilize grain boundaries, thus providing strengthening; however, excessive MC can result in stress concentration, reducing the alloy’s durability and contributing to crack formation [15]. For example, it was shown that the Ni-coated diamond abrasive is less efficient in removing material than an uncoated diamond in MAF of Ni-based superalloys [170]. Mass finishing processes Mass finishing is an abrasive fine-finishing technology used for simultaneous processing of multiple components in a container, usually with abrasive media and a compound solution. Here, a cyclic movement of the container causes media to vibrate and rotate against workpiece surfaces, or workpieces to rub against each other. This type of finishing is often used as a final step after the AM build cycle to achieve low surface roughness and reflective surfaces (characterised by smaller standard deviation of heights, Sq). Mass finishing can be classified into 5 methods: vibratory finishing (using bowl or tub), rotary barrel finishing (tumbling), centrifugal barrel finishing, centrifugal disc finishing and drag (spindle) finishing [172]. The geometry and kinematics of the vibratory finishing are not well understood; however, Hashimoto et al. [173] modelled the material removal mechanism by deriving the relative velocity vector and the impact angle in the contact. In this respect the geometry and kinematics of the abrasive interaction could also be derived from the theory of aggressiveness [174]. Hashimoto et al. determined the characteristic specific energy curve against equivalent chip thickness h_eq [150,173], which is difficult as one also needs to estimate the depth of cut. As in other abrasive processes, the total specific energy is comprised of a chip-formation energy and the specific energy required for sliding and ploughing [173]. The dominant force in the contact occurs in a normal direction and depends on hydrostatic pressure (vibration); the cutting speed hence predominantly depends on the impact velocity of media. In a drag finishing process, a workpiece is clamped to a rotating carrier in a barrel and submerged into a mixture of abrasive media and liquid compound. Malkkora et al. [175] recently developed a model that enables a simulation of abrasive media flow, considered as a homogeneous and continuous media around a workpiece, as well as its interaction with a workpiece. The numerical modelling approach was based on the Arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian formulation, allowing calculation of process mechanics (e.g., sliding velocity, normal and shear stresses) and to correlate these fundamental parameters to surface roughness. paper_id: Xia et al. 2024 - Study on Microstructure and Thermal Cracking Sensitivi ... 718 Composites Made by Two-Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing by Current
training_text: To study the effect of different heat inputs on the microstructure of the same composite material (VInconel 718: VTi6Al4V=2:1), the metallographic morphology of the samples was observed under different deposition currents using an optical microscope. Figure 4 displays the optical microscopy characterization for each deposition current. Figure 4a shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 35 A, with the Ti6Al4V/Inconel 718 composite in the upper part and the Inconel 718 layer in the lower part. The upper section is predominantly composed of columnar crystals, intermingled with some long black bars among the branches of the columnar crystals. In the WAM process, the solid–liquid interface gradually advances into the liquid phase region. During this advancement, the solute undergoes redistribution, resulting in a phenomenon of component supercooling within a certain distance. This instability of the flat solid–liquid interface ultimately leads to the formation of columnar crystals. As the liquid phase region is influenced by solute redistribution, solute aggregation occurs, which is manifested as microscopic segregation [27]. From the Figure 4a, it can be observed that tiny secondary dendrites are present on the sides of the columnar crystals, with an average distance of 5.16 μm between these secondary dendrites. With the increase in the deposition current, the columnar crystals in the deposited layer gradually undergo differentiation. Figure 4b shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 40 A. From the Figure 4b, it can be observed that some of the grains are arranged in an orderly manner, while a discontinuous black phase is present between the grains. In addition, long straight columnar crystals can be observed in the Figure 4b, which is formed due to the instability of the solid–liquid interface resulting from the supercooling of the composition. Under conditions of rapid cooling, columnar crystals are formed more readily. In comparison to Figure 4a, when the deposition current is 40 A, the heat input increases, leading to a longer temperature residence time on the workpiece under the same heat dissipation conditions. As a result, the cooling rate becomes relatively slower. At the microscopic level, the number of columnar crystals decreases, with some larger columnar crystals gradually transforming into smaller grains, leading to an increase in the spacing between columnar crystals. As some of the heat is conducted in the direction of the deposited additive, a negative temperature gradient develops in the liquid phase, perpendicular to the crystal axis. This results in the formation of a secondary crystal axis along the primary crystal axis [27]. The presence of secondary dendrites can be observed in the Figure 4b, with the average distance between the secondary dendrites measuring 6.38 μm. Figure 4. Optical microscope characterization of samples under different deposition currents: (a) 35 A, (b) 40 A, (c) 45 A, and (d) 50 A. Travel speed: 0.9 mm/s. Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

training_text: The as-built microstructures consisted of ferrite with grain boundary allotriomorph austenite and Widmanstätten austenite with varying amounts of secondary austenite or chromium nitrides depending on alloy composition, position in the build, geometry, and process parameters. Figure 2 is not representative for all microstructures but shows most of the microstructural constituents encountered in the as-built microstructures. The as-built 2509 super duplex material contained small amounts of sigma phase in the upper/warmer sections of the part, see Figure 4. Note how the combination of different composition, higher heat input, and heat accumulation in the upper section of the 2509 part has led to a considerably higher austenite fraction. In addition, secondary austenite and chromium nitrides have been completely suppressed, with all austenite being either grain boundary allotriomorph or Widmanstätten austenite. Figure 5 shows high-resolution stitched images from the top of as-built 2205 and 2509 specimens showing mainly grain boundary allotriomorph and Widmanstätten austenite in the top layer. These figures present how the austenite formation is impacted by reheating from subsequent layers, with heavy precipitation and growth of austenite in the reheated material. They also show how the alloy composition heavily influences the austenite morphology, with Widmanstätten austenite dominating in the 2509 specimen due to the higher nickel content enabling austenite to form at higher temperatures. The EDX analysis of these inclusions (Figure 10b,c) show the presence of Al and O, indicating that they are probably alumina. Interestingly, these inclusions were not initially detected through SEM imaging of the powder. As aluminum exhibits a significantly higher affinity for oxygen compared with other alloying elements, the presence of aluminum oxides may result from a small oxygen fraction within the powder or the atmosphere of the laser chamber. training_text: Safarzade et al. [50] examined the microstructure of Inconel 625 walls made using the DED-Wire Arc technique before and after heat treatment. Using an electric furnace, the solution heat treatment was carried out for six hours at a temperature of 1100 °C. Afterwards, the material was quickly cooled by immersing it in water. The alloy structure exhibited a micro structure featuring a dendritic phase primarily composed of a solid solution rich in nickel. Additionally, it showcased (Nb, Ti) C carbides, Laves phases, and secondary Ni3Nb phases. During the solution heat treatment, the Laves and Ni3Nb phases underwent disintegration, resulting in the replacement of dendrites with massive columnar grains. After subjecting the material to a heat treatment process that promotes ageing, a noticeable change occurred. This change involved the appearance of M23C6 carbides at the boundaries between the grains of the material, as well as the creation of γ' precipitates at the nanoscale. training_text: SEM images of the surface of HT LPBF-fabricated (a, c) and HT wrought 440C (b, d) samples after corrosion testing LPBF-fabricated 440C sample. This visual evidence aligns with the quantitative electrochemical data, conclusively demonstrating the enhanced corrosion resistance of HT LPBF-fabricated 440C stainless steel compared to its wrought counterpart. This superior performance highlights the potential of additive manufacturing to produce AISI 440C components with improved corrosion resistance, offering a compelling advantage over traditional manufacturing techniques. The findings of this study are consistent with previous reports regarding the absence of martensite in as-LPBF-fabricated 440C steel and its associated undesirable properties [28–30]. However, this work presents a systematic investigation into the mechanisms underlying the absence of martensite, which has not been explored previously. The results reveal that a high solute concentration in the austenite parent phase leads to a significantly reduced Ms temperature, without the formation of a substantial amount of carbides, as observed in wrought samples following heat treatment. These findings underscore the critical importance of applying a full heat treatment to LPBF-fabricated 440C steel to promote martensitic transformation and achieve desirable properties. Looking ahead, compositional modifications aimed at reducing the solute content in austenite and increasing the Ms temperature may provide a more efficient pathway to martensitic transformation, thereby minimising the need for extensive post-processing. training_text: The scanning electron micrographs in Figure 5 contrast the microstructure of the specimens. It is worth noting that the resultant solidified microstructures are very similar. The solidification structure is that of columnar grains containing colonies of submicrometric cells separated by low angle grain boundaries. These columnar grains arose due to partial remelting of the previous consolidated layers, as they allowed epitaxial growth. Therefore, this epitaxial growth from the parent grains encouraged the elongation of the columnar grains, which then resulted in a highly textured columnar microstructure, as confirmed later by the electron backscatter diffraction analysis. From the shown plane of view, microstructural features of periodically layer bands are common in L-PBF specimens [31–36]. Accordingly, the behaviour of the layer bands observed in Figure 5 resulted from reheat and remelt influence by the consecutive layer deposition. In summary, these layer bands were weak barriers to prevent columnar grain size growth. However, as observed from the high magnification inset micrographs in Figure 5, layer bands did effectively break the cellular structures into small colonies. Consequently, neighbouring colonies of cells grew rather misoriented to each other in response to the influence of the layer bands to the local maximum heat flux direction. Therefore, this randomised orientation of the colonies contrasted with the columnar grains anisotropy. The benefit of this is that such subgrain features could result in strengthening and toughening effects by impeding dislocation movement and altering the course of fracture and propagation paths. training_text: presents the analysis of the fracture surfaces for both the as-printed and HT700 specimens. Fracture models mainly exhibit transgranular fracture characteristics (Fig. 13a, b, c and d). The SEM image show crater fractures due to microcrack coalescence, leading to brittle failure as depicted in Fig. 13b. Cleavage facets and shallow dimples indicate both brittle and limited ductile fracture. Stair-like and layered fractures develop along grain boundaries, influenced by ductile dimples and intergranular cracking. The tensile stress direction is perpendicular to columnar grain boundaries, causing some grain extrusion at the necking location. The continuous \( \alpha \)-Ti around \( \beta \) grains restricts plastic deformation, increasing stress concentration at \( \beta \) grain boundaries. This stress concentration promotes void nucleation and intergranular fracture along the \( \alpha/ \beta \) interface. The HT700 sample primarily shows ductile fracture with large dimples, though some cleavage fractures remain (Fig. 13d). The fracture surface appears relatively flat with randomly distributed fractures. Heat treatment transforms the microstructure from martensitic \( \alpha' \) to lamellar \( \alpha + \beta \), improving ductility and tensile properties. Uniform transgranular fractures with pronounced dimples are evident in the HT700 sample as depicted in Fig. 13(d) (Ref 65). The mean microhardness of the as-deposited was measured at 400 ± 5 VHN, whereas the HT700 exhibited a microhardness of 451 ± 13 VHN. Consequently, the microhardness measured for the HT700 surpassed that of the as-received sample. The observed increase can be attributed to the transformation of twin boundaries and dislocations within \( \alpha' \) into the more refined \( \alpha \) phase (Ref 51). Furthermore, this enhancement in hardness can be attributed to the formation of \( Ti_3Al \) in the HT700 specimen because it acts as a barrier to dislocation motion and thereby enhancing strength. The formation of \( Ti_3Al \) results in an unusual increase in the strength of the titanium alloy (Ref 66). Scale bar: 20 µm µm.

training_text: Further, Fig. 7 represents the microstructural evolution in the case of multilayer deposition of ten layers of IN625 through DED under the no vibration condition and under two extreme vibration frequencies of 33 and 28 kHz. Figures 7(a) and 7(b) shows the microstructure of the deposited layers at the bottom and middle zones of the total deposition, respectively, under the no vibration condition. It shows long columnar grains at the bottom layers whereas shorter grains at the middle layers. However, the grain boundaries of the shorter grains are found to be interconnected. Similarly, Figs. 7(c) and 7(d) shows the microstructures for deposition at a 33 kHz frequency and Figs. 7(e) and 7(f) for samples deposited at a 28 kHz frequency. The microstructural changes observed because of the implementation of vibration in the case of multilayer deposition are similar to that observed for the single-layer pre-placed deposition. The higher vibration amplitude (i.e., at a lower frequency of 28 kHz) shows complete conversion of columnar grains to discrete equiaxed grains, as can be seen in Figs. 7(e) and 7(f). Furthermore, similar observations are obtained irrespective of the number of deposited layers. Puga et al. also reported the fragmentation of the Laves phase into small pieces due to the application of ultrasound as it generates high-intensity shock energy. The above observation also indicates the significance of vibration amplitude in the case of the microstructural changes, as the amplitude controls the strength of the acoustic shock waves generated due to vibration. training_text: A synergistic balance between strength and ductility for both regions is desired in HT3, where CoCrMo experiences solution heat treatment and extended aging at the expense of some grain coarsening in the maraging steel region. The microstructure in Figure 10 shows a continuous interface in HT3, avoiding the inconsistent lath formation in HT2 and the prominent lath growth in HT1. The maraging steel region in Figure 10(b) and (d) lost cellular features and traces of epitaxial growth since the initial heat treatment stages induced extensive homogenisation. Considering that the ε-phase transition and precipitate dissolution temperatures for CoCrMo were found at ~970°C and ~1140°C, respectively [45], all treatment combinations effectively removed the melt tracks within the maraging steel region. The focus of HT3, however, is on altering the ε-phase transformation mechanism in CoCrMo. Regions highlighted in red in Figure 10(c) showcase consistent, parallel ε-phase bands that are constrained within grains and previous melt pool boundaries. The added solution treatment step preserves the previous γ grain boundaries in the succeeding γ-ε transformation. The presence of some equiaxed regions that include grains free of striations and containing sharp edges can also be observed. Figure 10(e) displays coarse precipitates that are exclusively formed in grain boundaries, which are identified as carbide precipitates through EDS. Unlike HT2, the matrix now contains round and elongated precipitates aligned in a parallel manner. These precipitates trace the observed ε-hcp bands, implying that rearrangement occurred after a longer aging time. The melt pool morphology and refined microstructure in the as-built samples disappeared. paper_id: Gurol et al. 2024 - Fabrication and Characterization of Wire Arc Additively Manufactured Ferritic-Austenitic Bimetallic Structure
training_text: Optical and SEM micrographs showing LCS side (a, b) and SS316L side (c, d) acicular, Widmanstatten, polygonal, and grain boundary through various locations of the building direction (especially at the first and the last layers due to differences in cooling rate). However, the general microstructure at the middle region of the LCS side was found to be consisting polygonal ferrite (PF) with a small amount of pearlite at the grain boundaries due to continuous recrystallization by successive layers, as seen in Fig. 4a, b. On the other hand, the bottom regions of the bimetallic wall correspond to the SS 316L region (Fig. 4c, d). The stainless-steel alloys solidify in one of four possible ways: mode A—single-phase austenite, mode AF—austenite with secondary ferrite, mode FA—primary ferrite with secondary austenite, and mode F—single-phase Ferrite [42]. In this way, it is possible to predict the final microstructure and solidification mode of the austenitic stainless steel using chromium to nickel equivalent ratio \( \mathrm{Cr}_{eq}/\mathrm{Ni}_{eq} \) [43]. The SS 316L wire used in this study had a \( \mathrm{Cr}_{eq}/\mathrm{Ni}_{eq} \) ratio of 1.62, which considering Schaeffler’s diagram, corresponds to a ferritic-austenitic (FA) solidification mode: The δ-ferrite initially formed from the liquid phase via becoming the primary phase. Due to the rapid cooling, the austenite phases grow and gradually replace the primary ferrite phase [44]. In agreement with this finding, the as-built condition was characterized by δ-ferrite dendrites (dark regions) oriented perpendicular to the deposition direction in an austenitic (bright regions) matrix. The amount of δ-ferrite at the bottom, middle, and top regions of the SS 316L side was measured at five different points for each region using a ferrite scope to reveal the variation in the amount of ferrite along the WAAM wall. The middle region was found as about 5.2 ± 1.1 whereas the root and top were 6.2 ± 0.5 and 5.4 ± 0.3%, respectively. The slight increase in the amount of δ-ferrite at the bottom layers compared to middle and top regions can be explained by the higher cooling rates, which prevent austenite formation within the primary ferrite [45]. As reported in previous studies [46, 47], various δ-ferrite can form depending on the welding parameters. In this study, the mid-section of any specific SS 316L layers exhibited mostly skeletal-type ferrite in the non-remelted area (Fig. 4c). However, several types of ferrite morphologies namely skeletal, lathy, and columnar were obtained through the layer transitions, indicating microstructural heterogeneity. As seen in Fig. 5a, b, the fine columnar structure of δ-ferrites perpendicular to the deposition direction was found adjacent to the fusion line in the building direction (Layer n + 1) whereas skeletal and lathy ferrite morphologies were obtained adjacent to the fusion line just below the previous layer (Layer n) due to solidification rate as reported in previous studies [48, 49]. Scale bar: 100 µm µm.

training_text: Layer development; longitudinal cross section in the upright-built sample system with ytterbium-doped (Yb:YAG) fiber laser source has been used to manufacture a convenient number of cylinders (12 mm diameter, 90 mm height); an F-theta lens is used to focus and deflect the laser beam over the working area. Flat-, 45°-, and upright-built samples have been produced (Fig. 1) in 99.4% pure argon inert atmosphere; supporting structures have been required on downward facing surfaces, depending on the sloping angle with the building direction, hence for flat- and 45°-built samples. Operating laser power, speed, and hatching strategies are based on preliminary trials and are aimed to optimize LPBF and full dense structure (Table 1). A number of quality jobs have been performed to assess and fine-tune the beam offset and the scaling factor to address possible dimensional shrinkage. Namely, a scanning pattern with 67° rotation of the scanning direction between consecutive 20-μm-thick layers has been set to improve densification. To the concurrent purpose of stress relieving and ductility improvement [9], heat treatment as per AMS 5664 standard (i.e., solution annealing at 1065 °C for 1 h, aging at 760 °C for 10 h, cooling to 650 °C, and holding for 8 h in argon inert atmosphere) has been eventually conducted before removal of the parts from the building plate, as suggested by the powder manufacturer [32]. The typical cleavage river pattern in Fig. 12b indicates brittle fracture mode. Meanwhile, the dimples in Fig. 12c also confirm the occurrence of plastic deformation and ductile fracture. Some micro-cracks can be observed at the fracture surface, as shown in Fig. 12d. The initiation and propagation of these micro-cracks accelerated the failure of the tensile specimen, thereby limiting the increase in elongation. The deformation temperature has been shown to have a significant effect on the deformation mode of NiTi alloys due to the thermoelastic martensitic transformation [42]. The formation of stress-induced martensite upon loading and the reversible transformation upon unloading occurs only at temperatures above \( A_f \), contributing to the superelasticity. Thereby, to better reflect the superelastic behavior of the current WAAM NiTiTa alloys, cyclic tensile tests were carried out at 100 °C (above \( A_f \)), and the results are presented in Fig. 13. The WAAM NiTiTa sample shows obvious superelasticity during the loading-unloading process, as shown in Fig. 14a. The critical stress (\( \sigma_c \)) for stress-induced martensitic transformation is about 380 MPa at 100 °C, while at room temperature it decreases to 252 MPa. This is due to the increased thermodynamic resistance for the martensitic transformation, which is a function of temperature as expressed by the Clausius-Clapeyron relation [43]. The calculated recovery ratio as a function of the cycle times is shown in Fig. 13b. The reversible strain in the first cycle is about 1.8 %, and the corresponding recovery ratio (ratio of recoverable strain to total imposed strain) is 91.5 %. With the increase of the number of cycles, the recovery ratio gradually reduced and then maintained at nearly 86.8 % after 10 loading-unloading cycles. The reduced recovery ratio is due to the gradual accumulation of defects and retained martensite, which promotes the decrease of transformation strain and the increase of the volume fraction of untransformed austenite within the shear bands during cycling tests [44]. During the manufacturing process, certain powder particles were melted to form molten pools. As the laser beam moved and scanned, the molten pools rapidly solidified and connected with adjacent molten pools. Figure 4(a) displays a characteristic semicircular fish scale pattern, the average width of these features is 70 μm, and the average depth is 85 μm, corresponding proportionally to the size of the melt pool. While Fig. 4(b) shows a network of interconnected pools. These patterns arose due to the presence of large columnar grains within the molten pool, which grew along the thermal gradient at the boundary of pool. The microstructure characteristics of the molten pool boundary were observed at the square position indicated in Fig. 4(a) using a high-power SEM. These observations are presented in Figure 4(c) and (d). As shown in Fig. 4(c), the side-branching columnar dendrites, indicated by the blue arrows, can be observed. These dendrites represent the lateral growth of columnar crystals, with the molten pool structure exhibiting a distinct columnar pattern in the region marked by a black circle A. However, the other molten pool structure exhibits a distinct honeycomb pattern in the region marked by a circle B. This can be attributed to the rapid directional solidification process involved in laser melting of the metal powder (Ref 20). The varying depth of the molten pool leads to changes in the direction of grain growth. Studies by Andreau et al. (Ref 21) showed that deeper molten pools with higher thermal gradients resulted in grain growth in all directions, while shallower molten pools primarily underwent epitaxial growth. Additionally, the repeated melting and deposition of solidified layers, the transition from cellular dendritic to columnar solidification occurred as the rate of cooling during the phase transition increased (Ref 22-24). According to those findings available in the literature, the widely observed cellular structure was characterized by a high dislocation density and the precipitation of trace elements at boundaries. This phenomenon arose due to mechanical constraints imposed by the substrate on thermal expansion of the deposited material during the printing process (Ref 3). Consequently, it promoted plastic deformation and generated high dislocation densities, leading to formation of dislocation clouds at grain boundaries. It was suggested that such cellular structure significantly impacted the mechanical properties of printed parts, particularly in enhancing yield strength (Ref 25-27). These findings were further supported by experimental results of Wang et al. (Ref 11). training_text: An in-depth examination of the pin’s worn surface was performed to better understand the wear mechanisms active under these specific test conditions. The SEM images in Figs. 16, 17, 18, and 19 illustrate the worn pin surfaces of the WAAMed LCS sample at different load and speed settings. Figure 16 provides an SEM image of the wear test conducted on the WAAMed LCS sample. Figure 17 shows the EDS mapping for a sample subjected to a load of 3.5 kg at a rotational speed of 450 rpm, highlighting key elements detected on the surface. The primary elements identified in the EDS analysis include Fe, Mn, Si, P, O, and C. Figure 18 displays the SEM pictures of the WAAMed 316LSi SS samples under varying conditions. The EDS mapping scan performed on the locally magnified region of the WAAMed 316LSi stainless steel sample, subjected to a 3.5-kg load at a rotation speed of 450 rpm, is presented in Figure 19. The analysis identified the main elements present in the EDS spectrum, including Fe, Ni, Cr, S, Mn, Si, Cu, Mo, and O. The figure demonstrates the detection of Cr and Mo in the ferrite, while the austenite matrix primarily concentrates Ni. Cr and Mo are components that enhance the production of ferrite, while Ni is a constituent that promotes austenitic formation. Figure 16 and 18 show the worn surfaces characterized by parallel scratches and grooves that align with the direction of sliding. Material removal occurs as fragments and debris due to the interaction between the opposing surface and the sliding surface (refer to Fig. 16b and 18b). Additionally, plow marks are visible on the surface, suggesting that material has shifted in the direction of sliding. These surface features suggest that wear is primarily driven by a combination of adhesion and abrasion. Furthermore, the worn surfaces exhibited the presence of white layers and scattered debris [48, 49]. Fig. 16 SEM images of worn surfaces of WAAMed LCS under varying conditions The surface that experienced the most significant wear (as seen in Fig. 16c-d) had prominent grooves, plastic deformation, and delamination. Delamination is responsible for the production of fractures that originate from subsurface stress concentrations as a result of repetitive loading at different speeds (see Fig. 18c-d). As these fissures extend to the surface, they result in crater formation and material detachment in the form of flakes or laminar fragments (refer to Fig. 16b). Wear debris analysis verifies material removal as coarser laminates (Fig. 18c). The surface showed indications of plastic deformation, including material displacement, flow patterns, reshaping, and groove formation (refer to Fig. 16d). High loads during sliding generate significant frictional heat, which contributes to this plastic deformation. Frictional heat causes the pin surface to become more pliable and prone to deformation due to its high temperature [50]. The three main forms of wear that occur under situations of maximum stress are severe adhesion, abrasion, and delamination. Figure 16, 17, 18, and 19 shows that oxidation occurred during the sliding process, as evidenced by the white strata (confirmed with oxygen content in element analysis) and debris, which were composed primarily of oxides. The intense heat produced by friction during high-speed sliding leads to oxidation. This leads to the scattering of oxidized particles across the contact area, generating layers of oxide [51]. The reduction in direct metallic contact between the counter surface and the pin surface facilitated by these oxide layers results in a reduced rate of wear. These oxide layers primarily contribute to the decreased wear rate and the safeguarding of the pin surface. Under a higher load, the wear resistance of WAAMed LCS and WAAMed 316L ASS samples is significantly influenced, resulting in a more substantial amount of material being removed. These findings suggest that the load plays a more significant role in affecting the wear resistance of WAAMed LCS and 316L SS samples than the speed. The effect of speed on the durability of both WAAMed LCS and 316L SS was somewhat less pronounced than that of load, likely due to the limited speed range applied in this study. The heat of friction at higher load and speed levels mostly controls the amount of material removed by wear at ambient temperature [52]. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

training_text: The as-built microstructures consisted of ferrite with grain boundary allotriomorph austenite and Widmanstätten austenite with varying amounts of secondary austenite or chromium nitrides depending on alloy composition, position in the build, geometry, and process parameters. Figure 2 shows an example of as-built 2205 microstructure close to the substrate with Figure 3 presenting a close-up of the fine nitride precipitation. Figure 2 is not representative for all microstructures but shows most of the microstructural constituents encountered in the as-built microstructures. The as-built 2509 super duplex material contained small amounts of sigma phase in the upper/warmer sections of the part, see Figure 4. Note how the combination of different composition, higher heat input, and heat accumulation in the upper section of the 2509 part has led to a considerably higher austenite fraction. In addition, secondary austenite and chromium nitrides have been completely suppressed, with all austenite being either grain boundary allotriomorph or Widmanstätten austenite. Figure 5 shows high-resolution stitched images from the top of as-built 2205 and 2509 specimens showing mainly grain boundary allotriomorph and Widmanstätten austenite in the top layer. These figures present how the austenite formation is impacted by reheating from subsequent layers, with heavy precipitation and growth of austenite in the reheated material. They also show how the alloy composition heavily influences the austenite morphology, with Widmanstätten austenite dominating in the 2509 specimen due to the higher nickel content enabling austenite to form at higher temperatures. In the 2205 specimen, grain boundary allotriomorph and secondary austenite are the main austenite constituents, and chromium nitrides have precipitated inside the ferrite grains in the top layer alongside secondary austenite. A thin-walled cylinder was compared to a massive 32 × 32 × 33 mm cube to assess the impact of part geometry on the as-built microstructure. The lower section of the thin-walled 2205 cylinder experienced cooling rates sufficiently high to produce limited primary austenite. Where the reheating from the subsequent layer was low, chromium nitrides precipitated inside the ferrite grains as indicated by the white-highlighted field in Figure 6. training_text: In the un-peened Ti6242 control sample, the \( \alpha + \beta \) transformation microstructure consisted of fine ‘basketweave’ lamellar \( \alpha \) separated by very thin nanoscale retained \( \beta \) films, which is shown in the SEM micrographs in Figure 6. However, the transformation structure differed between the top of the deposit (Figure 6b) where the microstructure was produced by only cooling through the \( \beta \) transus (\( T_\beta \)), to the mid-bulk of a wall (Figure 6(d)) that had also experienced several reheating cycles below \( T_\beta \). Near the top of the wall, the as-transformed material consisted of a basketweave microstructure of fine, ~ 0.6 \( \mu \)m-thickness \( \alpha \) lamellae. A few small pockets of very fine \( \alpha \) laths (see inset in Figure 6(b)) of ~ 0.2 \( \mu \)m thickness were also found in some regions. However, after experiencing thermal cycling at temperatures below the \( \beta \) transus, the transformation structure in the lower, steady-state region of the wall had noticeably coarsened to give a slightly larger average inter-lamellar spacing of ~ 0.7 \( \mu \)m, and the much finer \( \alpha \) was no longer seen. It should be noted that the region shown in Figure 6(d) was taken avoiding the etched lines corresponding to the optically observable HAZ bands, but the transformation structure varied systematically across each layer in ND, as will be discussed farther below (Figures 7, 8). Small particles were also found throughout the transformed \( \alpha \) microstructure, which are shown in the secondary electron micrograph in Figure 6(c). These particles were ~1 \( \mu \)m in size and SEM–EDS analysis revealed that they contained a significant amount of silicon, and therefore could be identified as titanium silicides.[36,44,47] In order to quantify the heterogeneity seen in the \( \alpha \) inter-lamellae spacing throughout the full Ti6242 WAAM build, large SEM backscatter image tile maps (Section II–B) were automatically acquired along the build direction, up the wall centre line, and batch analysed using bespoke software.[48] A plot of the average (2D) inter-lamellar spacing measured by this method, with build height, is shown for the un-peened sample in Figure 7 from the area highlighted in the optical macrograph. For the bulk of the wall, the inter-lamellar spacing in Figure 7 exhibited a ‘sawtooth’ wave profile with a pitch equivalent to the layer height. At the top of the wall (> 16 mm in Figure 7), for the last 4 layers, where the material was fully reheated into the \( \beta \)-phase field during each pass of the heat source and only transformed during cooling, the \( \alpha \) inter-lamellar spacing showed no systematic variance across the added layers (other than from systematic noise). The sawtooth wave pattern seen in the bulk, and the lack thereof in the fully \( \beta \)-annealed top of the wall, are very similar to the behaviour reported formerly for similar Ti64 WAAM builds, which is discussed at length in Reference 5. It can also be noted that in the older Ti64 WAAM build analysed previously, there was a gradual increase in \( \alpha \) inter-lamellar spacing towards the bottom of the wall due to the heat accumulation experienced during deposition, which was a result of the build temperature not being actively monitored and used to control the heat-source return time. Nevertheless, from the data in Figure 7 it is still evident that the whole steady-state lower part of the wall, where the HAZ band sawtooth wave pattern is seen, had a coarser \( \alpha \) lamellar spacing on average than the top ~4 layers of the build that did not experience reheating below \( T_\beta \), after cooling from the \( \beta \) phase field. training_text: Euler maps and pole figures of LPBF and EBM materials are reported in Fig. 1 along and perpendicular to the build direction. V-shaped elongated grains along the build direction and equiaxed grains perpendicular to the build direction of about 60 ± 24 μm were measured for the LPBF specimen after heat treatment. This microstructure is consistent with the grain structure reported after annealing according to the standard H282 heat treatment.9,25 For the EBM alloy, elongated and equiaxed grains of about 110 ± 44 μm were measured along and perpendicular to the building direction. For both AM alloys, the pole figures in Fig. 1 revealed a textured microstructure along the [001] axis. In addition, the SEM images in Fig. 1c highlighted the absence of significant defects in the LPBF alloy with a few carbides along grain boundaries and a γ′ precipitate size of 45 ± 10 nm. As reported by Unocic et al.,11 for the as printed EBM H282, small voids were observed in the heat-treated EBM H282 with a few carbides in the grains and at grain boundaries and a γ′ size of 15 to 20 nm. Finally, much larger equiaxed grains 700 ± 210 μm in size were measured for the cast alloy. Isothermal Oxidation Behavior ThermoGravimetric Analysis (TGA) data acquired during isothermal oxidation at 800 °C in dry air for 72 h is reported in Fig. 2. Higher mass gains were observed for the AM alloys than for the cast material. After the transient oxidation period that lasted 5 h, parabolic oxidation behavior was observed (Fig. 2b). Oxidation rate constants were calculated using Eq. (1) confirming three to four times lower oxidation rates for the cast alloy compared to the LPBF and EBM materials, with the LPBF coupon exhibiting the fastest oxidation rate (Fig. 2b) with Δm mass change of the specimen (mg), a surface area of the specimen (mg cm⁻²), t time (h) and k_p oxidation rate constant (mg² cm⁻⁴·h⁻¹). Material: Ni Cr Fe Co Mo Nb Al Ti Si Mn C S Cast 58. Scale bar: 20 µm µm.

The results are shown in Figure 6. Table 4 lists the compositional analysis of the points (A~G) marked in Figure 6. Combined with the EDS point analysis in Table 4, the matrix (marked with A) corresponds to the NiTi phase with 0.87 at.% Ta solid solution, while the precipitate with a (Ti + Ta)/Ni ratio of 1.73 is highly likely to be the (Ti, Ta)2Ni phase. Besides the oval (Ti, Ta)2Ni phase (marked with H), a large number of irregular white precipitates (marked with G) appeared at the grain boundaries, as shown in Figure 6c. training_text: Detailed SEM analysis was carried out for the optimum sample (i.e., Sample #6) in the as-built and heat-treated conditions. Figure 5 shows the microstructure of the optimum as-built sample at different locations. In the CuCrZr side (shown in Figure 5a–c), solid-solution Cr elements with a diameter ranging from 0.4 to 1 μm were precipitated due to the low cooling rate during the deposition. This microstructure is specific to the LP-DED process while no or slight Cr precipitation was observed during the L-PBF of this alloy.[41] Figure 4. The SEM micrographs from the interface of IN718 and CuCrZr produced using different process parameters. Figure 5d–f show the interface between CuCrZr and IN718. As observed in the previous section, the interface revealed an uneven fusion line caused by the Marangoni convection of IN718 to the CuCrZr side. Figure 5e shows the Cr element was precipitated within the grain boundaries of CuCrZr, which resulted from prolonged heating of this region. The morphology of IN718 within the fusion zone consists of dendritic trees and spherical regions at a wide range of dimensions shown in Figure 5f. The dendritic trees were usually connected to the base IN718 material and elongated throughout the heat dissipation direction. Nevertheless, excessive thermal stress can cause free dendrite formation, as shown in Figure 5f. The origin of these structures is mainly the difference between the cooling rates and the solidification temperature of the two materials.[42] This usually happens when the cooling rate is higher than \(10^4\) K s\(^{-1}\) causing undercooling of the melted material before nucleation.[43] Lower solidification temperature for CuCrZr (i.e., 1065–1080 °C) allowed IN718 to grow within the liquid copper matrix and form the dendritic trees. [111]. Instead of increasing the current during the short circuit phase, the current is dropped, extinguishing the arc and limiting the amount of thermal energy transferred to the deposit [174]. The electrode is then retracted, pinching the molten material, depositing it into the melt pool. The current is then increased to reignite the arc and the process repeats [175]. The decrease in thermal energy transfer reduces the heat accumulation in multi-layer deposits, which can be characterized by the finer grain structures when compared to continuous welding techniques [111, 176]. This can be seen in Figure 5 [177], where the lower heat input and heat accumulation is characterized by the finer grain structure. Furthermore, the pulsing of the arc has been shown to sever dendrite arms, increasing the heterogeneous nucleation sites, further refining the microstructure [115, 132]. It also drastically reduces the dilution of previously deposited material, reducing the amount of material being melted with each pass and possibly reducing the number of thermal cycles [175, 178]. Thus these reasons make CMT the most viable option for wire and arc additive manufacturing (WAAM). It should be noted that although there is a reduction in heat input and thermal cycles compared to continuous welding, WAAM deposits still suffer from heat accumulation, cracking, porosity, delamination and anisotropic microstructures [179]. The first study of using GMAW for AM was conducted by Dickens et al., who tried to expand the realm of 3D welding from large pressure vessels, to more complex geometries [180]. Gas Tungsten Arc Welding is similar to the GMAW process, but the arc is struck between a non-consumable tungsten electrode and the workpiece. A filler metal can be fed manually or mechanically into the arc, where it melts and is deposited onto the substrate. training_text: Effect of TiB2 content on (a) wear, and (b) coefficient of friction of TiB/Ti-6Al-4V composite, and wear morphology of TiB/Ti-6Al-4V composite, (c) Ti-6Al-4V, and Ti-6Al-4V with (d) 0.1 wt.% TiB2, (e) 0.75 wt.% TiB2, and (f) 1.0 wt.% TiB2. wear loss of the pure Ti-6Al-4V samples is approximately 40% more than that of the 1.0-wt.% TiB2 sample. This indicates that the in situ-formed TiB particles provide significant wear resistance compared to the unreinforced Ti-6Al-4V alloy. The use of submicron-sized TiB2 for the formation of Ti matrix composite results in nano-sized in situ-formed TiB particles which are strongly bonded with the matrix and hence resist detachment during the wear test. This is also confirmed by the coefficients of friction (COFs) as shown in Fig. 11b. There is only a slight decrease in the COFs, which indicates that the TiB particles are firmly bonded. Also, the in situ-formed nano-TiB particles act as load-bearing members in general MMCs and inhibit the plastic deformation of the Ti matrix. The formation of the network of hard TiB whiskers in the Ti matrix, as shown in Fig. 4, resists deformation by acting as a barrier wall for sliding motion. The increase in temperature causes the softening of the Ti-6Al-4V matrix and leads to poor high-temperature wear properties. However, the homogeneously dispersed nano-TiB whiskers provide a remarkable improvement in the high-temperature wear properties.40 The increase in the stiffness of the material and the high hardness due to the presence of TiB whiskers contribute to the reduced wear of the TiB2-added samples.
