paper_id: Carrozza et al. 2022 - An investigation on the effect of different multi ... texture and mechanical properties of the DED-produced Ti-6Al-4V alloy
training_text: Moreover, the different heat treatment conditions induced significant microstructural variations, as visible in Fig. 3. The AB specimens provided a largely α’ martensitic microstructure. This feature is related to the very fast heating/cooling cycles, typical of the DED process. Conversely, the microstructural features found in the heat-treated samples were highly dependent on the cooling mean adopted. Since most transformations occurring upon cooling from the β field are diffusional (except β → α’), the cooling mean is one of the most important heat treatment-related parameter in order to control the final microstructure of a given titanium component [3,4,28]. The samples in the FC condition underwent the slowest cooling rate, approximately 1–2 °C/min, which resulted in a completely lamellar α + β microstructure in which α colonies were easily recognizable (Fig. 3b). Moreover, thick α layers in correspondence of the prior-β grain boundaries (dGB) were visible throughout the whole cross-section. Similarly, the specimens in the AC condition were characterized by fine α laths surrounded by a thin layer of β phase. Although, no clear colonies were detected, unlike in the previous case. In fact, a Widmanstätten morphology was recognized by the typical ±30°/60° angles between neighbor lamellae, typical of intermediate cooling rates (≈ 10 °C/min) [3,4]. Oppositely, the specimens in the WQ conditions provided a mainly martensitic microstructure, close to the AB case. However, a relevant number of α laths homogeneously dispersed throughout the whole sample were detected. The formation of such features via water quenching is possible, as the typical cooling rate achieved during water quenching is typically lower than 410 °C/s [29,30]. Nevertheless, the insurgence of a greater amount of α phase and its growth are more likely due to the possible decomposition of the martensite during the agine step of the heat treatment. In fact, the long duration and relatively high temperature facilitate the occurrence of diffusive phenomena, such as the α’ → α + β decomposition. During this transformation, the supersaturated martensite lattice expels the β-stabilizing elements (e.g. V, Mo), thus transforming into α laths and generating a thin β layer around itself [31,32]. In order to confirm the assumptions made during the microstructural analyses of the micrographs and to investigate more in details the phases involved, the XRD patterns of all the samples were gathered and studied, as visible in Fig. 4a. Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: compares the microstructure evolution in the middle section of the fabricated rods under various deposition conditions. This section is analyzed because it corresponds to the gauge length of the tensile sample, directly affecting mechanical properties like strength and ductility. The microstructure predominantly comprises a combination of WF and AF, creating a mixed-phase microstructure. However, their volume fraction varies slightly depending on the deposition condition, as illustrated in Fig. 13. When the coil current and WFS are set at 300 A and 150 mm/min, the resulting microstructure consists of an irregular pattern of ferrite and pearlite, as presented in Fig. 13a. The grains appear irregular or non-uniform arranged, which can be attributed to the unstable nature of metal transfer during deposition. This instability arises because the molten metal droplets do not fall uniformly due to the rotational effect created by the Lorentz force, leading to uneven cooling across the structure [42]. The grains are finer than the other deposition conditions (Figs. 13b, c), primarily due to the slow metal transfer rate associated with low WFS. A slower WFS results in less heat input per unit time, leading to faster cooling and fine grains. On the other hand, when the coil current is increased to 350 A, a significant change in microstructure is observed (Fig. 13b, c), compared to 300 A. An increase in WFS from 225 to 300 mm/min leads to more uniform structure due to more stable molten metal transfer. The optimized WFS and coil current ensure a consistent and controlled deposition process, which minimizes the disturbance caused by the Lorentz force induced by the interaction of the coil current with the magnetic field, which may affect the molten metal flow and solidification process. Since the rate of metal transfer under 350 A coil current is considerably higher than 300 A, the viscosity of the molten pool is higher, causing the cooling rate to decrease and, hence, the formation of coarser pearlite. Furthermore, under the same conditions of 350 A and 300 mm/min, when the gap between the induction coil (bottom) and the molten pool at the top surface is reduced from 25 to 20 mm, a more uniform and coarser pearlite structure is formed (Fig. 13d). This occurs because the reduced coupling distance exposes the top surface of the forming rod to a higher-intensity magnetic field, which maintains the higher rod temperature till the complete rod fabrication. Higher rod temperature for a longer time compared to 25 mm CD provides more time for carbon diffusion, promoting the growth of coarser pearlite layers. 3.2 Mechanical characterization Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: Effects of auxiliary ultrasonic vibration (USV) on the microstructure of the LDED-built (a) Inconel 718 [87], (b) Ti6Al4V [72], (c) Inconel 625 [72], (d) 316 L [83] and (e) Ti/TiB composite [84]. is still a challenge that needs to be resolved. Due to the micro-segregation of Nb and Mo, the Laves phase typically forms in these alloys during solidification, which deteriorates their mechanical properties [91]. To this end, Chen et al. [73] adopted an auxiliary USV in a WAAM-built Inconel 625 alloy. Interestingly, the dissolution of the Nb element is promoted, suggesting that the ultrasound reduces the elemental segregation in the alloy. This may be attributed to a combination of factors; the increased equiaxed growth ahead of the melt pool will result in finer interdendritic structures and therefore smaller regions of interdendritic fluid high in Nb and lower percentages of Laves phase. Additionally, the enhanced mixing promoted by the USV field will also offset the formation of a fluid of different elemental composition ahead of the solidification front. [84] adopted the auxiliary USV in the LDED of Ti–TIB composites and reported that the application of USV promoted the dispersion of TiB whiskers effectively (Fig. 14e). In fact, grain refinement and quasi-continuous network-shaped TiB microstructures were achieved in the Ti/TiB composite with auxiliary USV, as shown in Fig. 14e. Specifically, the COF of the direct-aged condition decreased by 6.66% at 100 °C, 5.76% at 200 °C, 8.33% at 300 °C, and 8.95% at 400 °C compared to their as-built counterparts. During aging, intermetallic precipitates such as Ni3Mo, Ni3Ti, and Fe2Mo form within the martensitic matrix [24,29]. These precipitates strengthen the material by hindering dislocation movement, which enhances the microhardness of the worn surface. The higher microhardness of the direct-aged samples reduces surface deformation and material removal during sliding contact, minimizing interaction and adhesion between the worn surfaces, leading to a lower COF. Conversely, the as-built maraging steel, lacking these strengthening precipitates, has a comparatively softer surface, making it more prone to deformation and resulting in higher COF values. Scale bar: 100 µm µm.

After that, a slight decrease in hardness was observed toward the top layer (390 HV1). This correlates well with the trends indicated by the etching colors in Figure 3. The differences in the maximum material hardness can be attributed to the different cooling rates and in situ preheating temperatures depending on the applied process parameters. Lower laser powers favor a faster cooling due to the smaller melt pool size, thus potentially resulting in a finer grain.[27] Furthermore, the decrease in material hardness along build direction for the highest laser power could be a cause of a sequential overheating. Due to the low thermal mass of the substrate, the excessive energy input will lead to higher in situ preheating temperatures. These promoted in situ temperatures will most likely result in a higher retained austenite content because the transformation to either martensite or bainite is not fully performed. This mechanism is temperature and time dependent and is therefore affected by the different processing times (due to the average weld track width) and the maximum temperatures (due to the energy input). paper_id: Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing – A revolutionary method in AM
training_text: Microstructure and grains distribution greatly affect the mechanical properties of fabricated parts produced through WAAM [140]. Min Qi et al. [141] explained that complex thermal cycling in the manufactured material from AM processes results in columnar coarse grains. Haden et al. [134] performed a wear scar of platinum in Z axis (facing towards test equipment) over the deposited MS, they performed SEM and FIB imaging and observed grain refinement immediately below the wear scar as shown in Fig. 17. Wang et al. [142] utilized H13 as feeder wire for the WAAM process with 4-Axis CNC-assisted MIG welding powder as shown in Fig. 18. They found multiple microstructural formations which was due to local heating histories. Also, the elongation and tensile strength were maximum which was farthest from the substrate. Liu et al. [143] developed an Al based fabricated part through TIG and MIG. They revealed that the GTAW welding of Al part results in higher hardness and strength over the GMAW welds due to the precipitate strengthening and less porosity development. In GTAW weldment, there are large amount of localised plasticity observed, while there is a considerable amount of porosity in GMAW weldments which could figure out the difference in mechanical characteristics between both the kinds. GTAW bonded Al part is mechanically more reliable than GMAW welded one [143,144]. However, cold metal transfer for Al based WAAM improves mechanical characteristics by allowing for better control of porosity formation, controlled metal deposition, and lower heat input. Lower welding heat input results in decreased weld pool temperature as well as fine grain structure, which minimizes H2 trapping and hence the porosity formation [145,146]. With WAAM microstructure and phase transformation is dependent on the materials used, High temperature developed, cooling rate and deposition rate [147]. Defects produced in the process also affect the mechanical properties [140]. To increase the mechanical properties, recent studies concentrated mostly on reducing the defects such as porosity, surface cracking, deformations and gas inclusions by introducing some post-processing techniques. This paper will see the recent post-processing techniques which have been done for the enhancing of mechanical properties of as-fabricated (AF) produced parts. Delamination is usually a visible deficiency which cannot be eliminated by post-processing techniques or heat treatments, but can be avoided by following proper process parameters in order to reduce repeated fluctuated stresses and also by considering the characteristics of deposited alloy [148,149], there are various categories of defects as can be briefly seen in Table 7. Scope of defect in WAAM processes with various metals can be seen in Fig. 19. Material: s GMAW 1400 NAB. Scale bar: 20 µm µm.

The gas porosity is also an indication of interlayer fusion leading to the entrapment of gases during the WAAM process. Course dimples are also an indication of brittle fracture [20]. These features suggest imperfections within the material structure and areas where the material has not adequately fused, potentially leading to compromised mechanical properties. Additionally, the absence of significant temperature fluctuations reduces the formation of new nucleation sites, allowing the columnar grains to grow in the inclined direction. During the high-energy pulses, the molten pool remains active and fluid, which promotes columnar grain growth similar to SP-GMAW. However, during the low-energy pulses, the rapid reduction in temperature results in localized undercooling, enhancing heterogeneous nucleation and promoting the development of cellular grains [48]. training_text: Ductility-dip cracking (DDC) is a cracking resulting from ductility drop of grain boundary at the intermediate temperatures (approximately 0.4–0.7 of liquidus temperature of material) in the Nickel-based superalloys with low fraction precipitates. The mechanism is complicated and sometime is categorized into strain-age cracking or liqation cracking [220]. DDC in fusion-based AM Nickel-based superalloy is referred to the cracking caused by creep like mechanism [226]. They concluded that during the reheating of welded Nickel-base superalloy, grain boundary sliding causes high strain and void coalescence. These voids segregate at the stress concentration sites such as triple point junction of grain boundaries and forms cracking eventually. It was noted that continuous carbide particles are harmful to ductility-dip cracking resistance since the voids near the carbide particles nucleate into the cracking [227]. Since DDC and SAC are only associated with solid phase, these two types of cracking are also referred as solid-state cracking. Fig. 22 presents the typical morphologies of solid-state cracking in AM processed Ni-superalloys [221]. 4.4.2. Residual stress As discussed earlier, although the layer-wise manufacturing manner of the laser-based AM processes allow complex design structures, it may also cause large thermal gradients due to the localized heat input and rapid solidification, which in turn may give rise to large internal stress (IS) induced during the process and consequently the residual stress (RS) at the end of production process generated within the AM components [228]. These internal stress and residual stress causes not only cracking but distortion to fusion-based AM Nickel-based superalloys, which degrades the dimensional precision of AM components. The anisotropic degree of the specimens after cyclic annealing is comparable to that of the equiaxed \( \beta \) grain microstructures fabricated by DED [14, 31]. Figure 13 shows the tensile fracture morphologies of the specimens after cyclic annealing in horizontal and vertical directions. The fibrous zone and shear rupture zone appear in both samples, and the dimples is also similar, which further demonstrates that the mechanical properties are almost isotropic. Although the yield tensile strength (YS) and the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) decrease after cyclic annealing, the EL, especially in horizontal direction, is significantly improved. The main reason for this may be attributed to the globularization of \( \alpha \) phase in prior-\( \beta \) grains and the elimination of grain boundary \( \alpha \) phase (\( \alpha_{GB} \)) between prior-\( \beta \) grains [32]. Dislocation theory can be applied to clarify the difference of the mechanical properties between the as-built and heat-treated specimens. For the as-built specimens, lots of dislocations pile up at the grains boundaries during the tensile test in horizontal direction due to the continuous \( \alpha_{GB} \) between prior-\( \beta \) grains (Fig. 10a), causing a high back stress to block the slip of dislocation. Besides, the pile up of dislocations also leads to a stress concentration triggering crack along the \( \alpha_{GB} \), which is detrimental to the ductility [32]. Therefore, the elimination of \( \alpha_{GB} \) after cyclic annealing (Fig. 10b) avoids the initiation of crack at the \( \beta \) grain boundaries and favors the improvement of ductility in the horizontal direction. On the other hand, the magnitude of elongation is also proportional to the glide distance of dislocations or to the size of \( \alpha \) in the direction of tensile axes. In the specimens after cyclic annealing, the shape of the primary \( \alpha \) is globular (Fig. 10b) and, thus, the slide distance is comparable in the vertical and horizontal tensile axes. In contrast, the shape of the primary \( \alpha \) is lamellar for the as-built specimens (Fig. 3), and the size of \( \alpha \) sections in different tensile directions is diverse, easily contributing to nonuniform dislocation slide and stress concentration in \( \alpha\text{-}\beta \) interfaces. Therefore, the anisotropy of tensile properties of the as-built specimens is higher than that of the cyclic annealing specimens. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

The as-printed body is a porous structure and contains micro-cracks mainly formed between the porosities. From the fracture cross-section (Fig. 8(a)), it can be observed that these cracks can propagate through the structure when the load is applied. The formation of micro-cracks in the sample is attributed to the brittleness of the alumina matrix and the differences in melting points and thermal expansion coefficients of alumina and steel components [51,63]. Due to the weak adhesion between steel and alumina matrix, steel particles were removed during polishing in some areas; these are distinguished in dark circles in the micrograph. It also can be understood from Fig. 7(c) that some of the alumina particles were melted during the printing process. A similar effect was noted on the fracture surface of the bars, as highlighted in Fig. 8(a). Besides, a long crack formed due to thermal gradients during solidification. Fig. 7(d–f) illustrates BSE images of the sintered sample. The images of the as-printed and as-sintered samples show no discernible difference between them. Due to the existence of the steel component in the fabricated composite and considering the steel area being melted at 1370 °C, liquid phase sintering must have occurred during the heat-treatment to achieve full densification. However, the mentioned phenomenon did not happen because of the poor wettability of the steel and alumina, the high interfacial energy between steel and alumina, and the presence of a thin layer of oxide on the surface of the steel, which prevents melted steel from moving between alumina particles [64–66]. From the fracture surface analysis (Fig. 8(c) and (d)), spherical steel particles can still be observed, confirming the stated phenomenon. It is evident from the SEM images of the polished cross-section that the melted metallic particles did not rearrange the alumina particles due to capillary action. On the other hand, it could be noticed that the as-sintered samples have relatively higher densification than the as-printed body. The reason could be associated with the densification of the alumina component during sintering. The onset of sintering temperature for alumina is around 1000 °C. Hence, alumina particles started to densify at this temperature through the solid-state sintering mechanism. training_text: Microstructure and grains distribution greatly affect the mechanical properties of fabricated parts produced through WAAM [140]. Min Qi et al. [141] explained that complex thermal cycling in the manufactured material from AM processes results in columnar coarse grains. Haden et al. [134] performed a wear scar of platinum in Z axis (facing towards test equipment) over the deposited MS, they performed SEM and FIB imaging and observed grain refinement immediately below the wear scar as shown in Fig. 17. Wang et al. [142] utilized H13 as feeder wire for the WAAM process with 4-Axis CNC-assisted MIG welding powder as shown in Fig. 18. They found multiple microstructural formations which was due to local heating histories. Also, the elongation and tensile strength were maximum which was farthest from the substrate. Liu et al. [143] developed an Al based fabricated part through TIG and MIG. They revealed that the GTAW welding of Al part results in higher hardness and strength over the GMAW welds due to the precipitate strengthening and less porosity development. In GTAW weldment, there are large amount of localised plasticity observed, while there is a considerable amount of porosity in GMAW weldments which could figure out the difference in mechanical characteristics between both the kinds. GTAW bonded Al part is mechanically more reliable than GMAW welded one [143,144]. However, cold metal transfer for Al based WAAM improves mechanical characteristics by allowing for better control of porosity formation, controlled metal deposition, and lower heat input. Lower welding heat input results in decreased weld pool temperature as well as fine grain structure, which minimizes H2 trapping and hence the porosity formation [145,146]. With WAAM microstructure and phase transformation is dependent on the materials used, High temperature developed, cooling rate and deposition rate [147]. Defects produced in the process also affect the mechanical properties [140]. To increase the mechanical properties, recent studies concentrated mostly on reducing the defects such as porosity, surface cracking, deformations and gas inclusions by introducing some post-processing techniques. This paper will see the recent post-processing techniques which have been done for the enhancing of mechanical properties of as-fabricated (AF) produced parts. Delamination is usually a visible deficiency which cannot be eliminated by post-processing techniques or heat treatments, but can be avoided by following proper process parameters in order to reduce repeated fluctuated stresses and also by considering the characteristics of deposited alloy [148,149], there are various categories of defects as can be briefly seen in Table 7. The etching also revealed the melt pools and their behaviour, but only in the unreinforced 316L specimens. Fine columnar grain bands observed from the specimen of Figure 8a were abruptly terminated at meltpool boundaries. Hence, it is possible that they have grown oriented towards the build direction. On the other hand, specimens of Figure 8a-c contained more complex columnar structures. Internal structure of columnar grains consists of colonies of cells [59]. In which, depending on growth direction, cells were either equiaxed or elongated [60]. This cellular structure is better observed in the high magnification micrographs of Figure 8, and they were formed because of complex heat transfer and large temperature gradients in the meltpool inherited from the ultrafast melting and solidification rates during laser processing. The highest temperature gradient is located on the bottom surface of concave shaped melt pools. Where, solidification of cellular structures starts perpendicular from the boundaries towards the centre of melt pools. Hence, cells are most likely to be oriented with its longitudinal direction parallel to the build direction. Whereas cells formed near the top of the meltpool boundaries can grow horizontally in response to the maximum heat flux direction. However, typically the structures formed on the top of melt pools are remelted during the fusion of the consecutive layer. Fluid dynamics of the melt pool driven by gas expansion and material evaporation, resulting from the recoil pressure [61] and the Marangoni flow effect on heat and mass transfer [62], can alter the heat flux direction. This is one of the reasons for the seen horizontal and arbitrary oriented colonies of cells. An example of a such complex growth behaviour was also observed on discontinuous melt pools, Figure 8a. Interestingly, colonies near the meltpool tip are oriented radially perpendicular to the tip planar boundary. A similar growth behaviour was also observed in Pham et al. single track study [63]. Therefore, it can be confirmed that the cells growth axis is closely perpendicular to the solid-liquid interface due to higher local thermal gradients and the maximum heat flux [64,65]. As illustrated in Figure 8b, the rapid rastering of the laser beam trough the sinusoidal path led to the formation of melt pools which have a “stack of dimes” type of look resembling weave bead patterns sometimes seen in metal welding [66–68], where each semicircle corresponds to a dab of filler formed during the welding [69]. The seen overlapping dabs resulted, therefore, from a dabber mode formation of material tracks. Factors such as laser, scanning and layer parameters and physical properties of the molten material such as surface tension and viscosity contribute to the spacing of the dabs. In contrast with the continuous mode, this interrupted action allowed for a faster cooling causing grain refinement and strong vertical texture. However, some grains persisted to go through multiple dabs, implying that the dabber mode does not completely prevent grains from elongating. Nevertheless, the colonies seen in this specimen are several orders of magnitude smaller than those of Figure 8a. The nonhomogeneous size of the refined structures seen in Figure 8c and 8Figure 8d resulted from the addition of SiC to 316L. Where, the degree of constitutional undercooling set by the composite composition, the distribution of SiC and thermal profiles in the liquid were associated with this phenomenon [70–72]. Therefore, based on the unreinforced specimens, here, those colonies decorated with slightly large structures correspond to a reinforcing phase. The observed porosity is probably associated with typical L-PBF defects, 316L, SiC and contaminants [73,74]. Therefore, the causes of porosity formation were either from entrapped gases (or absorption of surrounding gases), evaporation of certain elements, meltpool instabilities, shrinkage during solidification or other influencing factors such as powder humidity and oxygen content in the processing chamber. It is worth noting that pores were only found between grains, and where they resided there was a lack of grain boundary. Generally, solidification crack occurs along the grain boundaries and precipitated phases, aided by existing internal defects. Here, the presence of porosities made the specimens less ductile and offered an alternative pathway for crack to propagate. Cracking along cellular boundary is convoluted and often consumes more energy. In accordance with a previous study [75], fewer cracks were observed when using a relative high scanning speed. The 10000 mm/s scanning speed reduced the solidification time, which constrained aggregation of nano SiC particles and consequently reduced the degree of cracks. However, based on the density results of Figure 4, the increase in scanning speed correlated with an increase in porosity. Nevertheless, the tensile results of Figure 6 confirmed that higher scanning speed reflects on improvements in composite tensile strength and ductility. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

training_text: The microstructure of the layers deposited via L-DED-wire was investigated at various locations and under different magnifications using SEM, as shown in Fig. 8. The figure shows that the steel processed by the L-DED-wire method in this study had a hierarchical microstructure composed of various layers of metal deposited upon each other and separated by interlayer boundaries, marked by red lines in Fig. 8a. The Schaeffler diagram has been seen to be reliable for evaluating the overall microstructural features of the type of stainless steel filler wire used in this study processed via direct deposition techniques due to the similarities such methods share with conventional welding technologies [22]. Thus, the \( Cr_{eq} \) and \( Ni_{eq} \) values of the 316LSi were calculated following the nominal chemical composition of the alloy and marked on the Schaeffler diagram in Fig. 9; the results show that the filler wire used is expected to have a mixture of around 92% austenite and 8% ferrite after deposition. However, the low-magnification SEM images in Fig. 8a and b did not show any clear sign of ferritic features being present in the deposited metal, and the dominant microstructure seemed austenitic with a hierarchical structure of grains and subgrain features, as can be seen in Fig. 8b. The absence of ferrite Fig. 8(a) and (b) SEM images can be attributed to the relatively rapid cooling rates associated with L-DED, which potentially refined the ferritic features along the austenitic boundaries to the extent that they could not be detected in such magnifications. However, the presence of ferrite in the microstructure was experimentally confirmed since the deposited metal was noticeably ferromagnetic. Hence, the material was investigated using SEM under higher magnifications, as shown in Fig. 8c to f, and refined ferritic features with different morphologies were detected. The morphology of ferritic features was dependent upon the area of investigation. As shown in Fig. 8c, ferrite had mainly a vermicular network in the top section, while it turned into sporadic spots in the middle section. Furthermore, ferritic features in the bottom center are mainly lacy, trapped between austenitic dendrites and stretched toward the primary thermal gradient direction (Fig. 8e), while ferrite morphology turned into a combination of vermicular and lacy close to the bottom corner areas (Fig. 8f). Moreover, the austenitic grains, as the main phase, could be made out by backscatter electron channeling imaging, as can be seen in Fig. 8b, where they are separated by red dashed lines, while cellular and dendritic subgrain constituents are apparent within the grains, indicating the hierarchical nature of the main microstructure. Accordingly, the various ferritic morphologies were scattered between the hierarchical austenitic features. training_text: The scanning electron micrographs in Figure 5 contrast the microstructure of the specimens. It is worth noting that the resultant solidified microstructures are very similar. The solidification structure is that of columnar grains containing colonies of submicrometric cells separated by low angle grain boundaries. These columnar grains arose due to partial remelting of the previous consolidated layers, as they allowed epitaxial growth. Therefore, this epitaxial growth from the parent grains encouraged the elongation of the columnar grains, which then resulted in a highly textured columnar microstructure, as confirmed later by the electron backscatter diffraction analysis. From the shown plane of view, microstructural features of periodically layer bands are common in L-PBF specimens [31–36]. Accordingly, the behaviour of the layer bands observed in Figure 5 resulted from reheat and remelt influence by the consecutive layer deposition. In summary, these layer bands were weak barriers to prevent columnar grain size growth. However, as observed from the high magnification inset micrographs in Figure 5, layer bands did effectively break the cellular structures into small colonies. Consequently, neighbouring colonies of cells grew rather misoriented to each other in response to the influence of the layer bands to the local maximum heat flux direction. Therefore, this randomised orientation of the colonies contrasted with the columnar grains anisotropy. The benefit of this is that such subgrain features could result in strengthening and toughening effects by impeding dislocation movement and altering the course of fracture and propagation paths. training_text: We successfully fabricated dense β type Ti-42Nb alloy ingots via LDED by appropriately tuning the process parameters. The microstructure of the Ti-42Nb samples is displayed in the SEM micrographs in Figure 6. The analysis was performed on the XY cross-section at different heights (measured from the top of the substrate), and on the YZ cross-section. Coarser grains were observed on the top of the specimen, at z = 50 mm and 30 mm (Figures 6a and 6b, respectively) than on the bottom, at z = 10 mm (Figure 6c). The samples exhibited a dendritic segregation on the bottom that tended to disappear on the middle and top. These dendrites were aligned parallel to the building direction (Z-axis), which indicates that grains grow epitaxially from the parent grains in the molten pool as a consequence of the high thermal gradient (Figure 6d). This epitaxial columnar grain growth is a microstructural feature commonly observed in laser-deposited titanium alloys [32,34,37,44–46,48]. X-ray diffraction (XRD) studies were carried out on the same samples studied by SEM to confirm that their composition was primarily single β-phase. The diffractograms are shown in Figure 7. A sample of the powder employed as a precursor material, spherical pre-alloyed Ti-42Nb particles (63–105 µm), has been studied by XRD as well (Figure 7e). The Ti-42Nb powder was formed by randomly oriented single β-phase crystallites and its diffractogram has been employed as a reference pattern of a β-phase polycrystalline material with random crystallographic texture. It can be observed that some peaks were missed in the diffraction patterns of the samples generated by LDED (Figure 7a–d), and there were discrepancies in the relative intensity of the peaks in comparison to the reference pattern (Figure 7e). These variations were caused by two factors. Firstly, the microstructure of the laser-deposited samples was composed of coarse grains and the area studied by XRD did not comprehend a statistically relevant number of grains that contributed to the diffraction pattern. Secondly, the crystallographic texture of the laser-deposited Ti-42Nb was not random. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

Inconel 625 alloy has a face-centered cubic lattice structure, and the dendrites will grow preferentially along the orientation with the smallest angle between the temperature gradient. Moreover, the temperature gradient at the top of the molten pool will change in the laser scanning direction, which will cause the growth direction of the dendrites to change. Thus, turning dendrites are easily formed at the layer-to-layer interface. The performance of surfacing layer was mainly determined by the solidification structure, and that depended on the ratio \( G/R \) of the solidification speed \( R \) and the solid–liquid interface temperature gradient \( G \). The large temperature gradient \( G \) and the small solidification rate \( R \) were produced at the interface between the molten pool and the substrate, and a large \( G/R \) value could be obtained, which was conducive to the formation of planar crystals. As the solidified structure moved toward the surface of the cladding layer, the \( G/R \) ratio decreased, and a dendritic structure was produced. Nevertheless, the type and morphology of the precipitated phase in the deposition process changed with the chemical properties of the alloy elements. \( \gamma \)-NiFe phase formed in the interfacial zone between substrate and deposit layer due to a large amount of iron dissolved into the interface from base steel. However, the peaks related to three phases of \( \gamma' \), \( \gamma'' \) Cr- and Mo-rich phases did not be detected by XRD due to the low quantity of these precipitated phases. training_text: exemplifies the common features on side (vertically built), upward facing and downward facing surfaces of LPBF Ti-6Al-4V: (i) melt-pool flow patterns (primary roughness);[9] (ii) unmelted or spattered particles (secondary roughness);[9] (iii) surface fissures or cracks (Figure 1b); (iv) melt overflow bumps; and (v) dross formation - excessive adhering or sintering of particles on downward facing surfaces. In addition, oxidized regions (not shown in Figure 1) are common on a LPBF surface. These features change with component design features, LPBF parameters, powder quality, orientation, location, and gas flow condition. An indicative ranking on their severity for fatigue properties will be provided, following a detailed assessment of the influence of surface defects on fatigue performance. Figure 2 summarizes the important processing and design variables, indicative of the challenge to manage LPBF surface conditions. Fortunately, the influence of each of these variables has been assessed through the LPBF of one signature alloy, Ti-6Al-4V (wt.%), due to its broad industrial importance as well as its high buy-to-fly ratio by conventional manufacturing.[10] This offers a unique basis to systematically assess the design features and LPBF variables on surface conditions and the consequent influence on fatigue response.[11–14] The purpose is to formulate an essential knowledge base for LPBF of metal components for suitable applications subject to cyclic loading, with no or minimal post-AM surface processing. The remainder of this contribution is organized as follows. Section 2 succinctly discusses fatigue and fracture toughness assessment methods and their relevance to design for AM; Section 3 summarizes developments to date in characterizing a metal AM surface; Section 4 details the formation and potential features of a LPBF surface under various design and processing conditions; Section 5 discusses the influence of support structures on surface finish; Section 6 examines the fatigue performance of LPBF Ti-6Al-4V with as-manufactured surfaces; Section 7 focuses on post surface processing methods; Section 8 emphasizes the importance of following the ASTM standard practice to report fatigue data; and Section 9 concludes this work with recommended design considerations and identified outstanding research issues for LPBF with improved surface conditions and fatigue performance. Scale bar: 20 µm µm.

training_text: SEM images of 3D RTCO surface structures, viewed perpendicular (a,b) and parallel (c,d) to the building direction, highlighting a magnified region with cellular structure morphology (e). The potentiodynamic polarisation (CP) curves of Figure 9 show the comparison between the corrosion behaviour of polished bulk L-PBF and the two non-surface finishing RTCO structures (10% and 35%) in SBF solution, containing Cl⁻ ions. The Bulk CP curve presents a Tafel-like region before the passivation plateau, followed by an abrupt current enhancement associated with a local breakdown of passive films. This behaviour is similar to the ones found in literature [52]. The L-PBF bulk structure presents a passive plateau of ~500 mV, a pitting potential of about +676 mV (vs. SCE), and a passive current density of 612 mA/cm². However, the passive plateau is shorter for bulk L-PBF, revealing that the surface passive films are still protective but for lower potentials. The RTCO10 structure presents a pitting potential of about Epit +342 mV (vs. SCE) and RTCO35 a pitting potential of Epit +378 mV (vs. SCE), being the passive current density about 612 mA/cm² and 610 mA/cm², respectively. The bulk repassivation potential corresponding to pit repair by a passive layer is about +100 mV and more noble than the repassivation potential of RTCO structures. Repassivation behaviour is also similar for both RTCO (10% and 35%) structures, with a repassivation potential of Erept +61.2 mV (vs. SCE) and Erept +29.1 mV (vs. SCE), respectively. Moreover, for 3D structures after passive film breakdown, the current enhancement is not as abrupt as usual, but there is a significant current density increase with potential suggesting the effect of the porous lattice. The differences between RTCO10 and RTCO35 lattice structures observed in Figure 9 do not seem to induce major changes. Scale bar: 100 µm µm.

training_text: shows the fracture morphology of different areas of specimens at different interlayer temperatures. Figure 12(a), (b), (c) and (d) depicts that the through-crystal fracture dominates all the fractures of specimens. The fracture surface exhibits dimples of varying sizes distributed throughout the area, and the presence of deep and large tough sockets suggests a ductile fracture mode. Furthermore, sporadic second-phase particles were observed within the dimples. These observations demonstrate that the Laves phase particles are advantageous sites for macroscopic crack propagation. Upon cracking, rapid extension occurs along the path of Laves phase particles (Ref 40). The amount and morphology of the Laves phase significantly impact the fracture process. Figure 12(e) and (f) present the fracture morphology of the upper and bottom areas of specimens at 200 °C interlayer temperature, respectively. Compared to the coarse and interconnected Laves phase particles, the morphology of the Laves phase particles in the bottom region was finer and discrete, less harmful to the tensile ductility. Thus, the bottom region exhibits higher tensile strength. This observation aligns with the exceptional elongation depicted in Fig. 11. Furthermore, the microstructure contains micropores. Due to the large cooling rate of the material during the forming process of the metal part, the gases in the liquid metal cannot escape from the molten pool in time, and these gases were trapped inside the part to form micropores. During uniaxial stretching, the pores act as stress concentration points and are prone to the formation of microcracks, which expand with tensile loading, weakening the tensile strength. These enlarged and merged microcracks weaken the ductility of the material and reduce the mechanical properties of the part (Ref 41). 4. training_text: shows the microstructure in the xz-plane (parallel to the building direction) of the as-printed and heat-treated LPBF-IN718 using MHH and ER heating. In the as-printed microstructure in Figure 5(a and b), typical cellular/dendritic segregation is evident. Given the fast solidification during the printing process, refractory and heavy solutes, such as Nb and Mo, get rejected and segregated from the γ-matrix, forming dendrites inside individual grains as well as along the grain boundaries. The presence of these segregated solutes leads to the formation of Laves phases which are notorious degrading the mechanical properties of nickel-based superalloys [28,29]. However, it was found that the grain boundaries contain higher concentrations of the segregated elements as compared to the grain interiors, as shown in the inset image in Figure 5(b). To examine the elemental distribution in the as-printed condition, an EDS intensity map was acquired from the xz-plane, including the dendrites, inter-dendrites and grain boundary areas shown in Figure 6. It can be seen that the grain boundaries and inter-dendritic regions are rich in Nb, Ti and Mo and deficient in Ni, Cr and Fe, whereas in the dendrite zones, the opposite is observed. To quantify these segregates inside the grains and grain boundaries, an EDS line scanning was performed for 500 points within a distance of 25 μm and over a dwell time of 1000 s, as shown in Figure 7. High fluctuations were observed in the concentration of alloying elements in the dendrite, inter-dendrite and grain boundary regions. As can be seen, the mass fraction of Nb in the grain boundary and inter-dendrite regions reached up to ≈ 10.5% and ≈ 8%, respectively, whereas in the dendrite regions, it was ≈ 4%. Similar fluctuations of Mo and Ti are evident from Figure 7. It is interesting to note that the grain boundaries have a higher mass fraction of Nb segregates than the inter-dendritic regions, confirming the results shown in the intensity map in Figure 6. According to the investigation by Damien et al. [30], the segregation energy of Nb on grain boundaries is twice that in the matrix. Thus, Nb preferentially segregates along the grain boundaries than in the grain interior. Conversely, the mass fractions of Ni, Cr and Fe in the inter-dendrite and grain boundary regions dropped significantly as compared to the matrix, thus supporting the general observations from the elemental maps in Figure 6. To prevent changes in the local chemical composition of the LPBF-IN718 alloy caused by this segregation phenomenon, the phases/segregates need to be dissolved in the γ-matrix using heat treatments. training_text: To examine the elemental distribution in the as-printed condition, an EDS intensity map was acquired from the xz-plane, including the dendrites, inter-dendrites and grain boundary areas shown in Figure 6. It can be seen that the grain boundaries and inter-dendritic regions are rich in Nb, Ti and Mo and deficient in Ni, Cr and Fe, whereas in the dendrite zones, the opposite is observed. To quantify these segregates inside the grains and grain boundaries, an EDS line scanning was performed for 500 points within a distance of 25 μm and over a dwell time of 1000 s, as shown in Figure 7. High fluctuations were observed in the concentration of alloying elements in the dendrite, inter-dendrite and grain boundary regions. As can be seen, the mass fraction of Nb in the grain boundary and inter-dendrite regions reached up to ≈ 10.5% and ≈ 8%, respectively, whereas in the dendrite regions, it was ≈ 4%. Similar fluctuations of Mo and Ti are evident from Figure 7. It is interesting to note that the grain boundaries have a higher mass fraction of Nb segregates than the inter-dendritic regions, confirming the results shown in the intensity map in Figure 6. According to the investigation by Damien et al. [30], the segregation energy of Nb on grain boundaries is twice that in the matrix. Thus, Nb preferentially segregates along the grain boundaries than in the grain interior. Conversely, the mass fractions of Ni, Cr and Fe in the inter-dendrite and grain boundary regions dropped significantly as compared to the matrix, thus supporting the general observations from the elemental maps in Figure 6. To prevent changes in the local chemical composition of the LPBF-IN718 alloy caused by this segregation phenomenon, the phases/segregates need to be dissolved in the γ-matrix using heat treatments. training_text: To study the effect of different heat inputs on the microstructure of the same composite material (VInconel 718: VTi6Al4V=2:1), the metallographic morphology of the samples was observed under different deposition currents using an optical microscope. Figure 4 displays the optical microscopy characterization for each deposition current. Figure 4a shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 35 A, with the Ti6Al4V/Inconel 718 composite in the upper part and the Inconel 718 layer in the lower part. The upper section is predominantly composed of columnar crystals, intermingled with some long black bars among the branches of the columnar crystals. In the WAM process, the solid–liquid interface gradually advances into the liquid phase region. During this advancement, the solute undergoes redistribution, resulting in a phenomenon of component supercooling within a certain distance. This instability of the flat solid–liquid interface ultimately leads to the formation of columnar crystals. As the liquid phase region is influenced by solute redistribution, solute aggregation occurs, which is manifested as microscopic segregation [27]. From the Figure 4a, it can be observed that tiny secondary dendrites are present on the sides of the columnar crystals, with an average distance of 5.16 μm between these secondary dendrites. With the increase in the deposition current, the columnar crystals in the deposited layer gradually undergo differentiation. Figure 4b shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 40 A. From the Figure 4b, it can be observed that some of the grains are arranged in an orderly manner, while a discontinuous black phase is present between the grains. In addition, long straight columnar crystals can be observed in the Figure 4b, which is formed due to the instability of the solid–liquid interface resulting from the supercooling of the composition. Under conditions of rapid cooling, columnar crystals are formed more readily. In comparison to Figure 4a, when the deposition current is 40 A, the heat input increases, leading to a longer temperature residence time on the workpiece under the same heat dissipation conditions. As a result, the cooling rate becomes relatively slower. At the microscopic level, the number of columnar crystals decreases, with some larger columnar crystals gradually transforming into smaller grains, leading to an increase in the spacing between columnar crystals. As some of the heat is conducted in the direction of the deposited additive, a negative temperature gradient develops in the liquid phase, perpendicular to the crystal axis. This results in the formation of a secondary crystal axis along the primary crystal axis [27]. The presence of secondary dendrites can be observed in the Figure 4b, with the average distance between the secondary dendrites measuring 6.38 μm. Figure 4. training_text: The scanning electron micrographs in Figure 5 contrast the microstructure of the specimens. It is worth noting that the resultant solidified microstructures are very similar. The solidification structure is that of columnar grains containing colonies of submicrometric cells separated by low angle grain boundaries. These columnar grains arose due to partial remelting of the previous consolidated layers, as they allowed epitaxial growth. Therefore, this epitaxial growth from the parent grains encouraged the elongation of the columnar grains, which then resulted in a highly textured columnar microstructure, as confirmed later by the electron backscatter diffraction analysis. From the shown plane of view, microstructural features of periodically layer bands are common in L-PBF specimens [31–36]. Accordingly, the behaviour of the layer bands observed in Figure 5 resulted from reheat and remelt influence by the consecutive layer deposition. In summary, these layer bands were weak barriers to prevent columnar grain size growth. However, as observed from the high magnification inset micrographs in Figure 5, layer bands did effectively break the cellular structures into small colonies. Consequently, neighbouring colonies of cells grew rather misoriented to each other in response to the influence of the layer bands to the local maximum heat flux direction. Therefore, this randomised orientation of the colonies contrasted with the columnar grains anisotropy. The benefit of this is that such subgrain features could result in strengthening and toughening effects by impeding dislocation movement and altering the course of fracture and propagation paths. The remelting parameters were designed, the laser scanning direction was offset from each other by 67°, and the hatch distance was increased to 80 and 90 μm to achieve a reduced roughness effect. The design of parameters for the remelting strategy is based on different assumptions when the interaction of the laser beam with the powder is more efficient than the interaction with the bulk layer during remelting. The Mo interlayer deposited between the Ti6Al4V and SiAlN, provides a bonding role between the SiAlN coating and the Ti alloy substrate. training_text: SFE plays a crucial role in shaping the microstructure and properties of 3D-printed CoCrMo alloys. Lower SFE promotes the formation of partial dislocations and stacking faults, which impede dislocation motion and enhances alloy strength through increased dislocation density.[376] This lower SFE also facilitates the nucleation of hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lamellae at stacking faults during rapid cooling, resulting in a fine microstructure with improved mechanical properties. Conversely, higher SFE can inhibit the γ-fcc to ε-hcp transformation, leading to fcc phase dominance and potentially reduced wear resistance.[386] The formation of nanotwins and increased stacking fault density in low-SFE conditions creates additional barriers to dislocation motion, enhancing strength. These unique microstructural features, including cell boundaries and planar defects, are fundamental to optimizing the alloy’s mechanical performance.[387] Thermal history fundamentally shapes the phase composition of 3D-printed CoCrMo alloys through various mechanisms. In Material Extrusion (MEX), extrusion temperature and flow rate affect microstructural development and carbon content, where optimal thermal management prevents detrimental carbide precipitation, enhancing wear performance and biocompatibility.[374] LPBF creates rapid cooling rates that yield refined microstructures with fine grains and cellular structures, contrasting with traditional casting’s coarser grains and brittle sigma phase formation. These thermal gradients promote beneficial epitaxial grain growth, as shown in Figure 27.[376] The extreme cooling rates in SLM, reaching \(10^8\) °C s⁻¹, generate higher hcp phase fractions compared to conventional casting’s \(10^0\)-\(10^2\) °C s⁻¹ rates, enhancing hardness and wear resistance.[386] Rapid cooling in LPBF typically results in metastable γ-FCC phase dominance, with tungsten addition further stabilizing this phase.[387] In LDED, high cooling rates create cellular dendritic microstructures with selective molybdenum segregation at cell boundaries, producing both γ-FCC and ε-HCP phases, though post-processing heat treatment can transform ε-HCP martensites into stable γ-FCC phase.[388] Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

paper_id: Xu et al. 2025 - Improving High-Temperature Mechanical Properties of Additively Manufactured Inconel 718 Through Heat Treatment
training_text: SEM fractographs for Inconel 718 samples without and with various heat treatments for high-temperature tensile tests (650 °C) are presented in Fig. 10 and 11, respectively. As-deposited Inconel 718 fracture surface displays a dendritic structure along the Z direction (building direction), as presented in Fig. 10(a) and (b). Numerous long-chain Laves phase fragments are within the dimples oriented to columnar dendrites. The DA samples exhibit fracture steps, and the dimples are likewise oriented in the building direction, as depicted in Fig. 10(c) and (d). Laves phase cracking and fragments within the dimples can be seen. After DA, samples still retain their dendrite characteristics on their fracture surfaces and manifest the transgranular ductile fracture mechanism with obvious micro-void coalescence caused by second phase particles. The fracture surface of STA samples presents a distribution of linearly arranged dimples accompanied by “Laves + δ” fragments, as displayed in Fig. 11(a) and (b). This implies that fractures take place among the columnar dendrites. The “Laves + δ” fragments result in deeper and finer dimples that reveal an obvious ductile fracture mode with high ductility. The samples after HSTA heat treatment have degenerated dendritic structures and demonstrate a mixed fracture mode. As presented in Fig. 11(d), there are micro-cavities within the dimples from the transgranular fracture and the cleavage planes from the intergranular fracture. This occurrence is caused by the separation of small residual second phase particles from the \( \gamma \) matrix. Figure 12 depicts the magnified fracture morphologies and corresponding EDS mappings of the Inconel 718 samples after high-temperature tensile testing. It can be noticed that plentiful fragmented Laves phases aligning the inter-dendritic regions appear within the as-deposited fracture dimples and are remarkably enriched with Nb and Mo elements (Fig. 12a). These brittle Laves phases can serve as favorable sites for the development of micro-voids and the generation of fractures along inter-dendritic regions. As the samples undergo DA, STA, and HSTA heat treatments, respectively (Fig. 12b, c, and d), the number of remaining Laves phases interspersed among the dendrites pronouncedly decreases, and micro-segregation gradually diminishes. The element distribution becomes more homogeneous, and only several scattered Nb and Mo elements are enriched within dimples. Scale bar: 100 µm µm.

training_text: SEM fractographs for Inconel 718 samples without and with various heat treatments for high-temperature tensile tests (650 °C) are presented in Fig. 10 and 11, respectively. As-deposited Inconel 718 fracture surface displays a dendritic structure along the Z direction (building direction), as presented in Fig. 10(a) and (b). Numerous long-chain Laves phase fragments are within the dimples oriented to columnar dendrites. The DA samples exhibit fracture steps, and the dimples are likewise oriented in the building direction, as depicted in Fig. 10(c) and (d). Laves phase cracking and fragments within the dimples can be seen. After DA, samples still retain their dendrite characteristics on their fracture surfaces and manifest the transgranular ductile fracture mechanism with obvious micro-void coalescence caused by second phase particles. The fracture surface of STA samples presents a distribution of linearly arranged dimples accompanied by “Laves + δ” fragments, as displayed in Fig. 11(a) and (b). This implies that fractures take place among the columnar dendrites. The “Laves + δ” fragments result in deeper and finer dimples that reveal an obvious ductile fracture mode with high ductility. The samples after HSTA heat treatment have degenerated dendritic structures and demonstrate a mixed fracture mode. As presented in Fig. 11(d), there are micro-cavities within the dimples from the transgranular fracture and the cleavage planes from the intergranular fracture. This occurrence is caused by the separation of small residual second phase particles from the \( \gamma \) matrix. Figure 12 depicts the magnified fracture morphologies and corresponding EDS mappings of the Inconel 718 samples after high-temperature tensile testing. On the one hand, \( \delta \) phase may be formed when the Nb concentration at the grain boundaries (suitable nucleation positions) meets the requirements. Atoms close to grain boundaries have higher diffusion velocity and kinetic energy and deviate from the equilibrium position, which facilitate the \( \delta \) phase precipitation. Furthermore, metastable \( \gamma'' \) phases can directly transfer into stable \( \delta \) phases above 650 °C (Ref 30). Although \( \delta \) phases belong to the orthorhombic crystal structure system, \( \delta \) phases (Ni3Nb) and \( \gamma'' \) phases have the similar elemental composition. The existence of \( \delta \) phases at grain boundaries exerts a robust pinning effect on the movement of grain boundaries. This can effectively inhibit the expansion of grain boundaries and hence refine grain sizes (Ref 31). For HSTA heat treatment, homogenization heat treatment (1100 °C/1.5 h) acts in order to dissolve deleterious Laves phases, homogenize the element distribution, and eliminate micro-segregation. The HSTA sample exhibits a fuzzy dendritic structure and smooth grain boundary morphology, as presented in Fig. 2(d) and 6(d). And only a few MX particles and fine granular Laves phases remain in the \( \gamma \) matrix. The uniform element distribution is conducive to uniform and adequate \( \gamma'' \) and \( \gamma' \) strengthening phase precipitation with a large proportion of Nb during subsequent aging heat treatment. These can be indicated that heat treatments at 1100 °C cannot completely diminish the dendritic microstructures and decompose Laves phases. Higher homogenization temperatures or longer holding time than the conventional-fabricated ones are required to completely eliminate Laves phases for as-deposited Inconel 718 samples by DED, which is in reasonable agreement with the previous studies (Ref 32). High-temperature homogenization temperature promotes high atomic kinetic energy and helps more atoms overcome energy barriers, leading to a higher atomic diffusion rate and higher grain boundary migration rate (Ref 18). training_text: Stereo microscopy of the X2CrNiMoN25-7-4 cubes (4 × 4 × 5 mm³) built with various process parameters. The irregular pores, known as lack of fusion pores, are caused by insufficient melting and fusion of the powder particles. paper_id: Prass and D'Oliveira 2026 - Effect of Cu Additions on Microstructure and Wear Performance of AISI 316L Manufactured by PTA
training_text: The microstructure and solidification mode of stainless steels are influenced by the chemical composition of the feedstock and the thermal conditions imposed by the processing technique. According to the literature (Ref 34, 35), the solidification of the melt pool generated by the PTA process leads to the formations of distinct microstructures along the height of the deposited layer, driven by variations in cooling rate. Typically, a planar growth region forms near the unmelted substrate, which transitions into columnar dendrites in the middle of the layer and equiaxed dendrites at the top of the deposit. Figure 4 presents the microstructure of the topmost layer in the as-deposited single walls. As expected, the overall microstructure produced by PTA-DED shows a columnar dendritic solidification pattern, with dendrite growth direction aligned with the built direction (Fig. 4b). As the heat source moves during the deposition, different solidification conditions occur throughout the melt pool. And near the top of the melt pool, a transition from columnar dendritic to equiaxed dendritic can be observed, regardless of the powder mixture (Fig. 4a). The welding of austenitic stainless steel can result in two distinct solidification modes, primary ferrite and primary austenite. In the primary ferrite mode, solidification begins with the formation of Cr-rich \( \delta \)-ferrite crystals, causing Ni to segregate to the remaining melt pool. In contrast, the primary austenite mode initiates with the formation of \( \gamma \)-austenite, which is depleted both in Cr and Ni; therefore, enriching the liquid phase with these elements (Ref 36, 37). Cu in stainless steels, similar to Ni, acts as an austenite-stabilizing element; thus, its addition to the powder feedstock is expected to promote primary austenite solidification (Ref 37–39). In the SEM images using a SE detector (Fig. 4c), the dendritic zones appear darker than the interdendritic zones, suggesting the segregation of corrosion resistance elements occurred due to the rapid cooling rates during solidification (Ref 40, 41). This interpretation is supported by semi-quantitative EDS analysis on both dendritic and interdendritic zones (Table 6), which confirms the segregation of both Ni and Cr during solidification, strongly suggesting that the deposition of the powder mixtures with PTA-DED resulted in the primary austenite solidification mode. It is also worth noting that in austenitic stainless steels, the solubility of Cu in austenite is approximately 7.5 wt.% at 1100 \( ^\circ \)C and 3.0 wt.% at 835 \( ^\circ \)C (Ref 36). This behavior contributes to the observed accumulation of Cu in the interdendritic zone, an average increase of 50% of Cu content, particularly noticeable for the single-wall deposited with a powder mixture containing 5 wt.% Cu MP. Cu additions impacted grain refinement, as assessed by measuring the equiaxed dendrite size (Fig. 4c, d, e, f, and g). Compared to the deposits processed with 316L, which exhibited a mean equiaxed dendrite size of 183 \( \pm \) 49 \( \mu m^2 \), additions of 1 wt.% and 5 wt.% Cu MP reduced dendrite size to 167 \( \pm \) 42 and 119 \( \pm \) 21 \( \mu m^2 \), respectively. Similarly, a microstructure refinement was measured in single-walls processed with powder mixtures containing 1 wt.% Cu NP and 1 wt.% CuO NP, with dendrite sizes of 153 \( \pm \) 42 and 152 \( \pm \) 31 \( \mu m^2 \), respectively. These findings can be accounted by different operating mechanisms depending on the feedstock used; higher Cu content enhances thermal conductivity and increases cooling rates, producing more refined microstructures. training_text: After the aging heat treatment and nitriding treatment, the metallographic structures of the cross-sections of various samples are shown in Figure 4. Compared with the non-aged sample, as is shown in Figure 3a, it can be seen from the results that after the aging heat treatment, the typical fusion channel structure inside the sample is still vaguely visible but appears less distinct than that in the non-aged as-built state. After the nitriding treatment, similarly to in the non-aged specimen, the fusion channel structure disappears. After 24 h of nitriding, a nitrided layer of approximately 81 μm thickness appears on the sample surface, which is slightly thicker than the ~79 μm layer in the non-aged 24 h nitrided sample. After 48 h of nitriding, the depth of the nitrided layer increases significantly to about 211 μm, showing a slight difference from the ~212 μm measurement in the non-aged 48 h nitrided sample. When the nitriding time is further extended to 60 h, the depth of the nitrided layer increases slightly to about 231 μm, which is thinner than the ~238 μm measurement in the non-aged 60 h nitrided sample. Figure 4. Metallographic structures of L-PBF manufactured 18Ni300 after different heat treatments: (a) aging heat treatment; (b) aging heat treatment +24 h nitriding; (c) aging heat treatment +48 h nitriding; and (d) aging heat treatment +60 h nitriding. The analysis of the pre-aged specimen reveals that, under nitriding conditions of 500 °C and 500 Pa pressure, ammonia decomposes into nitrogen and hydrogen, and that nitrogen primarily reacts with the Fe element in 18Ni300 at high temperatures to form an Fe-N solid solution, which appears darker than the matrix after etching. Figure 2 is not representative for all microstructures but shows most of the microstructural constituents encountered in the as-built microstructures. The as-built 2509 super duplex material contained small amounts of sigma phase in the upper/warmer sections of the part, see Figure 4. Note how the combination of different composition, higher heat input, and heat accumulation in the upper section of the 2509 part has led to a considerably higher austenite fraction. In addition, secondary austenite and chromium nitrides have been completely suppressed, with all austenite being either grain boundary allotriomorph or Widmanstätten austenite. Figure 5 shows high-resolution stitched images from the top of as-built 2205 and 2509 specimens showing mainly grain boundary allotriomorph and Widmanstätten austenite in the top layer. These figures present how the austenite formation is impacted by reheating from subsequent layers, with heavy precipitation and growth of austenite in the reheated material. In the calculations, coherency and coalescence have been assumed to occur at \( f_{s,0}=0.900 \) and \( f_{s,co}=0.990 \), based on the limits applied in a similar analysis by Tomus et al. [7] for L-PBF of Hastelloy X. It can be seen from Fig. 11 that the predicted tendency to solidification cracking is greater for batch A than batch B, which is in agreement with the experimental results. The figure also clearly demonstrates a positive correlation between increasing crack susceptibility and Si content, which was also found for L-PBF of IN738LC [23]. In addition to extending the final solidification interval when liquid feeding is restricted in the mushy zone, higher Si levels lead to the formation of the Laves phase at ~1150 °C [18]. It is proposed that the presence of the Laves phase further contributes to increased crack susceptibility by (i) embrittling the mushy zone and (ii) further reducing the permeability of the mush, exacerbating the liquid feeding issue. This appears to be reasonable, given the presence of localized Si, Nb, and Cr enrichments observed on the crack surfaces. The influence of the Nb content on the crack susceptibility is not as obvious from Fig. 11. Cieslak [18] noted that there was a small positive correlation between Nb content and crack susceptibility of IN625, but this effect was determined through comparison of a sample containing 3.6 wt% Nb and a Nb-free sample; the effect of Nb content is not as obvious when smaller differences are considered (i.e., between powders A and B). Nevertheless, the interaction between Si and Nb on crack susceptibility which was noted by Cieslak [18] can also be seen in Fig. 11 by the intersection of the trendlines for different Nb contents as the Si content increases; the solidification cracking tendency rapidly increases as Si and Nb increase simultaneously. This is a reasonable prediction, as Ni-based alloys with high Nb and Si but low C have a large mushy region, which leaves the alloy susceptible to the propagation of cracks [24]. It should be noted that the CSI_E results must be carefully interpreted. First, the indicator does not suggest a threshold value below which cracking does not occur. Powder batch B was found to be crack-free for all processing conditions in this study, while cracks were observed in all conditions with powder batch A. The CSI_E for powder batch A is 142.7 °C and 105.8 °C for powder batch B (i.e., a reduction of 25.9%). Therefore, it is expected that crack-free samples can be obtained for alloy compositions resulting in a CSI_E between these limits, but it is not clear what the threshold value is. training_text: SEM image of the microstructure – (a) at the interface between the (W7Ni3Fe) sec. 1 section and the (Ti6Al4V) sec. 1 section (BSE detector). (b) Zoomed image of the selected area from (a); (c) at the interface between the (Ti6Al4V) sec. 1 section and the (W7Ni3Fe) sec. 2 section (BSE detector). (d) Zoomed image of the selected area from (c); (e) at the microstructure at the (W7Ni3Fe) sec. 2 section (BSE detector) and, (f) at the (Ti6Al4V) sec. 2 section (BSE detector). 4b and c are the SE and BSE-SEM images at the interface between the Ti6Al4V substrate and the W7Ni3Fe (sec. 1) section. Based on Figure 4b, acicular Widmanstätten α-Ti laths were seen near the interface region of the Ti6Al4V substrate. The formation of acicular Widmanstätten α-Ti laths was caused by reheating and the rapid cooling rate by the laser deposition and scan motion on top of the substrate (Zhang et al. 2009). In Figure 4c, the bright spherical microstructures were W composition. The spherical W particles were embedded in the Ni-Fe matrix, typically found in the LPS processed W7Ni3Fe (Gurwell et al. 1984; Srikanth and Upadhyaya 1984; Şahin 2014; Zhou et al. 2021). Figure 4b and c show that no visible defects occurred at this interface. Figure 4d illustrates the microstructure at the (W7Ni3Fe) sec. 1 section. A significantly higher volume fraction of W composition over the Ni-Fe composition was found in this section. Compared to Figure 4c, the W particles in Figure 4d coalesced and formed large W grains. Since the DED processing involves rapid solidification from the molten phase, the duration of a solution-reprecipitation in the W composition was extremely short. The W particle morphology results were smaller and less spheroidal than the W particle processed by conventional LPS methods due to the breaking of the agglomerated particles (Zhou et al. 2021). Figure 5a and b show the BSE-SEM images at the interface between the (W7Ni3Fe) sec. 1 section and (Ti6Al4V) sec. 1 section. Micropores were found in this region, suggesting further optimisation of the processing parameters; however, some studies have developed efficient methods of optimising the parameters to obtain the lowest possible porosity (Rao et al. 2022). Although the DED system used in this study has two powder feeders, both powder feeders share the same powder feeding line. The W7Ni3Fe in the (Ti6Al4V) sec. 1 likely came from W7Ni3Fe particles that remained in the powder feeding line. No micro cracks could be found at this interface. Figure 5c and d illustrate the morphology at the interface between the (Ti6Al4V) sec. 1 section and the (W7Ni3Fe) sec. 2 section. Micropores were again seen in the (W7Ni3Fe) sec. 2 sections near the interface. Figure 5d is a magnified BSE-SEM image of the selected area from Figure 5c. The spherical W particles were embedded in the polygon-shaped grains of the Ti6Al4V matrix. Figure 5e shows the microstructure at the (W7Ni3Fe) sec. 2 section, similar to the morphology found in the (W7Ni3Fe) sec. 1 section (Figure 4d). Figure 5f demonstrates the microstructure at the (Ti6Al4V) sec. 2 sections, similar to the microstructure shown in Figure 5d. The evolution of the W7Ni3Fe microstructure during the DED processing can be concluded in three stages: (a) rearrangement stage, (b) solution-reprecipitation, and (c) solid-state. The Ni-Fe and Ti6Al4V compositions are melted in the rearrangement stage due to the laser energy input, forming a small molten pool with W particles. The W particles are rearranged under the capillary force as in the DED process, and other forces, such as Marangoni force, buoyancy force, and the impact force from the powder carrier gas (Zhang et al. 2009; DebRoy et al. 2018). After the laser moves away, the dissolved W begins to reprecipitate at the solution-reprecipitation stage. The W can be reprecipitated either on residual W particles or forming individual nuclei in the liquid. Due to the rapid cooling rate of the DED process, the reprecipitated W grains could grow into irregular or dendritic shapes. Due to the rapid movement of the solidification front, the Ti6Al4V and Ni-Fe matrices grow into polygon shape grains. The powder carrier gas delivering the powders gathers and escapes from the molten pool. The powder carrier gas is trapped in the solidified molten pool during the solid-state stage due to the rapid solidification, resulting in micropore formation (Zhang et al. 2009). Note that the S214 was deposited on 316L stainless steel substrate, and a small amount of 316L melted and entered S214 deposition layer. Star-like or flower-like iron-rich phases appeared on \( \alpha \)-Cu as shown in Fig. 4(i) and (l). The surface of S214 deposition layer melted more with high heat input. The melted S214 and IN625 at a fast-cooling rate were not completely mixed and solidified. There was a significant compositional non-uniform transition zone near the interface, and its width was approximately 150-200 \( \mu \)m as demonstrated in Fig. 4(g) and (h). Figure 5 presents the microstructure morphology of S214 / IN625 bimetallic deposition samples. A small amount of IN625 melted and infiltrated the S214 deposition layer with depositing S214 on the IN625 deposition. The solubility of Cr, Fe, and Mo elements in IN625 in \( \alpha \)-Cu was low, and quiet a few of them dissolved into \( \alpha \)-Cu to form a supersaturated solid solution, and some of them underwent segregation to form an elementally enriched phase, whereas Ni dissolved in \( \alpha \)-Cu to form a Cu(Ni) continuous solid solution. The S214 deposit layer was composed of columnar dendrites (Cu(Ni) solid solution) and large eutectic phases. Furthermore, the IN625 deposition layer was columnar dendritic, with obvious segregation stages at the grain boundary. As heat input increased, the granules of the S214 deposition layer coarsened, and the precipitated phase grew larger. As depicted in Fig. 5, with low heat input, a small transition layer (partial melting zone) formed between the IN625 and S214 deposits, followed by a continuous composition transition zone (CTZ) from the bonding contact upward. Under low heat input, the molten substrate was not fully mixed with the IN625 molten pool due to a faster cooling rate. Although more S214 deposits were melted in high heat input, the molten pool stirred vigorously and the elements of IN625 and S214 were mixed evenly. Figure 5(a) and (d) shows columnar dendrites in the S214 deposition layer. Elements segregated during solidification due to low solid solubility and inadequate diffusion of Cr, Mo, and Nb in \( \alpha \)-Cu basal phase. training_text: presents the microstructure morphology of S214 / IN625 bimetallic deposition samples. A small amount of IN625 melted and infiltrated the S214 deposition layer with depositing S214 on the IN625 deposition. The solubility of Cr, Fe, and Mo elements in IN625 in \( \alpha \)-Cu was low, and quiet a few of them dissolved into \( \alpha \)-Cu to form a supersaturated solid solution, and some of them underwent segregation to form an elementally enriched phase, whereas Ni dissolved in \( \alpha \)-Cu to form a Cu(Ni) continuous solid solution. The S214 deposit layer was composed of columnar dendrites (Cu(Ni) solid solution) and large eutectic phases. Furthermore, the IN625 deposition layer was columnar dendritic, with obvious segregation stages at the grain boundary. As heat input increased, the granules of the S214 deposition layer coarsened, and the precipitated phase grew larger. As depicted in Fig. 5, with low heat input, a small transition layer (partial melting zone) formed between the IN625 and S214 deposits, followed by a continuous composition transition zone (CTZ) from the bonding contact upward. Under low heat input, the molten substrate was not fully mixed with the IN625 molten pool due to a faster cooling rate. Although more S214 deposits were melted in high heat input, the molten pool stirred vigorously and the elements of IN625 and S214 were mixed evenly. Figure 5(a) and (d) shows columnar dendrites in the S214 deposition layer. Elements segregated during solidification due to low solid solubility and inadequate diffusion of Cr, Mo, and Nb in \( \alpha \)-Cu basal phase. Figure 6 illuminates the microstructure of IN625-S214 bimetallic single-wall deposition at different deposition sequences. As displayed in Fig. 6, the interface fluctuations were substantially greater for IN625 deposition on S214 than for S214 deposition on IN625, with clear signs of melt pool flow and inhomogeneous component distribution visible. Because of high heat conductivity of S214, the melted IN625 and S214 were not fully mixed before solidifying, resulting in composition inhomogeneity dis the transition zone, as illustrated in Scale bar: 50 µm µm.
