training_text: To study the effect of different heat inputs on the microstructure of the same composite material (VInconel 718: VTi6Al4V=2:1), the metallographic morphology of the samples was observed under different deposition currents using an optical microscope. Figure 4 displays the optical microscopy characterization for each deposition current. Figure 4a shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 35 A, with the Ti6Al4V/Inconel 718 composite in the upper part and the Inconel 718 layer in the lower part. The upper section is predominantly composed of columnar crystals, intermingled with some long black bars among the branches of the columnar crystals. In the WAM process, the solid–liquid interface gradually advances into the liquid phase region. During this advancement, the solute undergoes redistribution, resulting in a phenomenon of component supercooling within a certain distance. This instability of the flat solid–liquid interface ultimately leads to the formation of columnar crystals. As the liquid phase region is influenced by solute redistribution, solute aggregation occurs, which is manifested as microscopic segregation [27]. From the Figure 4a, it can be observed that tiny secondary dendrites are present on the sides of the columnar crystals, with an average distance of 5.16 μm between these secondary dendrites. With the increase in the deposition current, the columnar crystals in the deposited layer gradually undergo differentiation. Figure 4b shows the optical microstructure at a deposition current of 40 A. From the Figure 4b, it can be observed that some of the grains are arranged in an orderly manner, while a discontinuous black phase is present between the grains. In addition, long straight columnar crystals can be observed in the Figure 4b, which is formed due to the instability of the solid–liquid interface resulting from the supercooling of the composition. Under conditions of rapid cooling, columnar crystals are formed more readily. In comparison to Figure 4a, when the deposition current is 40 A, the heat input increases, leading to a longer temperature residence time on the workpiece under the same heat dissipation conditions. As a result, the cooling rate becomes relatively slower. At the microscopic level, the number of columnar crystals decreases, with some larger columnar crystals gradually transforming into smaller grains, leading to an increase in the spacing between columnar crystals. As some of the heat is conducted in the direction of the deposited additive, a negative temperature gradient develops in the liquid phase, perpendicular to the crystal axis. This results in the formation of a secondary crystal axis along the primary crystal axis [27]. The presence of secondary dendrites can be observed in the Figure 4b, with the average distance between the secondary dendrites measuring 6.38 μm. Figure 4. training_text: depicts the SEM images of the MSS specimens in different states. Apparently, the MSS specimens primarily consisted of lath martensite. Moreover, the number density of precipitated particles increased with the extension of tempering time, while the precipitated particles were significantly coarsened when the tempering time was 2.0 h (Figure 4h). This is due to the fact that the precipitated second-phase particle continued to aggregate and grow, generating a significant ripening process [24]. Figure 4. SEM morphology of the MSS specimens: (a,b) as-deposited, (c,d) as-tempered 0.5 h, (e,f) as-tempered 1.0 h and (g,h) as-tempered 2.0 h. Further detailed microstructure characterizations of the as-tempered 1.0 h MSS specimen were conducted via TEM (Figure 5). As seen in Figure 5a–c, the as-tempered 1.0 h MSS specimen was composed of lath martensite, austenite and nano-precipitates. Among them, the film-like and bulk austenite (A) was present in the lath martensite matrix. The incomplete martensitic transformation could be promoted because of the rapid cooling rates during LDED process together with the existence of the austenite-forming element Ni, leading to the appearance of bulk retained A [17,25]. The formation of reversed A during tempering process could be attributed to two aspects: (i) The synergistic effect between Cu and Ni. The diffusion of Ni can be promoted by the segregation of Cu at the martensite lath-boundaries by decreasing stacking fault energy, which can provide the nucleation energy for reversed A [26,27]. Also, the existence of Ni promotes the enrichment of Cu and thus facilitates the formation of reversed A [17,26]. (ii) The existence of retained A. The driving energy for reversed A nucleation can be alleviated by the retained A [28]. Consequently, the retained A and reversed A were observed in the as-tempered 1.0 h MSS. Furthermore, nano-sized precipitates were dispersed in the M matrix (Figure 5c). These particles were confirmed as the coexistence of ε-Cu and Cr23C6 via the SAED pattern (Figure 5d). Moreover, the particle 1 with the size of 17 to 23 nm (Figure 5e) and particle 2 with the size of 3 to 11 nm (Figure 5f) marked in Figure 5c was recognized as Cr23C6 carbide (Figure 5g) and ε-Cu (Figure 5h) via the EDS analysis, respectively. paper_id: Zhang et al. 2022 - Microstructure and Fatigue Properties of Ti-48Al Alloy Fabricated by the Twin-Wire Plasma Arc Additive Manufacturing
training_text: To investigate the fatigue fracture mechanism of WAAM-produced TiAl alloys at room temperature, the fatigue morphologies of fatigue specimens are analyzed at different deposition locations. According to previous reports(Ref 29), the room-temperature fatigue fracture of TiAl alloys mainly contains three modes: (1) delamination fracture during crack propagation along lamellar interfaces, (2) translamellar fracture, where the fracture is perpendicular to lamellar microstructure, and (3) the stepwise mixed fatigue fracture mode. SEM fracture morphology performance of the Ti-48Al alloy fabricated by TW-PAAM after fatigue testing are shown in Fig. 10 and 11. These results show that after fatigue testing, translamellar fracture characteristics are observed on all the fracture surfaces at different locations of deposition. In addition, no plastic deformation is evident on the fatigue fracture surface. The fracture surfaces of U-3 specimen are shown in Fig. 10. The fatigue fracture process exhibited three stages. In Fig. 10(a), some fatigue source zone can be observed in the fracture surfaces, and fatigue fracture preferentially along the interlamellar interface proceeds with formation of frequent branches. The fatigue source zone initiates along the lamellar interface in the equiaxed lamellar colony, exhibiting smooth features along the surface, and the area was also small as shown in Fig. 10(b). There are a small number of facets and fractures in the fatigue fracture propagation area, the fatigue fracture morphology with obvious tear edges, and Figure 10(d) shows the typical topography of river-like patterns in the fatigue fracture area, and the fracture propagates along the river-like direction. Figure 10(e) shows fatigue striations that are perpendicular to the direction of crack propagation. The fracture in Fig. 10(f) represented traces of microslip of the parallel delamination strip. The fracture surfaces of L-4 specimen are shown in Fig. 11. There was obvious principal crack; a small amount fatigue source zone in the fracture surface is shown in Fig. 11(a). The cracks of fatigue originate on the interior defects or initiated by a translamellar way in a equiaxed lamellar colony as shown in Fig. 11(b). In the fatigue crack propagation area, multiple crack initiations were frequently observed on the fracture surface, which may cause a reduction in resistance to crack initiation. The fracture of Fig. 11(d) shows that the fatigue fracture zone is also dominated by delamination. Moreover, there are some tearing edges left by the tearing connection between cracks and secondary cracks formed by interlayer separation. The fractography in Fig. 11(e) shows the cracks stop at the boundary between misoriented lamellar colonies and propagates along the colony boundary. However, this crack propagate way does not found in the upper part. Additionally, secondary crack can also be observed. No fatigue striations and rubbing are observed in the fracture surfaces. Figure 11(f) shows the microcrack propagate along the interlamellar. Meanwhile, twinning traces and microslips also can be observed. Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: To investigate the fatigue fracture mechanism of WAAM-produced TiAl alloys at room temperature, the fatigue morphologies of fatigue specimens are analyzed at different deposition locations. SEM fracture morphology performance of the Ti-48Al alloy fabricated by TW-PAAM after fatigue testing are shown in Fig. 10 and 11. These results show that after fatigue testing, translamellar fracture characteristics are observed on all the fracture surfaces at different locations of deposition. In addition, no plastic deformation is evident on the fatigue fracture surface. The fracture surfaces of U-3 specimen are shown in Fig. 10. The fatigue fracture process exhibited three stages. In Fig. 10(a), some fatigue source zone can be observed in the fracture surfaces, and fatigue fracture preferentially along the interlamellar interface proceeds with formation of frequent branches. The fatigue source zone initiates along the lamellar interface in the equiaxed lamellar colony, exhibiting smooth features along the surface, and the area was also small as shown in Fig. 10(b). There are a small number of facets and fractures in the fatigue fracture propagation area, the fatigue fracture morphology with obvious tear edges, and Figure 10(d) shows the typical topography of river-like patterns in the fatigue fracture area, and the fracture propagates along the river-like direction. Figure 10(e) shows fatigue striations that are perpendicular to the direction of crack propagation. The fracture in Fig. 10(f) represented traces of microslip of the parallel delamination strip. The fracture surfaces of L-4 specimen are shown in Fig. 11. There was obvious principal crack; a small amount fatigue source zone in the fracture surface is shown in Fig. 11(a). The cracks of fatigue originate on the interior defects or initiated by a translamellar way in a equiaxed lamellar colony as shown in Fig. 11(b). In the fatigue crack propagation area, multiple crack initiations were frequently observed on the fracture surface, which may cause a reduction in resistance to crack initiation. The fracture of Fig. 11(d) shows that the fatigue fracture zone is also dominated by delamination. Moreover, there are some tearing edges left by the tearing connection between cracks and secondary cracks formed by interlayer separation. The fractography in Fig. 11(e) shows the cracks stop at the boundary between misoriented lamellar colonies and propagates along the colony boundary. However, this crack propagate way does not found in the upper part. Additionally, secondary crack can also be observed. No fatigue striations and rubbing are observed in the fracture surfaces. Figure 11(f) shows the microcrack propagate along the interlamellar. Meanwhile, twinning traces and microslips also can be observed. Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

It suggests that the L12–Al3Ti phase is tougher than D022–Al3Ti [25,26] and thus L12–Al3Ti phase is more desired in Al alloys for better mechanical performances [11]. In the tensile fracture surface morphology of the AlZnMgCu–Ti alloy, we observed the fracture of the brittle lath-like D022–Al3Ti phase (Figure S2(a)). In contrast, the bottom of the dimples in the tensile fracture of the AlZnMgCu–Ti@C alloy revealed a cubic morphology of the L12–Al3Ti phase, with no observed fractures (Figure S2(b)). Therefore, in the present study, the significant improved ductility of AlZnMgCu–Ti@C alloy was reasonably resulted from the disappearance of brittle D022–Al3Ti phase. Moreover, the C addition led to the finer size of L12–Al3Ti phase, which is beneficial to Orowan looping strengthening [27,28], contributing to the improved strength of the AlZnMgCu–Ti@C alloy. Therefore, the addition of C-induced Al3Ti phase structure change resulted in the improved mechanical properties of the AlZnMgCu–Ti alloy (Figure 1). The next question is that why the L12→D022 transformation of Al3Ti phase could be suppressed by the C addition in LPBF AlZnMgCu–Ti alloys? In LPBF Al alloys, the stable D022–Al3Ti phase structure was a result of the formation of antiphase boundaries (APBs) displacing (001) planes in the unstable L12–Al3Ti phase with a vector of \( \frac{1}{2} [110] \) [29]. Therefore, it can be deduced that the disappearance of the D022–Al3Ti phase in the AlZnMgCu–Ti@C alloy is related to the inhibition of APB formation in the L12–Al3Ti by the C element. In order to accurately characterize the crystal structure of the C rich L12–Al3Ti phase, atomic phase and EELS analysis were performed on a typical L12–Al3Ti particle (Figure 4) using ACTEM. As shown in Figure 4(b), the L12–Al3Ti phase doped with C atoms are arranged neatly and no defects are formed, indicating that the C element does not exist in the lattice in the form of replacement atoms. The atomic intensity profiles of the (002) plane are presented in Figure 4(c), and the calculated interplanar spacing is 2.12 Å, which is larger than the L12–Al3Ti phase (2.02 Å, [30]). EELS high-energy loss spectrum can observe peaks of C, Al and Ti (Figure 4(d–f)). These results suggest that C atoms in the L12–Al3Ti phase were in the form of interstitial solid solution. paper_id: Geethapriyan et al. 2025 - Enhance the microstructure and mechanical pro ... -Arc (DED-Arc) stainless steel 308L using laser shock peening process
training_text: SEM micrographs showing the microstructure of WAAM created SS308L specimen with different types of deposition in various regions: a U-DD b B-DD and c B-DD with LSP more prominent at the fusion lines between adjacent layers in the MR due to heat accumulation. This heat originates from the preceding layer, which affects the subsequent layer, extending the cooling period and enabling larger grains to form at fusion lines compared to MR. TR, on the other hand, has smaller grain sizes since it is preheated by the previous layer but does not receive additional heat, leading to faster cooling. Consequently, both columnar and equiaxed grains are present in TR. In B-DD, BR shows columnar intermediates emerging in multiple directions due to faster cooling as depicted in Fig. 2b. The heat is rapidly transferred to the MS substrate at ambient temperature, resulting in coarser grains compared to other regions. In MR, columnar ferrite structures are prevalently close to the fusion boundary but disappear moving further into MR, where vertically arranged columnar dendrites characterize the microstructure. The cooling rate diminishes as more deposition layers accumulate, resulting in a coarser microstructure in the MR than in BR. In TR, equiaxed grains are distributed randomly due to atmospheric contact. The grain direction in B-DD samples is different from U-DD, with smaller grains and crossed microstructures. This difference arises because the B-DD method does not extinguish the arc between layers but instead moves in the opposite direction, decreasing cooling time and yielding a finer grain structure. For the B-DD + LSP samples, the shock pressure applied via laser shock peening refines the grain structure, particularly at the surface shown in Fig. 2c. Grain size analysis conducted using ImageJ software indicates a reduction in grain size from BR to TR: in the BR, from 14.51 μm to 8.91 μm; in the MR, from 13.59 μm to 8.19 μm; and in the TR, from 13.57 μm to 7.9 μm. This grain refinement is attributed to the LSP-induced shockwaves, which increase grain numbers, reduce slip and dislocation, and thereby enhance the material’s surface morphology. Figure 3 presents the EDS analysis of the DED-Arc fabricated SS308L specimen across the BR, MR, and TR under different deposition methods: unidirectional-direct deposition, bidirectional-direct deposition, and bidirectional-direct deposition with laser shock peening. Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

Figure 6 shows the wear tracks of DED-built, DED-HT, and Wrought-HT D2 steels after wear testing under a 20 N load. In all three samples, typical plowing grooves and fish-scale surface features were observed, primarily caused by the sliding motion (yellow arrows). These fish-scale surfaces are known to result from fine particles, detached during wear, adhering to the surface (Ref 51). Luo et al. reported that dry sliding conditions commonly lead to self-mating adhesive wear on the worn surface (Ref 52). Therefore, it can be inferred that all three samples exhibited a similar adhesive wear behavior under the 20 N load condition. Figure 7 presents the SEM images and EDS results of the wear track areas obtained under the 20 N load condition. No evidence of carbide pullout was observed in any specimen, whereas localized adhesion of oxide films was detected in several regions of the worn surfaces, indicating that mild oxidative wear was dominant under this condition. Figures 8 and 9 present the SEM observations and EDS results of the wear tracks obtained under the 30 N load condition. The wear tracks formed under this condition exhibited characteristic plowing grooves aligned with the sliding direction in both DED-built and DED-HT samples (Fig. 8a, b). All specimens showed distinct regions where oxides were concentrated around carbide-depleted zones, suggesting that carbide detachment facilitated both the formation and accumulation of oxide debris and the occurrence of abrasive plowing on the worn surfaces (Fig. 9). The uniformly distributed fine secondary carbides in DED-HT and Wrought-HT samples likely contributed to enhanced wear resistance (Ref 53). In contrast, coarse carbides in the Wrought-HT D2 sample were observed to detach from the matrix in certain regions (Fig. 8c), which could remove the surrounding matrix during sliding and result in wider plowing regions. Consequently, this wear behavior may lead to higher wear loss and an increased wear rate compared with the 20 N condition. Furthermore, the Wrought-HT specimen exhibited locally formed Al-rich oxide layers originating from the wear of the counterpart, whereas such counterpart-derived oxides were rarely observed in the DED-built and DED-HT specimens (Fig. 9). training_text: The scanning electron micrographs in Figure 5 contrast the microstructure of the specimens. It is worth noting that the resultant solidified microstructures are very similar. The solidification structure is that of columnar grains containing colonies of submicrometric cells separated by low angle grain boundaries. These columnar grains arose due to partial remelting of the previous consolidated layers, as they allowed epitaxial growth. Therefore, this epitaxial growth from the parent grains encouraged the elongation of the columnar grains, which then resulted in a highly textured columnar microstructure, as confirmed later by the electron backscatter diffraction analysis. From the shown plane of view, microstructural features of periodically layer bands are common in L-PBF specimens [31–36]. Accordingly, the behaviour of the layer bands observed in Figure 5 resulted from reheat and remelt influence by the consecutive layer deposition. In summary, these layer bands were weak barriers to prevent columnar grain size growth. However, as observed from the high magnification inset micrographs in Figure 5, layer bands did effectively break the cellular structures into small colonies. Consequently, neighbouring colonies of cells grew rather misoriented to each other in response to the influence of the layer bands to the local maximum heat flux direction. Therefore, this randomised orientation of the colonies contrasted with the columnar grains anisotropy. The benefit of this is that such subgrain features could result in strengthening and toughening effects by impeding dislocation movement and altering the course of fracture and propagation paths. training_text: SEM of high-temperature fracture surface of different samples: (a) AB, (b) ST + AT, (c) HIP, (d) HIP + ST + AT, (c') the magnification figure of rectangular area in Fig.19c, (d') the magnification figure of rectangular area in Fig.19d. strengthening mode of the HIP and HIP + ST + AT samples was precipitation strengthening. We concluded that the contribution of the HIP treatment to the mechanical properties at room temperature was not obvious. However, at a high temperature (800 °C), the tensile properties of the LPBF-fabricated Inconel 738 alloy were significantly improved by the HIP treatment, especially in terms of yield strength and elongation (Fig. 15). For the AB sample, owing to the formation of a great number of original defects of such as cracks and pores during the LPBF process, as well as to the high and unstable dislocation density at high temperatures, brittle fractures occurred before yielding of the sample at 800 °C. The AB samples have poor plasticity, resulting in a severe mismatch of strength and plasticity. As shown in Fig. 19a, the fracture surface of the AB sample contained a large number of typical smooth cleavage step, which is mainly intergranular fracture. For the HIP sample, although the HIP treatment significantly increased the grain size of the AB Inconel 738 alloy, the lower defect density and stable cubic γ’ phases may have hindered the movement of dislocations, increasing the strength of the alloy. The uniform distribution of carbides at the grain boundaries also hindered dislocation movement, which further increased the strength. In addition, the equiaxed grains ensured good plastic deformation. Thus, the high-temperature (800 °C) tensile properties of the AB Inconel 738 alloy (σUTS = 487.4 MPa) were significantly improved (σUTS = 808.4 MPa, σY = 733.8 MPa, εf = 6.1%) via the HIP treatment, which is primarily attributed to uniform carbide formation, lower defect densities and stable γ’ phases. It also can be identified in Fig. 19c and e’, the fracture surface of the HIP sample changes to a mixture of brittle and ductile fracture surface with several visible dimples and a few tearing edges, indicating the extent of uniform plastic deformation. Some micro-cracks can be observed at the fracture surface, as shown in Fig. 12d. The initiation and propagation of these micro-cracks accelerated the failure of the tensile specimen, thereby limiting the increase in elongation. The deformation temperature has been shown to have a significant effect on the deformation mode of NiTi alloys due to the thermoelastic martensitic transformation [42]. The formation of stress-induced martensite upon loading and the reversible transformation upon unloading occurs only at temperatures above \( A_f \), contributing to the superelasticity. Thereby, to better reflect the superelastic behavior of the current WAAM NiTiTa alloys, cyclic tensile tests were carried out at 100 °C (above \( A_f \)), and the results are presented in Fig. 13. The WAAM NiTiTa sample shows obvious superelasticity during the loading-unloading process, as shown in Fig. 14a. The critical stress (\( \sigma_c \)) for stress-induced martensitic transformation is about 380 MPa at 100 °C, while at room temperature it decreases to 252 MPa. This is due to the increased thermodynamic resistance for the martensitic transformation, which is a function of temperature as expressed by the Clausius-Clapeyron relation [43]. The calculated recovery ratio as a function of the cycle times is shown in Fig. 13b. The reversible strain in the first cycle is about 1.8 %, and the corresponding recovery ratio (ratio of recoverable strain to total imposed strain) is 91.5 %. With the increase of the number of cycles, the recovery ratio gradually reduced and then maintained at nearly 86.8 % after 10 loading-unloading cycles. The reduced recovery ratio is due to the gradual accumulation of defects and retained martensite, which promotes the decrease of transformation strain and the increase of the volume fraction of untransformed austenite within the shear bands during cycling tests [44]. training_text: The microstructures of the samples after different treatments were observed using a SEM, as shown in Figure 4. The microstructure of the TA15 titanium alloy predominantly consists of the α phase, characterized by a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure, and the β phase, characterized by a body-centered cubic (bcc) structure. Due to the LDED fabrication method, the microstructure features layered α and β phases, forming a distinctive mesh-like morphology. After cryogenic treatment, notable changes were observed in the microstructure. The α platelets became thicker, while the quantity and volume of the β phase decreased. However, no significant morphological changes were detected in the overall structure of the ULT samples compared to the as-built samples. A quantitative analysis of the β phase was performed using Image Pro Plus software, based on SEM images captured at 5000× magnification (Figure 4b). After calibrating the image processing parameters, the β phase content in the untreated as-built samples was measured to be ≈42.1%, whereas cryogenic treatment reduced this content significantly to about 21.4%. These findings indicate that cryogenic treatment facilitates the transformation of the metastable β phase into the α phase and stable β phase, consistent with previous research.[27] Energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was used to conduct point scan analysis on samples subjected to different treatments, as shown in Figure 5. Point 1 corresponds to the α phase, and Point 2 corresponds to the β phase; all points were selected randomly. The results indicate that, in the as-built sample, the elements were nearly uniformly distributed. The EDS line scan results of as built sample and ULT sample, corresponding to the microstructure, are presented in Figure 6. It is evident that the elemental content of Mo and V in both the α and β phases is quite prominent. After ULT, significant segregation of elements occurred, with the Mo and V contents in the β phase decreasing markedly compared to the as-built sample. Specifically, the Mo content decreased from 3.4% to 1.7%, representing a 50% reduction, while the V content decreased from 4% to 2.5%, a 37.5% reduction. The elemental compositions of the β phase are detailed in Table 2. These changes in the β phase content are closely linked to the reduction in the β-stabilizing elements Mo and V. 3.3. training_text: The characteristic features of the fracture surface of the cyclically strained AB 316L were examined using SEM to describe the underlying fatigue deterioration process of the AB structure in AM 316L. It is well established that fatigue crack initiation and propagation in a material are substantially influenced by the microstructure, grain and phase structure, and strength of the matrix [56]. However, fatigue studies of AM materials have mainly correlated the fatigue damage of metallic materials additively manufactured with internal defects, large pores, lack-of-fusion [57,58], and surface roughness [6,59,60]. Fig. 7 shows distinct regions on the fracture surface of AB 316L cyclically strained at a stress amplitude of 150 MPa. A crack initiation zone located at the surface edge of the fatigued specimen is shown in the SEM image in Fig. 7(a). Surface particles, labelled (P), adhered to the outer surface, and another partially melted particle was located directly under the surface, which is highlighted by the yellow square. A magnified view of the particles highlighted particle in (a) is shown in Fig. 7(b). Interestingly, a fatigue crack was initiated in the particles located under the surface. This was attributed to the localised strain at the defect site [61]. Another crack initiation region without defects was observed at the surface, as shown in Fig. 7(c). Crack initiation sites were arranged by identifying traces of persistent fatigue slip bands (PSB). It is well established that PSBs comprise extrusions–intrusions, that is, a tongue-like topography [62]. At a high magnification, intrusion roots and protrusions of PSBs were observed at the crack initiation site, as shown in Fig. 7(d). During the cyclic straining of FCC structural materials, such as steel 316L, these localised strain bands (PSBs) are preferentially formed from favourably oriented slip planes. Consequently, extrusions and intrusions on the specimen surface promoted a dislocation pile-up that impinged on the structural boundaries. Hence, fatigue cracks nucleate because of the local high cyclic plastic strain in PSBs [63,64]. In Fig. 7(e), crack tortuosity along the melt-pool boundary is observed, as indicated by the arrow. Simultaneously, an array of elongated layers is shown, as highlighted by the yellow oval. This is attributed to crack propagation along Fig. 7. training_text: To further understand the tensile fracture behaviour of L-PBF TA15 before and after annealing, the fracture morphology of each condition is studied, as shown in Figure 8. The fracture surface of the as-built tensile (Figure 8a) is dominated by flat cleavage surfaces, cleavage steps and tear edges, with a few small and shallow dimples, which is a typical mixed brittle–ductile fracture. Figure 8b suggests that the fracture morphology of the TA15 sample after annealing (HT1) at 630 °C is quite similar to the as-built condition, mainly composed of intergranular fracture cleavage surfaces and small dimples. These two conditions showed similar mechanical properties, such as high strength and low ductility. Figure 8c–e are L-PBF TA15 after annealing at 800 °C (HT3), 850 °C (HT4) and 900 °C (HT5), respectively. Each of them shares very similar fracture morphologies. The surface is covered with small dimples, which is a typical sign of ductile fracture. As the annealing temperature increases, the dimple radiuses increase notably. When the annealing temperature increases to 950 °C (HT6), it can be noticed in Figure 8f that some brittle fractures reappear, accompanied by large size dimples. Correspondingly, a decrease of ductility has been observed in this condition. Scale bar: 20 µm µm.

Mass finishing processes Mass finishing is an abrasive fine-finishing technology used for simultaneous processing of multiple components in a container, usually with abrasive media and a compound solution. Here, a cyclic movement of the container causes media to vibrate and rotate against workpiece surfaces, or workpieces to rub against each other. This type of finishing is often used as a final step after the AM build cycle to achieve low surface roughness and reflective surfaces (characterised by smaller standard deviation of heights, Sq). Mass finishing can be classified into 5 methods: vibratory finishing (using bowl or tub), rotary barrel finishing (tumbling), centrifugal barrel finishing, centrifugal disc finishing and drag (spindle) finishing [172]. The geometry and kinematics of the vibratory finishing are not well understood; however, Hashimoto et al. [173] modelled the material removal mechanism by deriving the relative velocity vector and the impact angle in the contact. In this respect the geometry and kinematics of the abrasive interaction could also be derived from the theory of aggressiveness [174]. Hashimoto et al. determined the characteristic specific energy curve against equivalent chip thickness h_eq [150,173], which is difficult as one also needs to estimate the depth of cut. As in other abrasive processes, the total specific energy is comprised of a chip-formation energy and the specific energy required for sliding and ploughing [173]. The dominant force in the contact occurs in a normal direction and depends on hydrostatic pressure (vibration); the cutting speed hence predominantly depends on the impact velocity of media. In a drag finishing process, a workpiece is clamped to a rotating carrier in a barrel and submerged into a mixture of abrasive media and liquid compound. Malkkora et al. [175] recently developed a model that enables a simulation of abrasive media flow, considered as a homogeneous and continuous media around a workpiece, as well as its interaction with a workpiece. The numerical modelling approach was based on the Arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian formulation, allowing calculation of process mechanics (e.g., sliding velocity, normal and shear stresses) and to correlate these fundamental parameters to surface roughness. Moreover, the authors also proposed a testing procedure, to identify the Drucker-Prager plasticity model, which has a demonstrated potential to investigate the effects of media (geometry, size, lubricant) on the rheological properties. training_text: EP can be further used to machine internal surfaces. A recent study by Zhao et al. [204] was concerned with ECM of internal holes of PBF-LB/304L stainless steel, where the electrolyte was a 10 wt% NaNO3 salt solution. The material-removal mechanisms responsible for removing semi-sintered particles/powder from the internal surface of the hole are shown in Fig. 21. The microscopy here reveals that the adhered powders and the band protrusions were dissolved simultaneously, where the most protruded surface irregularities – where the current density is localised and highest – were broken first to form half-spheres/craters and basin shapes, according to known smoothing mechanisms. In this case, the surface roughness was reduced by 55% from Sa = 14.151 μm to Sa = 6.287 μm. Further reduction of surface roughness, could be possibly achieved by optimising the EP system parameters, including the selection of the electrolyte. ECM processes are widely established and have been used in the aerospace and medical sectors for more than 30 years [194]. An early example of ECM industrial application was Rolls-Royce’s production of compressor blades for jet turbines, where ECM implementation was driven by the possibility of producing blades in smaller batch sizes and the process capability to machine complex geometry while achieving damage-free surface integrity, as the parts are not subjected to mechanical or thermal stresses. Similarly, ECM is also a long-established process in the production of artificial hip joints made of Ti and CoCr alloys. The ECM application areas are gaining a new momentum with the advent of AM, making EP a capable finishing technology for post-processing AM parts. For example, EP of PBF-LB/Ti6Al4V was able to uniformly smooth the highly scattered initial roughness values (Ra = 4–25 μm) due to different build-orientation angles down to Ra = 1–3 μm [205]. This result suggests that EP is capable of finishing parts with different (initial) levels of surface roughness, and that the amount of dissolved material is largest on the workpiece surface with the highest surface roughness (with the largest quantity of semi-sintered particles on the surface). The reported surface-thickness reduction time here was between 5 and 8 μm/min. Furthermore, 20 min of processing were required to achieve Ra<4 μm target, while removing 0.12 μm from the 0°-oriented surface and 0.28 μm from the 135°-oriented surface. This necessitates careful tolerancing of dimensional allowances for the as-built parts. Build angle also affected the achievable Rsk values. These were either positive or negative, indicating different levels of final surface isotropy (and level of the contact area). The recent wider adoption of EP for post-processing AM metal parts is further driven by the availability of the commercially available turnkey post-processing solutions, such as the trademarked “Hirtisation” technology package developed by RENA Technologies Austria. “Hirtisation” is hence not a commercial name for electropolishing, but a three-step electrochemical post-processing spanning, (a) electrochemical jet machining (hydrodynamic electrochemistry) capable of removing support structures as well as powder cake, (b) EP smoothing (e.g., levelling the surface to Ra = 2 μm), and (c) EP brightening (e.g., achieving Ra = 0.5 μm). Other machine-integrated auxiliary operations include cleaning and a vacuum-drying process. Their patented EP [206] combines a 1) steadily-increased/ramped DC current with a 2) pulsed current – in a single-anodic pulse. The process, however, is controlled by the whole (input) pulse sequence, i.e., both anodic and cathodic pulse. In general, the anodic pulses have a wide current-density range, between 0.5 and 30 A/dm². In practice, the process is voltage controlled and the voltage increase of the ramp pulse depends on the initial surface roughness. The number, amplitude and frequency of the pulsed currents that follow the ramp pulse are material dependent. Examples of EP process design are illustrated in Table 3. Scale bar: 100 µm µm.

training_text: The HIP treatment was applied to nine different samples of PBF-LBed IN939, with varying combinations of temperature (1270 °C, 1280 °C, 1290 °C), pressure (100, 125, 150MPa), and holding time (80, 160, 240min), according to the DOE setup. Analyzing the HIPped samples collectively, a clear trend emerges regarding the influence of temperature, pressure, and holding time. Figure 9 shows the microstructure of all 9 HIPped samples with highest temperature at the top and lowest to the bottom, as indicated in each picture label. Treatments at 1290 °C consistently produced the best results in terms of porosity closure and recrystallization. However, the effectiveness was modulated by pressure and time: higher pressure (150MPa) and longer duration (240min) synergistically enhanced the homogenization process. At this temperature, pores volume fraction ranges between 0.023 and 0.032%, lower than in the as-built condition. On the other hand, grain size (105, 72 and 88 μm, respectively) changes as a function of pressure and soaking time i.e. 150 MPa – 240 min, 125 MPa – 160 min and 100 MPa – 80 min, ca. 50-55% larger than those obtained at atmospheric pressure. In contrast, samples treated at 1270 °C showed comparable level of porosity (ca. 0.025-0.042%) but, the PBF-LB-induced columnar grain structure was not fully modified. These results indicate that 1270 °C is insufficient to trigger significant recrystallization in PBF-LBed IN939 under the conditions tested. Moreover, grain size was not altered significantly, ranging between 34 and 35 μm for 100 MPa – 160 min and 150 MPa – 80 min, while when no pressure was applied grains were able to coarsen up to 127 μm. Conversely, when lower pressure is applied together with long soaking times, i.e. 125 MPa – 240 min, a considerable larger grain size is obtained i.e. 134 μm. This means that at lower temperatures, other HIP parameters become more impacting in triggering material recrystallization. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

paper_id: Li et al. 2024 - Effect of Heat Treatment on Fatigue Performance of 316L Stainless Steel Fabricated by Laser Powder Bed Fusion
training_text: Crack initiation at the boundary of the molten pool: (a) fracture diagram of the initiation area of the 450 °C AT sample, (b) molten pool morphology diagram of the 450 °C AT sample (black and white colors represent different grains), (c) substructures with different orientations at the molten pool boundary, and (d) load-depth curve of molten pool boundary and molten pool interior (Fig. 9(b)), regardless of their morphology or size (203.1 μm and 192.2 μm; 38.4 μm and 44.3 μm), are very similar, so it is believed that the low strength of the molten pool boundary is the cause of crack initiation. In Fig. 9(c), the dashed line represents the boundary of the molten pool, with the interior of the molten pool on both sides. It can be seen that the substructure orientations on both sides of some molten pool boundaries are different. In dynamic deformation, the resistance to deformation on both sides of the molten pool is different, resulting in inconsistent deformation. By measuring the deformation capacity of the molten pool boundary and the inside of the molten pool through nanoindentation samples, Fig. 9(d) shows the load-displacement curve. It can be seen that the mechanical properties of the interior and boundary are different. The average ultimate compressive strength of the molten pool boundary is 2.78 GPa, which is 10% lower than the 3.05 GPa inside the molten pool, so the mechanical properties of the molten pool boundary are lower. The inconsistent deformation capacity on both sides of the molten pool leads to the formation of micropores and microcracks. Adjacent micropores grow and merge to form microcracks. When the crack extends to the boundary of the sample (Fig. 6(b)) or reaches a certain extent (Fig. 6(e)), the initiation area tears, and the initiation stage ends and the growth stage begins. In addition, the grain boundary is also a low-strength area. When the grain boundary overlaps with the molten pool, the strength of this area will be further reduced. As shown in Fig. 9(b), there are multiple overlapping areas of grain boundary and molten pool boundary, and the overlapping areas are very likely to become microcracks. The width of the molten pool is positively correlated with the strength of the molten pool, so different spot diameters, scanning spacing, and scanning strategies can be used to control the width of the molten pool, thereby increasing the strength of the molten pool and extending the initiation life. Scale bar: 50 µm µm.

training_text: A synergistic balance between strength and ductility for both regions is desired in HT3, where CoCrMo experiences solution heat treatment and extended aging at the expense of some grain coarsening in the maraging steel region. The microstructure in Figure 10 shows a continuous interface in HT3, avoiding the inconsistent lath formation in HT2 and the prominent lath growth in HT1. The maraging steel region in Figure 10(b) and (d) lost cellular features and traces of epitaxial growth since the initial heat treatment stages induced extensive homogenisation. Considering that the ε-phase transition and precipitate dissolution temperatures for CoCrMo were found at ~970°C and ~1140°C, respectively [45], all treatment combinations effectively removed the melt tracks within the maraging steel region. The focus of HT3, however, is on altering the ε-phase transformation mechanism in CoCrMo. Regions highlighted in red in Figure 10(c) showcase consistent, parallel ε-phase bands that are constrained within grains and previous melt pool boundaries. Unlike the dense striations in HT2, these bands mostly terminated at grain boundaries and displayed no overlap. The added solution treatment step preserves the previous γ grain boundaries in the succeeding γ-ε transformation. The presence of some equiaxed regions that include grains free of striations and containing sharp edges can also be observed. Figure 10(e) displays coarse precipitates that are exclusively formed in grain boundaries, which are identified as carbide precipitates through EDS. Unlike HT2, the matrix now contains round and elongated precipitates aligned in a parallel manner. These precipitates trace the observed ε-hcp bands, implying that rearrangement occurred after a longer aging time. The EBSD analysis of the HT3 specimen presented in Figure 11 also revealed a sophisticated multi-phase interface which reflects the targeted phase transformation in both alloys. In the maraging steel region, the two-stage solution HT led to the formation of martensite blocks that are continuous and randomly oriented, with block widths averaging 2.7 ± 0.6 μm. The melt pool morphology and refined microstructure in the as-built samples disappeared. The redistribution of interface alloying elements also formed residual austenite islands scattered along bcc boundaries, shown in Material: Fe Co Cr Ni Mo Ti Mn Si C Maraging Balance 9. In contrast to the STAed specimens, the low microhardness of the as-printed specimen is due to the lath martensitic microstructure without any strengthening precipitates (Ref 22). This is due to the fact that the particular aging temperature and exposure time influence the precipitation kinetics. A longer aging duration causes coarsening of precipitates; as a consequence, a lower microhardness value is obtained. Moreover, the particular aging temperature and associated holding duration decide the formation of reverted austenite within the alloy. The trace of reversed austenite within the over-aged maraging steels was reported in the literature (Ref 13, 39). Similar observation is made through XRD analysis in the present study (Fig. 14). The austenite, being a soft and ductile phase, reduces the strength of the alloy. Therefore, with increase in the aging duration, the transformation of martensite-to-austenite (austenite reversal) is surely increased, which causes a decline in the microhardness value. However, reverted austenite is considered to be a desired phase constituent because by controlling the proportion of reverted austenite, the required combination of the ductility and toughness can be achieved (Ref 35). Past researchers extensively studied the phenomenon of austenite reversion, and they reported that alteration in the tensile strength and ductility in maraging steels is greatly influenced by the precipitation of nano-scaled particulates (Ref 7). On the contrary, some other research groups concluded that reversed austenite plays an important role for improving mechanical properties, especially, elongation at break through the Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) effect. As reported by Ooi et al. (Ref 30), the beneficial role of reverted austenite is mainly to increase work hardening during the tensile tests. training_text: To understand the mechanism of microstructural development during the L-PBF of the current materials, single track laser melting of powder particles was conducted on the top surfaces (with a powder layer upon them) of some bulk L-PBF-processed samples using different laser exposure durations. Figure 10 shows the microstructures of some cross-sections of the solidified tracks. These sections actually correspond to longitudinal sections of solidified melt pools and thus are very useful for understanding the microstructural evolution during L-PBF. It is clear that for the L-PBF-processed Ti1023, the single solidified melt pool was fully dominated by several large columnar grains which grew epitaxially from a previous layer, whereas for the L-PBF-processed Ti1023 + 7 wt.% ZrN, the solidified melt pools tended to show columnar grains in the lower regions but fine equiaxed grains in the upper regions. Obviously, columnar grains seem quite liable to be developed at the interlayer interfaces due to epitaxial grain growth. Moreover, it is noted that a number of particles accumulated in the upper regions of the solidified melt pools of the L-PBF-processed Ti1023 + 7 wt.% ZrN sample (see Figure 10b–d). These particles, according to the point EDX analysis (Figure 10e,f), were enriched in Zr and N, and the chemical compositions of some particles in the as-fabricated Ti1023 + 7 wt.% ZrN alloy are listed in Table 6 according to the EDX results, suggesting that they could be unmelted ZrN particles. Table 6. Chemical composition (at. %) of the particle shown in Figure 10e obtained using SEM-EDX analysis. Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

It is apparent that many secondary cracks appear on the side surface of the HC specimen, compared with the HU specimen. The number of cracks decreased gradually and the average length and depth increased significantly with increased hydrogen charging time. In order to clarify the correlation between microstructures and initiation and propagation of cracking in the presence of hydrogen, the microstructure features of the side surface of HU and HC-168 h specimens were characterized and given in Fig. 9. Comparing Fig. 9a, b, it is easy to find that the deformation degree of dendrite near the HU specimen's outer surface is significantly higher than that HC-168 h specimen. In addition, the fragmentation of Laves phase in the interdendritic area was observed, while MC carbides showed no signs of fracture. Laves phase may promote the formation of cracking during SSRT. It is noteworthy that microscopic voids form between the γ-matrix and Laves phase of the HU specimen and these voids could be expanded into cracks in the presence of H (Fig. 10). Figure 9c shows all cracks propagate along γ-matrix/Laves phase interfaces and are connected through the γ-matrix to form the large crack. Slip bands were also observed around the crack tip, as shown in Fig. 9d, which could be attributed to the intensive dislocation movement. 4 Discussions In this study, the HE behavior of the WAAM Inconel 625 has been investigated. It is interesting that WAAM Inconel 625 specimens nearly have a little necking deformation during SSRT in the presence of hydrogen, but they still have a high strain value compared with HU specimen. Hydrogen charges the fracture of WAAM Inconel 625 from ductile microvoid coalescence to brittle fracture dominated by quasi-cleavage. The initiation and propagation of hydrogen-assisted cracking are closely related to the Laves phase. Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

training_text: demonstrates the microstructures of the transverse cross section of the as-deposited IN718 sample. Staggered individual deposit layers can be observed from the low-magnification microscopy picture (Figure 5(a)). The deposition layers are delineated by bands of thin remelted nucleation zones formed at the layer interface. Extensively grown dendritic grains across a number of deposit layers (several millimeters) can also be seen occasionally. A high-magnification SEM picture in Figure 5(b) shows the detailed microstructure of the as-deposited material, where fine secondary dendrites are formed within a grain with an averaged dendrite arm spacing around 5 μm. In contrast to the dark austenite matrix, small white particles in globular and irregular shapes that have precipitated along the interdendritic boundaries can be seen. They are identified as the Laves phase and some minor MC and TiN phases that are segregated during the fast solidification process. Figure 6 shows the EDAX analysis on the major phases appearing in the as-deposited microstructure. Comparing Figures 6(b) and (c), one can observe that the matrix of the dendrite’s core area is rich in Fe, Cr, and Ni, while the white segregation particles are rich in Nb, Mo, and Ti, which are the major compositional elements of the Laves phase. Figure 7 shows the microstructure that went through a direct age heat treatment. Compared to the as-deposited microstructure, the direct-age treatment did not change the size of the dendrites and the morphology of interdendritic Laves phase. training_text: The microstructure of laser-deposited IN718 alloy exhibited various grain morphologies and size distributions. This was obviously caused by the dynamic heat transfer of the moving heat source and layered material formation mechanism. During laser deposition, material is built up layer by layer. When depositing a new layer of material, a thin top portion of the previous layer is remelted. As the molten pool solidifies, a thin nucleation zone at the layer interface is formed. As a result, layer boundaries consisting of fine grains can be observed, clearly delineating the deposit layers in the cross-sectional microstructure (Figure 5(a)). These layer interface regions are usually associated with sharp changes in grain size and degree of microsegregations; therefore, they can be the weak sites of tensile stress. Figure 16 compares the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)–generated grain/twin boundary overlay maps on the standard STA and homogenized STA microstructures, where the differences of grain morphologies and size distributions from the two heat treatments can be clearly seen. The layer interface regions can still be identified in the STA-treated material as bands of agglomerated fine grains (Figure 16(a)). This feature of layer boundaries disappeared in the homogenized microstructure, where the grains have been recrystallized and have a more isotropic appearance (Figure 16(b)). Figure 17 shows the microstructures of STA-treated material. It can be observed that bands of segregation-depleted regions are formed and also delineate the staggered deposition layers. It is also noticed that the edges of the deposit sample consist of relatively larger size grains (left areas in Figure 16(a)). This is a result of 30 pct higher energy input (high laser power and slower speed) used on the periphery contour of the rectangular sample in order to maintain good geometric accuracy. This portion of material was mostly removed during the preparation of tensile specimens; however, if the final specimen contained this microstructure, it may have contributed to deviations of the tensile properties. paper_id: Afkhami et al. 2022 - Effects of manufacturing parameters, heat treatmen ... 13Cr10Ni1·7Mo2Al0·4Mn0·4Si steel processed by laser powder bed fusion
training_text: Fresh gas-atomized CX stainless steel powder from EOS GmbH was used as the raw material in this study. The chemical composition of the powder is presented in Table 1. The specimens were manufactured using an EOS M 290 machine, equipped with a 400 W Yb-Fiber laser, under optimized parameters provided by the manufacturer. These parameters were also used in some previous studies on CX using the same AM machine to achieve fully dense parts [1,3–5,12,15–17]. The samples were manufactured along both the horizontal and vertical orientations to investigate the effects of the building direction (BD). Consequently, the BD and loading axis (LA) in mechanical tests were normal in the horizontal and parallel in the vertical samples. Further detail on the geometry and dimensions of the specimens are available in Supplementary Fig. 1 and Fig. 2.1 Once manufactured, horizontal and vertical specimens were subdivided into two groups based on their post-processing: as-built (without post-processing) and heat-treated. Subsequently, heat-treated specimens were post-processed following this procedure: solution annealing at 850 °C for 30 min, then air cooling to room temperature (20 °C) and aging for 120 min at 525 °C, and, again, air cooling to room temperature (Supplementary Fig. 3). In other studies, as examples, the solution annealing was performed for 60 min at 1000 °C and 900 °C in Refs. [10, 14], respectively. Furthermore, the aging step lasted for 180 min at 530 °C in [14]. However, the heat treatment used in this study was optimized following the instruction provided by the powder manufacturer [16]. The heat treatment was planned to reach the best material performance in a shorter time and by consuming less energy than the treatments used in the preceding investigations available in the literature. Consequently, the duration of the solution annealing and aging treatments were shortened at least 50% and 30%, respectively, compared to the procedures used in, e.g. Refs. [2,5,10], and [14]. The heat treatment was carried out in a sealed furnace under the pure argon atmosphere to avoid any unwanted reaction in the material. In addition, one horizontal and one vertical sample were subjected to dilatometry with a Gleeble 3500 thermomechanical simulator to investigate the phase transformations triggered by the heat treatment. Scale bar: 10.0 µm µm.

training_text: FESEM micrographs of sample before (a) and after annealing at b 910, c 960, and d 990°C Figure 7 presents the XRD patterns of as-built samples before and after annealing at 960°C and 990°C. The XRD patterns of the as-built samples reveal Bragg reflections corresponding to the Ti-hcp planes. Notably, no evidence of β-phase nanoprecipitates is observed in the XRD patterns of as-built samples. The absence of detectable β-phase peaks might be attributed to the nanoprecipitates' small size, which causes significant peak broadening and reduced intensity, making them undetectable by conventional XRD techniques. After annealing at 960°C and 990°C, reflections corresponding to the α, β, and α′ phases become evident. The formation of the β-phase after annealing can be explained by the diffusion of vanadium atoms from the α′-phase, which facilitates the nucleation of the α-phase along the α′-boundaries and the subsequent precipitation of the β-phase. The Bragg reflections in the as-built samples exhibit broader peaks compared to those in the annealed samples. This peak broadening can result from several factors, including instrumental effects, small crystallite sizes, and the presence of significant lattice strain in polycrystalline materials [26]. In the case of as-built samples, the broadening is primarily attributed to high levels of residual stresses and strains inherent to SLM-fabricated parts, caused by the steep thermal gradients and rapid cooling rates during SLM processing. Upon annealing, these residual stresses and strains are relieved, leading to a reduction in the peak integral breadths, as demonstrated in Fig. 2. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

training_text: Solidification cracking forms in the mushy zone of molten pool, where solid dendrite grows into the molten material and inhibits the liquid flow at the inter-dendrite. The remaining liquid is the cracking initial site when the residual stress or solidification shrinkage tear up the liquid region. Solidification cracking thus creates an opening dendrite structure to the cracking surface. Solidification cracking could be observed in any kind of fusion-based AM superalloy, especially the non-weldable Nickel-based superalloys. The susceptibility of Nickel-based superalloys to solidification crack is closely related to the segregation and formation of dendrites within the material. Fig. 20 presents the typical morphologies of solidification cracking in AM processed CM247LC [221]. Hot tearing occurs when fast cooling induces the formation of a large thermal gradient that results in uneven thermal contraction along solid–liquid interface [222]. Although the semi-solid material during solidification can accommodate this thermal strain via plastic deformation, creep, and filling of porosities, the lack of sufficient time due to fast solidification rate during AM fabrication will inhibit this thermal strain accommodation and hence lead to crack propagation along the inter-dendritic structure. Since hot tearing mainly occurs when solid and liquid phases coexist, alloys that present a high tendency for micro-segregation (e.g., Nickel-based Mar-M–247 alloy) are more susceptible to hot tearing. If the materials fail to inhibit the crack propagation through the deposited layers, more severe delamination would occur. Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

training_text: Representative fracture surface after tensile tests within different regions is shown in Fig. 12. The fractography of all samples is dominated by transgranular fracture, which is the typical feature of ductility. The fracture surface comprises typical dimples of different sizes spread throughout. training_text: Porosity is one of the major concerns with WAAM since it may significantly reduce the density of the components produced and degrade their mechanical properties. Slight, uniformly dispersed hydrogen holes with a diameter of up to 100 μm and large, unevenly distributed process pores are the two basic types of pores that can be distinguished [99]. Fig. 7 shows the presence of a typical porosity defect in IN718. The type of arc welding method, process variables, inter-pass temperature, composition and quality of the wire alloy and shielding gases, and others all contribute to porosity [100]. Larger pores may emerge in the generated part due to increased process arc instability and rate of energy input. The two concurrent mechanisms volumetric shrinkage, changed solubility, and accompanying hydrogen precipitation during solidification are what create gas porosity [101]. Pore defects generally are classified as raw material-induced & process-induced [102]. The main sources of hydrogen that are easily evaporated in the arc and then transformed into atomic hydrogen include hydrocarbon impurities, grease, and moisture on the wire surface. The molten pool that is trapped after solidification is then filled with it [103]. Gas pores having spherical geometry can be formed by hydrogen rejection, while large and irregular or flat pore shapes are generated by a lack of fusion in the weld zone [104]. The appearance, volume, and distribution of the porosity were significantly influenced by the feedstock wire’s quality and batch-to-batch irregularity [105]. High gas flow and high solidification rates in the weld pool may cause the pore concentrations in the metal alloys formed to increase. Porosity is the result of pre-occurrence flaws in the wires, such as impurities, supersaturated hydrogen, composition segregation, etc. being carried into the molten pool as well [106]. Pores significantly undermine the overall mechanical properties, substantially diminishing the ductility & strength of manufactured components [108]. Pores may eventually become the main source of stress concentration in the component, leading to the initiation, propagation, and eventual failure of fractures during production or even during part operation [109]. Because of the microcrack damage caused by porosity, a component has poor mechanical strength and frequently has inadequate fatigue properties [101]. According to Kinderman et al. [110], strain localization during tensile testing was induced by solidification flaws like porosity and hot cracking. Moreover, the ultimate tensile strength was decreased. When Rajput et al. [111] analyzed the impact of deposition techniques in the WAAM of IN 625, they found that in every mode of analysis, the macroscopic examination revealed an absence of cracks, porosity, and any other forms of defects. Three types of \( \alpha \) are formed based on the cooling level and solute capacity during the cooling process after passing through the \( \beta \) phase. The high cooling rate causes typically martensite phase alteration (\( \alpha' \)), medium cooling level causes the limited distance diffused alteration (massive conversion) and low cooling rate causes long distance diffused (\( \alpha \)) phase transformation. Various morphological features are therefore seen according to the cooling rate. Lathlike martensite and massive martensite \( \alpha' \) structures are attained when the cooling rate is over 500 °C/s (see Fig. 5) as mentioned above. The microstructure of cp-Ti is predominantly plate-like \( \alpha \) and acicular \( \alpha \) in cp-Ti if the cooling rate is below 90 °C/s, also, it is fine-wavy acicular and basket-weave \( \alpha \) from 90 °C/s to 500 °C/s [12,69–72]. The iron content is also highly effective in cp-Ti phase transformation as well as the cooling rate. Iron contributes to massive alterations along with quick cooling. Moreover, adding iron delays the long-distance diffusional alteration at low cooling temperatures. The surface topography of \( \alpha \) alloys forms dispersed \( \beta \) phase recrystallized \( \alpha \) grains that presents each cp-Ti grade content has a certain amount of iron, which is a strong \( \beta \) stabilizer. As shown in Fig. 7, the results demonstrate a clear dependency of the Young’s modulus on both the material processing route and the loading direction applied. The highest stiffness is observed near 45° and 225°, whereas the lowest modulus values are recorded around 150° and 330°. This unexpected anisotropic behaviour in the wrought material, while more pronounced than in the LPBF-printed samples, may arise due to loading-path sensitivity or microscale heterogeneities introduced during manufacturing processes, which become evident under multiaxial loading. Additionally, Fig. 7 shows that the XY- and ZX-oriented specimens exhibit a similar trend of variation of the effective Young’s modulus as observed in the wrought specimen. An opposite trend was observed in the Z-oriented specimen. The XY- and ZX-oriented specimens maintain a relatively high Young’s modulus (186–191 GPa) in the axial loading directions; however, they show a reduction near 120° and 300°. This behaviour suggests that the XY- and ZX-oriented specimens retain significant stiffness in the loading paths dominated by axial tension and compression but exhibit reductions in the effective stiffness under shear-dominated conditions. The Z-oriented specimens display a relatively low fluctuation, being within the range from 181 to 191 GPa. The stronger modulus variation suggests that the mechanical response in the LPBF-printed SS316L is more sensitive to the underlying grain orientation, defect distribution, and residual stress accumulation, which may result from the repeated laser scanning and subsequent cooling cycles. training_text: In this investigation, two types of microstructures were observed on the cross-section samples depending on the L-PBF process parameters utilised, which for simplicity have been represented by the calculated VED during processing. One type represents where the VED used produced an interface zone (interlayer) between the NiTi alloy and 316L parts. In the other type, the VED did not lead to the presence of an interface zone in the microstructure. Samples, where the VED were below 50 J/mm³ resulted in the absence of an interface layer, whereas samples processed with ≥ 50 J/mm³ resulted in the interface zone. This behaviour was observed to be independent of the phase(s) of the sample and layer thickness during printing. In general, above the interface zone, the microstructure of the NiTi was a complex one. For example, Fig. 5 compares the microstructures of two samples. The phases of the samples in Fig. 5 (a) & (b) were martensite and austenite, respectively. The presence of needle-like and plate microstructure; indicative of the martensite phase of NiTi, was predominantly present. These martensitic structures were a combination of fine and coarse needle-like and plate microstructures and have been observed previously by several researchers [46,47]. It could be observed in Fig. 5 (c) that the fine structures were predominantly found at the region close to the interface layer. Coarse structures were observed as one moved away from the interface region. It has been reported that during L-PBF processing of NiTi with similar chemical composition, the melt pool temperature was higher at the first layer (that is, the region closest to the 316L build plate) when compared to the top layer of the build [23]. It was further reported that these differences in temperature across the layers, resulted in obtaining fine martensitic microstructures at higher melt pool temperature zone, and coarse martensitic microstructures at low temperature level zone in their samples [23]. As such, it could be assumed that the zones close to the interfaces as well as the interface zone in the samples used in this investigation would be at a higher temperature compared to the rest. This would explain the presence of fine martensitic microstructures close to the interface zone (Fig. 5 (c)). In order to confirm the phases present at the different zones of the samples, EBSD analysis results is presented in the next subsection. 3.4. Such a microstructure in WAAM process is attributed to a more stable and consistent thermal mechanism due to faster cooling with the substrate during the initial deposited layers. Moreover, very small voids can also be seen along the building direction with varying proportions; representing slightly lower concentration at the bottom compared to the middle and top regions of the wall. Presence of such pores are likely due to continuous deposition in multi-layer structures where contaminations after previously deposited layers are trapped within the melt-pool, potentially leading to such defects [57]. In addition, pores are considered as material-induced or process-induced. Material-induced pores are produced due to contamination of wire or substrate with moisture, grease and certain hydrocarbon compounds that are hard to extract completely, while process-induced pores occur due to poor path planning or unstable deposition and are usually non-spherical [58]. The observed pores across the wall appear to be non-spherical. However, the pore sizes are very small, typically less than 3 microns. Moving to the middle section of the wall, shown in Fig. 15b, the microstructure changes, exhibiting elongated grains. A magnified segment, represented with “B” in the middle part, is shown in Fig. 15e, further detailing the corresponding microstructure. The dark region probably resulted from over etching during the sample preparation. The presence of small porosity is also evident in the middle. Furthermore, an SEM image of the top section is shown in Fig. 15c. A more detailed and magnified segment from the top section is also represented in Fig. 15f. These images present a heterogeneous and coarser morphology compared to the middle and bottom regions. Particularly, equiaxed and elongated grains are dominant, and an evident increase of size is observed in some grains. Such a variation of microstructure is likely due to slower cooling, causing a reduced thermal gradient at the top section of the wall. Scale bar: 10 µm µm.

training_text: Differences in distortion or deflection response can be loosely correlated with different microstructural features in each alloy. For example, Inconel® 625 does not undergo any solid-state transformations after solidification. As a result, it displays a columnar dendritic microstructure with secondary phases, such as laves phases and carbides, forming in the inter-dendritic regions where solutes can segregate.[10,21,22] Figure 1 shows common microstructural features of Inconel® 625 produced using a laser-based DED process.[15] Primary dendrites, secondary dendrites, and secondary phases are labeled. The cooling rate during solidification often dictates the manner in which these dendrites form. Slower cooling rates allow for secondary dendrite arms to form, while higher cooling rates produce microstructures with only primary dendrites.[10] The secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) can be used to provide a measure of the cooling rates during solidification, with a decrease in spacing corresponding to an increase in cooling rate.[23] Ti-6Al-4V, on the other hand, undergoes an allotropic phase transformation from a BCC phase at high temperatures to an HCP phase during cooling, resulting in a two-phase microstructure.[24] Beta grains form immediately after solidification begins and orient themselves along the steepest thermal gradient.[11,25] As the temperature decreases further, the beta phase undergoes a solid-state phase transformation to the alpha phase, but evidence of the size and shape of these beta grains remains. In DED, the final microstructure is typically colony or basketweave alpha grains, depending on processing parameters.[11,24,25] Figure 2 shows common microstructural features of Ti-6Al-4V produced using a laser-based DED process.[15] Prior beta grains and alpha lath structures are labeled. The structure is partially dependent on the solid-state cooling rates which dictate the formation of grain boundary alpha and the width of the alpha lamellae.[5,26] A higher cooling rate with short times spent in the beta range favors the formation of basketweave alpha, while a lower cooling rate over the beta phase field favors the formation of alpha lath colonies.[11] Scale bar: 20 µm µm.

training_text: To further verify the results of XRD observation, the corresponding SEM images were taken. The results are presented in Fig. 6 and Fig. 7. It is observed that the specimens fabricated with and without in-situ heat treatment all show two phases: the light gray (NiTi) and the dark gray (Ti2Ni) phases. The detailed phase composition analysis is performed using EDS and plotted in Fig. 8(a). The atomic ratio of Ni to Ti is close to 1:2 in dark gray phases and close to 1:1 in light gray phases, representing the Ti2Ni and NiTi phases, respectively. Similar results were reported in our previous research [53] and by other researchers [54, 55]. The corresponding volume fractions of the Ti2Ni phase in the cross-section of as-deposited specimens are counted using ImageJ and presented in Fig. 8(b). For samples fabricated without in-situ heat treatment, when the scan speed is constant, the volume fraction of the Ti2Ni phase decreases with the increase in laser power. The higher power energy is beneficial to improve the uniformity of chemical composition in the molten pool, suppressing Ti2Ni phase precipitation. When the laser power is constant, the volume fraction of the Ti2Ni phase increases along with the increase in scan speed. This phenomenon is ascribed to the suppressed fluid convection in the molten pool. The higher scan speed accelerates the molten pool solidification. The local composition unevenness then cannot be effectively eliminated through mixing, resulting in more Ti2Ni precipitation in the structure. For the samples fabricated with in-situ heat treatment, a similar trend is also observed when the laser power is constant. However, the volume fraction of the Ti2Ni phase decreases with the laser power when the scan speed is constant at 2 mm/s but increases with the laser power when the scan speed is constant at 4 mm/s. This observation may be related to the total energy input in the deposition process. Due to the largest laser power input and the largest number of deposition layers, sample #8 has the maximum total energy input in the whole fabrication process. Its equilibrium temperature is closest to the precipitation temperature range (300°C~700°C) and the holding time is the longest, which provides more time for the precipitation of the Ti2Ni phase. Therefore, the volume fraction in sample #8 has a certain degree of increase relative to sample #7. Fig. 6. Phase composition of as-deposited sample: a (#1), b (#5), c (#2), d (#6); (a, c) without in-situ heat treatment, (b, d) with in-situ heat treatment. Scale bar: 5 µm µm.

The abundance of the granular carbide phase in the GB of alloy C compared to alloy B is related to the higher content of carbide forming elements in the former alloy. The high level of alloying in C increased its hardenability and therefore suppressed the formation of ferrite and pearlite during cooling. Figure 2. As-received microstructures of alloys A, B and C. This ploughing action develops the appearance of fine-grooved and aligned scratch marks on the surface of the wear pin [48–51]. SEM images of both walls display these abrasive wear marks in the direction of the wear track. With the increase in load, delamination emerges as the dominant wear mechanism in the wall, surpassing abrasion which occurs as a consequence of dislocation pile-up, leading to the formation of voids and subsequent cracks. Thereby here also, even with a constant sliding distance of 2000 m for all values of loads, delamination becomes visible over the worn surface upon increasing the load. Furthermore, on higher load, the frictional action between the pin and disk results in a temperature rise producing large heat. This heat softens the material of the pin and further increases the chances of delamination wear [48,50,52]. Adhesive wear marks its presence on increasing the load from 30 N to 40 N as at a higher, load more surface contact takes place between pin and disc. Because of the occurrence of adhesive wear among the pin and disc, wear debris detached from the interface surface and subsequently shattered into smaller fragments due to the rubbing of opposing surfaces. Figure 14 reveals that the WAAM wall displays this mechanism at both lower (30 N) and higher (40 N) load values. On the contrary, the WAAM+FSP wall displays this mechanism only at the higher load (40 N). This can be explained by the formation of smaller grains in the FSP-treated wall due to the microstructure refinement. This refinement occurs in the stirred zone as the alloy undergoes stringent plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization. This finer grain size results in increased hardness, a phenomenon consistent with the Hall–Petch effect [13,40,51,52]. The higher hardness in FSP treated leads to enhanced wear resistance. Additionally, the high-intensity presence of Mg2Si and Mg in the WAAM+FSP wall further contributes to its high hardness compared to WAAM wall. It is also true from the SEM image that more debris and plough of different shapes and sizes have been formed in the WAAM specimen compared to FSP-treated specimen due to the continuous relative motion between the pin and disc. This grain refinement, specifically in techniques like FSP, is enabled by different mechanisms like Discontinuous Dynamic Recrystallization (DDRX), dynamic recovery (DRV), Continuous Dynamic Recrystallization, and particle-stimulated nucleation (PSN). Each contributes to the formation of finer grains, which mainly happens during plastic deformation. Continuous Dynamic Recrystallization (CDRX) involves the formation of new grains without nucleation as subgrains develop into grains with high-angle boundaries, while in DDRX, new grains form through nucleation and growth mechanisms, typically at high temperatures and large strains. As in DRV, the material experiences a rearrangement of dislocations into lower energy configurations, which results in the reduction of internal stress without forming new grains. Secondary particles or inclusions in the material promote the nucleation of new grains during the recrystallization process, enhancing its performance during the PSN mechanism [16,17]. These mechanisms combine to form finer grains during FSP and aid in improved mechanical properties. Peng et al. [16], Liu et al. [19], and Zhang et al. These stresses result in partial accommodation by some grains, leading to local orientation changes and the formation of LAGBs. The GB diagrams show that a large number of LAGBs are distributed at the boundary of the molten pool, with LAGBs accounting for 66% in LPBF 316L. As shown in Figure 3(a-c), the proportion of LAGBs decreases with increasing annealing temperature, dropping to 59.4% after annealing at 1200 °C. Kernel average misorientation (KAM) diagrams in Figure 2(e-h) illustrate the evolution of strain within the microstructure. The KAM value in Figure 3(d, e) reflects the orientation difference between adjacent points within the grain. Higher KAM values typically indicate more local misorientation within the grain, caused by dislocations. Therefore, higher KAM values are generally associated with higher dislocation density, while lower KAM values imply less dislocation density. The KAM value at the molten pool boundary is relatively high because the molten pool boundary is enriched with many LAGBs and dense dislocations. By comparing the average values of samples, it can be seen that the KAM values gradually decrease with the increasing temperature, indicating a reduction in dislocation density. Figure 2(g-i) depict different microstructural distributions, with blue indicating recrystallized (R) grains, yellow representing substructured (S), and red for deformed (D) grains. As shown in Figure 3(f), recrystallized structures are rare after annealing at different temperatures, but substructures increase, and deformed structures significantly decrease after annealing at 1200 °C.
